2.s:
Robert Lee Bell Jr. was born in 1961 in Birmingham, Alabama, the first son of Robert Lee Bell Sr. and Willie Joyce Stephens. The Birmingham News printed his birth that week under the names “Mr. and Mrs. Robert Lee Bell (Willie Joyce Stephens).” His father was four years into a nine-year enlistment in the Air Force, so his first years were lived around postings — his younger brother was born at Fort Worth, Texas, in 1964 — and the earliest photograph of him is from the weeks after his birth, in the arms of his grandmother Margaret Beatrice Eaken.

His parents separated when he was about eleven. His mother married again in 1980 and died in 1982, at forty, when he was barely twenty-one. A school portrait survives from the late 1970s.

A photograph from the late 1980s catches him in a suit at a pharmacy career fair, at the booth of SuperX, the Cincinnati drugstore chain — by then he had made his life in Cincinnati.

He and Cynthia Katharine Tuttle, a registered pharmacist, married in Hamilton County, Ohio, in 1992. Their son Alexander was born in Cincinnati in 1997. A photograph from a spring afternoon about 2000 or 2001 shows him in a yard with his own father, his wife and his two sons — three generations of Bells together, not long before his father died. He has since retired, and lives in Palm Springs, California.

3.s:
Cynthia Katharine Tuttle was born in 1959 in Evanston, Illinois, the daughter of Richard Clark Tuttle and Judith Katharine Frost. Her parents had met at Evanston, where her mother took a degree at Northwestern, and when they were expecting her they bought a house in Deerfield, a northern suburb of Chicago. She was the first of four children, and to her family she has always been Cindy.

In 1971, when she was eleven, the family moved to Cincinnati: her father had taken a job with H. S. Crocker, a label printer, after his Chicago firm closed. She grew up there, in the Indian Hill schools where her mother taught and painted portraits, and she graduated from Indian Hill High School with the class of 1977, a member of the National Honor Society. Her grandmother Velma Roush Frost had died when she was not yet five, and she kept what the family remembered of her.

She trained as a pharmacist, and has spent her working life as a registered pharmacist licensed by the Ohio Board of Pharmacy in Cincinnati.

In 1992, at thirty-two, she married Robert Lee Bell Jr. in Hamilton County, Ohio. Their son Alexander was born in Cincinnati in 1997. She lives in Cincinnati still, and is retired.

4.s:
Robert Lee Bell Sr. was born on 5 November 1935, the fourth child of John Henry Bell, a house painter, and Margaret Beatrice Eaken. He may never have been certain himself which city he was born in: his family was moving between Birmingham and Atlanta in that very year, and his own papers say both. Atlanta is what his obituary gave, and Georgia is what the family said about where they had been living when he was small.

His father walked out about 1942, when he was six, and never came back. The family went north to Wheaton, Illinois, where in January 1944 his eldest brother Thomas was killed in a car crash at sixteen. The death notice in the Birmingham papers listed him among the brothers left behind as “Bobby, 8.”

He joined the United States Air Force on 12 February 1953, three months past his seventeenth birthday and young enough to need a parent’s consent, while the Korean War was still being fought, and served until 17 July 1956, leaving as an Airman Third Class. Seven months later, on 4 February 1957, he enlisted in the Army, and he stayed nine more years, to 14 February 1966, rising to staff sergeant. Thirteen of the twenty years between seventeen and thirty were spent in uniform, and his marker names both branches and both wars, Korea and Vietnam. None of it was handed down in the family; not one word of any of it survives in the family’s own papers.

He married Willie Joyce Stephens on 26 August 1960, when he was a private first class stationed at Fort Benning, Georgia, three and a half years into his Army enlistment. The marriage was recorded at Fort Payne, in DeKalb County, though the Birmingham News reported the wedding in Birmingham; its six-line notice called him “Pfc. Robert Bell, son of Mrs. Claude B. Smith of Fitzgerald, Ga.,” for his mother and stepfather had moved to Georgia by then, and it ran her picture beside it. Their first son was born at Birmingham in 1961, announced in the Birmingham News as a son to “Mr. and Mrs. Robert Lee Bell (Willie Joyce Stephens)”; the second came at Fort Worth, Texas, in 1964, while he was still in the Army, which is probably how an Alabama family came to be in Texas at all. So the first six years of that marriage were Army years, lived at postings. It ended about 1972–73, and he married again afterwards. By January 1983 he was living at Mobile, Alabama, one of his mother’s four surviving children.

The later years were not quiet ones. On 20 November 1989 police in Blount County, Tennessee, searched a pair of massage businesses called Sue Lynn’s Health Studio and the 129 Health Studio, a mobile home and a dumpster, and he was charged with running them as brothels. In March 1990 he was convicted on five counts of promoting prostitution, for offences committed between 1987 and 1989, and sentenced to five consecutive two-year terms — ten years — and a $3,000 fine. The appeals court affirmed every part of it in August 1991, describing an operation that reached at least seven establishments across several states, from Sevierville and Chattanooga to Fort Lauderdale, Florida. He had pleaded guilty to possessing cocaine before that, and he would not give the probation officers an employment history; the consecutive terms were upheld on the finding that he had made crime a major source of his livelihood. He went to prison in Tennessee — six foot two, 170 pounds, blue eyes, grey hair — with the sentence running out on 29 April 1999, which is very likely why he spent his last years in Chattanooga.

He died at Chattanooga on 14 February 2001, aged sixty-five — thirty-five years to the day after his discharge from the Army. The Chattanooga Times Free Press carried his obituary three days later. Four photographs survive from his last years: beside a Tennessee lake in winter, deep-sea fishing in a straw hat, a plain portrait in a blue polo shirt, and one taken in a spring yard about 2000 or 2001, where he stands with his son, his daughter-in-law and his two grandsons. His name is cut on a white marble marker in the memorial section at Chattanooga National Cemetery, Section MA, site 36, beneath a cross and the words IN MEMORY OF. It is a cenotaph, not a grave: the markers in that section honour men whose remains were never recovered, or were buried at sea, or given to science, or burned and the ashes scattered. Where he actually lies, nobody now knows.

5.s:
Willie Joyce Stephens was born on 19 March 1942 at York, her father’s town in Sumter County, Alabama, the daughter of Jess Steve Willard Stephens, a mechanic who went by “Willard” and “J. W.,” and Grace Estelle Truett of Coffeeville in Clarke County. Her parents’ marriage did not last, and she was raised in Birmingham.

She went to Ramsay High School and transferred to Phillips in her third term, graduating there in 1960. Her senior year was a busy one: a Senior Y-Teen and its treasurer, a member of the Student Representative Council, a Red Cross representative and a Marshal. Her photograph in the Phillips yearbook is the earliest likeness of her there is, and it was taken only months before she married.

On 26 August 1960, aged eighteen, she married Robert Lee Bell at Fort Payne, in DeKalb County. Her first son was born in 1961, and a second followed in 1964 at Fort Worth. Her husband left the family about 1972 or 1973.

On 24 May 1980 she married again, to John Duncan Lammon, in the same town where she had married the first time. It was a home wedding, not a church one — a hired brass arch dressed with pink and blue flowers set up in somebody’s living room, white tapers in candelabra on either side, the bride in a full-length ivory gown with long sheer sleeves and the groom in a pale blue three-piece suit. She was thirty-eight.

She moved south with him to Jackson, in Clarke County, and there she kept her own clothing shop. She died on Tuesday 27 July 1982, aged forty; what took her is not known. Her husband survived her, and so did her mother Grace and her stepfather Charles L. Roberts of Birmingham, and her two sons and a daughter. The funeral was at Latham Funeral Chapel the next day. She was buried at Mount Gilead Cemetery in Clarke County — Lammon ground, where her second husband and the Lammon generation before him also lie. Her stone calls her simply JOYCE STEPHENS LAMMON, and under the dates it carries the whole of Micah 6:8: “He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good: and what doth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.” In the lower corner, in smaller letters, someone had two more words cut: AN ANGEL.

6.s:
Richard Clark Tuttle — Dick, all his life — was born at Terre Haute, Indiana, on 29 or 30 July 1929, the second son of Gifford Herman Tuttle and Helen May Knott, who were then living at 2266 Warren Street. His people had been in and around Terre Haute since the 1850s.

He grew up with an older brother, Robert Dale; a photograph from about 1938 has the two of them on a patch of spring grass, Dick at nine in a sweater and short trousers. When he was ten his grandmother Martha was living in the house as well — a woman he spent years under one roof with, and about whom almost nothing came down in the family afterwards.

About 1944 or 1945, when he was fifteen, his father moved the family north to Evanston, Illinois, and this branch of the Tuttles left Indiana after nearly a century. He graduated from Evanston Township High School in the class of 1947 — his senior portrait is on the class pages of The Evanstonian of ’47, and the family still has his own copy of the book with his name printed in the corner — and went on to take classes at Northwestern.

He enlisted in the United States Army and was certified at Fort Lee, Virginia, on 3 August 1951 as a quartermaster supply-records specialist, then served in occupied Germany; a photograph kept in the family shows him in uniform beside the sign for the Headquarters, Heilbronn Sub Post. He was still there at the end of 1952, sending his congratulations home to Terre Haute for his grandparents’ golden wedding.

Back in Evanston he met Judith Frost, who had come up from Marion, Indiana, to take a degree at Northwestern; they were introduced, the family says, through a friend. They married in the middle fifties, and in 1959, expecting their first child, bought a house on Dartmouth Avenue in Deerfield, Illinois. He worked for a Chicago label printer until the owner of the firm killed himself with carbon monoxide, and in 1971 he moved the family to Cincinnati to take a job with H. S. Crocker Co., another label company. He lived out his life there, and died at Cincinnati in 2015, two years after Judith.

7.s:
Judith Katharine Frost was born on 5 July 1934 at Parkersburg, West Virginia, the only child of Alan Chalmers Frost, who managed dime stores, and Velma Gladys Roush, a Mason County girl who had run away from home at sixteen. At two and a half, about 1936, she sat for a studio portrait, grinning in a knitted sweater-dress, ankle socks and white lace-up shoes.

Her father’s work moved them. By 1940 the family was renting on Stocking Road in Mansfield, Ohio, for thirty dollars a month; by 1950 they were at Marion, Indiana, where he ran the S. S. Kresge store seventy hours a week. In March 1947, when she was twelve, her mother took her to Akron to stay with her aunt Florence, and the two of them went on to Mason, West Virginia, to the bedside of her grandmother Bertha, who lay ill at home; another aunt came up from Georgia to join them.

As a sophomore she was one of the hundred girls of the Booster Club, who cheered the teams in gold slip-over sweaters, each girl buying her own. She graduated from Marion High School in 1952 — Latin Club, Booster Club, Y-Teens, Student Council, and co-chairman of the Mother-Daughter Christmas Tea — and went on to Earlham College at Richmond, Indiana, for her freshman year, 1952–53, and then to Northwestern. By her junior year at Marion she had also been on the Student Council and in the Art Club, which sent members to the Art Institute of Chicago. It was at Evanston that she met Richard Clark Tuttle. Their engagement was announced in April 1957, her engagement portrait ran in the Marion paper in May, they took out a licence in Cook County on 26 June, and they were married at three o’clock on Saturday 29 June 1957 in St. Luke’s Chapel, Evanston, by the Rev. St. John Brown. A photograph of her at a college formal in the early 1950s — a dark floor-length gown, a young man beside her in a dark suit with a white boutonnière — belongs to the few years before that. Their first home was at 536 Michigan Avenue, Evanston.

They bought a house on Dartmouth Avenue in Deerfield, Illinois in 1959, and moved to Cincinnati in 1971 when Richard took a job with the label printer H. S. Crocker. There were four children. She taught at the Indian Hill Schools, where she was remembered as “a positive early influence for hundreds of small children,” and she was a portrait painter and a maker of very fine dollhouse miniatures. To her grandchildren she was Mimi.

She died at Cincinnati on 31 October 2013, after fifty-six years of marriage. Her funeral was held on 5 November at St. Barnabas Episcopal Church on Montgomery Road.

8.s:
John Henry Bell was born on 4 August 1901 in Barbour County, Alabama, the eldest son of Thomas Jefferson Bell and Alice May Bradley, who farmed near Louisville. At home he was simply Henry, and that is how he grew up in his parents’ house through the 1900s and 1910s. He was sixteen in September 1917 when his father was shot in the back in the street at Louisville and partly paralysed; his father lived four more years, and the man who shot him got off with a hundred-dollar fine.

By 1925 he had left the county for Birmingham, and when his grandfather’s estate was divided seven ways among his father’s children the court set him down as “Henry Bell, Birmingham.” Two years later, on Friday the thirteenth of May 1927, he married Margaret Beatrice Eaken. Both Birmingham papers thought a couple marrying on such a date worth a humorous column, and the News ran a feature on the fearless bridegroom. Their first son arrived six months later, and he named the boy Thomas J., for his own father.

He drove a truck for a dry cleaner, out of a house on Huntsville Road in Birmingham, then painted houses — in Birmingham, and in Atlanta through the middle thirties, at 71 Ormond Avenue SE. There were six children. The second, a daughter named Marion, was born and lost in 1932 and buried at Forest Hill in Birmingham — his wife’s family ground, and the one family burying place he would not be laid in either. In June 1940 he was convicted in Jefferson County of desertion and non-support and sentenced to twelve months; he served four. The prison ledger put him at 163 pounds, physical condition good, teeth bad. He was released on 17 October 1940 by order of Judge Emmett Perry.

Sometime in the year that followed, he left for good. On 23 February 1942 he registered for the draft at Cincinnati, before Local Board No. 19 on Baymiller Street — five foot nine, 160 pounds, blue eyes, brown hair, a knot on his left leg near the hip — and when the form asked for someone who would always know where he was, he gave his mother at 118 North Street, Dothan. It is the last thing he is known to have put his name to.

His wife and children moved north to Wheaton, Illinois, where in January 1944 his eldest son Thomas, sixteen, was killed driving four friends to a skating pond in a car he had bought for fifty dollars that afternoon, against his grandfather’s orders; the certificate called the father simply “Henry Bell.” In December 1945 his wife sued him for divorce in the Jefferson County court at Birmingham, swearing that where he lived “is unknown and cannot be ascertained after reasonable effort,” and the court’s notice calling on him to answer was printed in the newspaper. She filed again in September 1948, through a solicitor, in the same words. When his own mother died in December 1956 her obituary named six surviving children, and he was not among them. He lies in neither of the family cemeteries — not at Forest Hill with his wife and his baby daughter, and not at Bethlehem with his parents. What became of him is not known. He was very probably the Henry Bell, fifty-one, born in Alabama and calling himself separated, who was lodging at the Mount Airy home for the homeless outside Cincinnati in April 1950 — the only man of that description in the whole county.

9.s:
Margaret Beatrice Eaken was born on 10 July 1908 at Cuba, in Sumter County, Alabama — her mother’s home ground, the small town on the Mississippi line where her father would be buried fourteen years later. She was the eldest child of Andrew Jackson Eaken and Maggie Dillon Swain. By 1910 the family had moved to Mobile, where her father had found work and her young uncle Langford Swain lodged in the house with them; she was one year old. She was thirteen when her father died and the family took him home to Cuba to bury him.

She was eighteen when she married John Henry Bell on Friday the thirteenth of May 1927, and both Birmingham papers thought a couple marrying on such a date worth a humorous paragraph. Their first son was born that November. There were six children; a daughter, Marion, died in infancy in 1932 and was buried at Forest Hill. In 1940 her husband was convicted in Jefferson County of desertion and non-support and served four months, and about 1942 he left for good.

By January 1944 she had taken the family north to Wheaton, Illinois, where her mother and stepfather were living, and there her eldest son Thomas Jackson — sixteen, and named for her brother — was killed in a car crash. She married again in 1948, to Claude B. Smith, and by 1950 she was at Lineville, in Clay County, Alabama, with her four surviving Bell children in the house.

Her later years were spent in Georgia. In July 1962, when her stepfather died, she was living at Fitzgerald in the south of the state and was styled “Mrs. Beatrice E. Smith”; her three brothers were then at Providence, Rhode Island, in Germany with the Army, and at Birmingham. Later she was at Clarkston, outside Atlanta, where she retired as a saleswoman at Rich’s department store, and she belonged to Vestavia Alliance Church. A cousin who had known her all her life said she “always had a larger-than-life personality”; a grandson remembered “such a refined lady.” In one snapshot she sits out in the cold in a dark coat on a wooden trestle in a bare winter yard, an iron fence behind her.

She died on Sunday 16 January 1983 at Clarkston, aged seventy-four, and was brought back to Birmingham to lie at Forest Hill, in Section 19, near the infant daughter she had buried half a century before. Her flat granite marker, carved with praying hands and a flower, reads MARGARET E. SMITH, JULY 10, 1908 — JAN. 16, 1983, GONE TO REST. Her death was announced in both cities, naming her husband, her four children, her mother and her two surviving brothers; neither notice mentioned John Henry Bell. Her mother outlived her by two years.

10.s:
Jess Steve Willard Stephens was born on 29 April 1917 at York, in Sumter County, Alabama, the son of John Willis Stephens and Mary Price Williams. His parents named him for Jess Willard, who had been heavyweight champion of the world for thirteen months when he was born. The name stuck twice over: he signed himself “Willard” and “J. W.” by turns, his father’s initials exactly.

The York he grew up in was small and plain — 1,651 people in 1924, electric street lights, streets not paved and, in the blunt shorthand of the fire-insurance surveyors, “Water Facilities: None. Fire Dept: None.” In 1920 the family was living at Election Precinct 6, York, the same small precinct where the Swains — the family his daughter would one day marry into — had lived twenty years before.

On 8 April 1939, aged twenty-two, he married Grace Estelle Truett at Fort Payne, in DeKalb County, at the other end of the state; she was twenty. The Montgomery Advertiser announced that “Mr. Stephens holds a position with the State” and that the couple would make their home in Livingston. By December 1941 they had a house on West Main Street there, and his sister Clara Mae was married in it. Three months later the two of them were at the Stephens-Williams reunion at his parents’ house in Livingston, entered on the guest list as “Mr. and Mrs. Willard Stephens, Livingston.” Their daughter Willie Joyce was born on 19 March 1942. The marriage did not last; Grace married again in 1947.

When he registered for the draft at Tuscaloosa on 16 October 1940 he was twenty-three, living with Grace at 521 Thirteenth Avenue and working for the Perry Creamery Company — five foot ten, a hundred and thirty pounds, fair-haired and blue-eyed — and he signed the card “Willard Stephens.” He worked as a mechanic. In April 1947, when his father died, he was in the Army and stationed at Washington, D.C.; by 1957 he was living at Birmingham. On 11 July 1958, at Arlington, Virginia, he married again. He was forty-one, divorced, and an auto mechanic at Parkway Motors; she was Jessie Eliza Comstock, born Svedberg at Charleston, South Carolina, forty-three and divorced too, and the two of them were already sharing an address on First Street S.E. in Washington. With her he moved to Charleston.

He was shot in the chest at his house on Sweetgum Street in Charleston on the afternoon of 18 March 1971 and died there at a quarter to five, aged fifty-three. The county coroner certified the death a homicide and entered the circumstances as undetermined; there was no autopsy, and the record does not say who fired. His wife gave the particulars. He lies at Magnolia Cemetery there under a low granite stone he shares with Jessie, who followed him in 1990. The cutter put four words under his name that say where he came from: BORN YORK, ALA.

11.s:
Grace Estelle Truett was born on 14 January 1917 in Clarke County, Alabama, the eldest daughter of Thomas William Truette and Sennie Lawrence. The family lived at Coffeeville, and in 1920 she was a toddler in the house there, called “Gracie E.,” with a younger sister, Gladys; a third sister, Jewel Rae, came after. Her father died before she was thirteen. Her mother was a widow for four years and then married again in the next county.

By January 1939 she was working as a clerk-typist in the Farm Security Administration’s Sumter County office, one of six people on a New Deal county payroll. On 8 April 1939, aged twenty, she married Willard Stephens; the marriage is recorded at Fort Payne in DeKalb County, two hundred and fifty miles north-east of the Clarke County villages her family had lived in for four generations, though the Montgomery Advertiser reported that it was “quietly solemnized in Montgomery.” Their daughter Willie Joyce was born on 19 March 1942. The marriage did not last. In 1947 she married Eugene Raiford Rivers Jr. at Montgomery, and later Charles Leroy Roberts; she also went for a time by the name Grace Tru Morgan, so there was probably one more marriage still.

She outlived her daughter, who died at forty in 1982. Grace herself died on Monday 9 November 1992 at Irondale, in Jefferson County, aged seventy-five. The notice in the Birmingham paper on the Wednesday morning set the graveside service for eleven o’clock that same day — the family drove west for it — and named the two sisters who survived her: Gladys, who had never left Clarke County and was living at Jackson, and Jewell, four hundred miles away at Lawton, Oklahoma.

She lies at Tuscaloosa Memorial Park under a bronze companion marker cut with roses and the words TOGETHER FOREVER. Her plate reads only GRACE T. — the T for the Truett name she had been born with seventy-five years earlier and had not used in half a century. Charles L. Roberts, who died in 1999, lies beside her under the other plate.

12.s:
Gifford Herman Tuttle was born at Indianapolis on 7 October 1903, the first child of Dennis Clark Tuttle and Leona Marie Alexander, who had married on New Year’s Eve nine months and six days before. His name was a quiet thank-you: his father Dennis had lost his own father before his first birthday and had been raised by a stepfather, Gifford H. Spear.

He grew up in Terre Haute, where his father repaired freight cars for the Pennsylvania Railroad, his widowed grandmother Mary Alexander lived under the same roof, and a younger sister, Dorothy, came along after him. On Saturday 8 October 1910, the day after his seventh birthday, his small friends gave him a surprise party: games and contests with prizes, ice cream and cake, and thirteen children — Grace McKee, George Hoffman, Raymond Lier, Opal Smith, Mary Hoffman, Kenneth Tucker, Margaret Dooley, Ron Dooley, Frank Hoffman, Edward McKee, Francis McKee, A. Tucker and the honoree. The birthday cake was a present from his grandmother. In August 1914, aged ten, he went out to West Terre Haute for the weekend with his parents, his sister and old Mrs. Alexander; and in February 1916 he was one of twenty-one children at Gretchen Cunningham’s birthday party at Twelfth and Mulberry streets, where the house and the ices were done up in pink and white. At Wiley High School he played on the line. The 1921 yearbook, The Red Pepper, photographed him standing with four other linemen in a striped jersey and moleskins, listed him as a guard on the second and third teams, and gave him one line: “It’s hard to get around him.” The next year he was on the roll of the Class of 1923, which he never graduated with: he married that spring.

On 2 April 1923, at nineteen, he married Helen May Knott in Rush County, Indiana. They had two sons, Robert Dale and Richard Clark. About 1944 or 1945 he moved the household out of Terre Haute to Evanston, Illinois — the moment this branch of the family left Indiana, where Tuttles and Fuerstenbergers had lived since the 1850s. The parish they joined was St. Luke’s Episcopal, at Lee and Hinman Streets, and they were still at Evanston in 1952. By 1970 he and Helen were at Highland Park. A photograph of the two of them from the early seventies, hand in hand and wearing flowers, was most likely taken at their fiftieth anniversary.

He died suddenly on 18 December 1974 at Highland Park, aged seventy-one. His body rested at St. Luke’s, where a requiem mass was sung on the Friday evening of 20 December; the interment was private, and the family asked that flowers be omitted. His father Dennis, then ninety, outlived him by eight months.

13.s:
Helen May Knott was born on 12 June 1905 in Indiana, the younger daughter of Joseph McGee Knott, a heater in a Terre Haute steel mill, and Martha Ellen (Lamb) Ford Knott. Her sister Mildred was seven years older; a half-brother, Percy Ford, was a grown man by the time Helen could walk. She grew up with all three of them under one roof in Terre Haute — in 1910 Helen was four, Mildred eleven and Percy twenty-four.

Three photographs survive of her childhood about 1911 to 1913: one on the lawn beside her big sister, which their mother sent as a postcard inscribed “My too sweet dauters, Mildred and Helen”; and two of Helen with her friend Grace, both girls in wide straw hats. Grace was almost certainly Grace Estella Schomer, born six months after her in December 1905, the daughter of the man who ran Terre Haute’s dancing school — a child performer the local paper once called “the miniature Pavlowa.” She lived to be ninety-seven.

In the autumn of 1920 she started at Garfield High School, Terre Haute, where the yearbook listed the new freshmen as the “Cradle Roll” of the Class of 1924, under a cartoon of a howling baby in a high chair; she had left by the next year. On 2 April 1923 Helen married Gifford Herman Tuttle in Rush County. Two sons followed, Robert Dale in 1925 and Richard Clark — Alec’s grandfather — in the last days of July 1929, when the family were living at 2266 Warren Street and the Terre Haute paper announced him in a single line: “to G. H. and Helen Tuttle, 2266 Warren street, a son, Richard Clark.” They raised the boys in a rented house in Terre Haute through the Depression, with Helen’s widowed mother living under the same roof.

Her father died in January 1932 at her sister’s house in Cedar Rapids, and lay in Highland Lawn Cemetery across the city under a flat granite marker cut simply Joseph Knott 1851 1932; her mother joined him in the same grave in 1945, under a matching stone.

About 1944 or 1945 the family moved north to Evanston, Illinois, and into St. Luke’s Episcopal Church, which they belonged to for thirty years. A hand-tinted studio portrait shows Helen in her late thirties, dark hair set in rolled waves; another photograph catches her with Gifford in the early 1970s, near their fiftieth anniversary. Gifford died in 1974, and Helen lived on as a widow in Wilmette.

She died on Sunday evening, 24 April 1977, at Evanston Hospital, aged seventy-one. The Chicago Tribune carried her two mornings later under her own maiden name — “Helen Knott Tuttle of Wilmette” — naming her two sons, her seven grandchildren and her sister Mildred Cooper of Cedar Rapids, and setting the visitation and a requiem eucharist for that evening in the Lady Chapel of St. Luke’s. The notice ends with two words that explain why no grave of hers has ever been found: “Interment private.” Terre Haute had not forgotten her either: the same morning her old home-town paper ran her among its DEATHS, word having reached a sister-in-law still living in the city. Where she was buried is not known. Mildred followed her six months later.

14.s:
Alan Chalmers Frost was born on 10 February 1903 at Paterson, New Jersey, the third child of Harry B. Frost, an English-born silk manufacturer, and Katharine Chalmers of Orange. His middle name was his mother’s maiden name. In a photograph of about 1903 or 1904 he is an infant in a long white gown and bonnet, propped on a stool between his sister Katherine, six or seven, and his brother Harry, three or four.

In 1905, aged two, he was living in a Paterson household that kept a live-in servant. By 1910 the family had moved out to Wyckoff, in Franklin Township, Bergen County, and that is where he grew up; in 1915 he was twelve and at school.

By the time his father died in December 1930 he was living at Wilmington, Delaware, and he was still there in January 1932, when he came up to spend a Sunday and Monday with his widowed mother on Wyckoff Avenue. She died three weeks later. By that summer he was working at Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, and came home to Wyckoff Avenue for the Fourth of July and again for a two-week vacation.

Some time in the early 1930s — when and where is not known — he married Velma Gladys Roush of Mason County, West Virginia, and their daughter Judith was born at Parkersburg in July 1934. He was with S. S. Kresge by the mid-1930s, at Sandusky, Ohio, and in October 1937 he came to Mansfield, Ohio, as assistant manager of the company’s Dollar store; in January 1939 he took over as manager. In July 1940 “the A. C. Frosts of Linden road, and their daughter Judy” were vacationing with relatives in New Jersey, and in February 1942 he had two men jailed for thirty days for stealing ten pairs of men’s socks from the store. He registered for the draft on 16 February 1942 from 1506 West Fourth Street, Marion, working for the S. S. Kresge Co.: five foot ten, a hundred and forty-five pounds, light complexion, brown hair, blue eyes, and the person who would always know where to find him was Velma Gladys Frost. He spent his whole working life in that chain, running the Marion store for many years at seventy hours a week, until Jupiter took over the location about 1962 and the Frosts moved to Flint, Michigan.

Velma died at Flint on 3 October 1964; they were living then at 316 West Dartmouth. He outlived her by eighteen years. His last home was 456 Glover Road, Clyde, a village in Wayne County, New York, where his elder brother Harry had married a Clyde girl, Esther Baird, in the village’s Episcopal church in December 1933, and where Harry lies in the Maple Grove cemetery. Alan joined that same church, St. John’s, by then Christ Community Church, and the Galen Historical Society. He died after a short illness at the North Wayne Community Hospital in Newark on 18 May 1982, aged seventy-nine, and the memorial service was held in the church chapel at Clyde three days later; the notice asked for gifts to the historical society or the village fire department’s ambulance squad. Where he is buried is not known.

⭐⭐ Velma Frost was born Velma Roush — now carried by records, not memory [FROST-33–36], adversary-upheld 17 Sep 2026. Her paid death notice (Flint Journal, 5 and 6 Oct 1964) gives her birth as 21 June 1907, West Virginia — the exact date of the Roush birth register — and names 2 sisters, Mrs. Joseph Walk of Akron and Mrs. William Kirton. Those two women are Florence and Della (Claudia) Roush, whose own Summit County, Ohio marriage records (1926, 1930) name their parents as John G. Roush and Bertha Nease. Velma herself married Alfred Hesterberg at Greenup, Kentucky, on 6 Sep 1931 as “Velma Roush,” parents John Roush and Bertha Nease; he divorced her at Akron in October 1933, when she was living in Charleston, W. Va. Her husband’s 1942 draft card names her “Velma Gladys Frost.” ⭐ And a second, independent statement seventeen years earlier: in March 1947 both Marion, Indiana papers reported that “Mrs. A. C. Frost and daughter, Judy” had visited “the former’s sister, Mrs. Joseph Walk, Akron,” and gone on to Mason, W. 15.s:
Velma Gladys Roush was born on 21 June 1907 in Mason County, West Virginia, the daughter of John G. Roush, a coal miner, and Bertha Ellen Nease.

She was fifteen months old on the evening of Saturday 12 September 1908, when her father tried to fill a coal-miner’s lamp from an oil can that had been standing by a hot cook stove, and the house at Broad Run went up. Her eldest sister, who had been ironing beside the table, died within hours; a second sister died five days later; the house and everything in it burned, including the family’s clothes. Velma was the infant asleep in the room, and a six-year-old sister carried her out through the smoke to their grandparents’ house, unseen and unaided. Her father died of his burns on 21 October. She can never have remembered any of it, and within six weeks the two people best able to tell her were dead.

Her widowed mother kept the four surviving girls together. In May 1909, before Velma was two, Bertha went to the Mason County court and qualified as guardian of “Iva Roush, Florence Roush, Velm Roush and Della Roush, infant children of John G. Roush, deceased,” on a $500 bond, with the girls’ grandfather Moses Roush standing surety. In 1910 the household at Wagner, Mason County, was Bertha at its head with Iva, Florence, Velma and the baby Claudia; in 1920 Velma was still in the county, about thirteen. She ran away from home at sixteen. She was five feet tall, and somebody wrote in her school yearbook, “She’s small but oh my!”

On 6 September 1931 she married Alfred Hesterberg at Greenup, Kentucky, signing as Velma Roush. He divorced her at Akron in October 1933, when she was living at Charleston, West Virginia. Her daughter was born at Parkersburg in July 1934. By 1940 she was at Mansfield, Ohio, married to Alan C. Frost, and by 1950 at Marion, Indiana, where he managed the S. S. Kresge dollar store on the square and worked seventy hours a week.

In Marion the family lived at 914 South D Street, and she went with her husband to the staff parties: a Valentine dinner for the employees at the Marion Hotel in February 1947, and in May 1949 a dinner for both Marion stores’ staff to mark the fiftieth anniversary of the Kresge chain, where she won a prize. In March 1947 she and her daughter drove to Akron to see her sister and went on to Mason, West Virginia, where her mother was ill. She took a few days with relatives at Cleveland in 1951. On a Monday morning in May 1953 she cut one of the ribbons at the opening of a new Marion store, standing in for the town’s retail trade beside the mayor’s wife and the wives of the president and vice-president of the Chamber of Commerce. At Christmas 1953 she and Alan put up a neighbourhood tree with the Drummonds at the corner of Ninth and D Streets, and the neighbours held a party round it; the Marion paper printed a photograph of it lit up at night. She spent a whole month in Florida in the spring of 1954. In August 1955 she gave a lawn shower for a bride-elect at her own house, her daughter helping as assistant hostess, with an umbrella and a miniature bride and bridegroom over the gift table.

Her health was failing well before the end; she was admitted to a Marion hospital twice within nine days in November 1959. About 1962 the family moved to Flint, Michigan, when another chain took the Kresge location over, and she belonged to the Episcopal church there. She had arthritis, and the treatment of the day was aspirin in high doses, which is hard on the stomach. She died on 3 October 1964 at Hurley Hospital in Flint, aged fifty-seven, of a perforated duodenum, and was cremated at White Chapel three days later. She left two sisters, Mrs. Joseph Walk of Akron and Mrs. William Kirton of Boynton Beach. Two photographs of her survive: a studio portrait, and a colour snapshot of her in her fifties, laughing in a red-and-black plaid coat with the autumn leaves down behind her.

16.s:
Thomas Jefferson Bell — Tom to everyone who knew him — was born in Barbour County, Alabama in the autumn of 1875, one of the eleven children of John T. Bell and Sallie Cox, and he farmed all his life near Louisville, on the country six miles south of Clayton where his grandparents had settled in about 1830. He married Alice May Bradley on 13 August 1895, when she was eighteen and newly out of the guardianship the county had placed her in as an orphan.

They had nine children. Seven were living in January 1920, when the whole household was under one roof at Louisville — Henry at eighteen, Ray at sixteen, William at twelve, Ethel at ten and little Juanita at two — and two were already buried in the churchyard at Bethlehem Baptist, the congregation his people had belonged to since thirteen of their neighbours gathered it in April 1824. His cotton went to Clayton, a county town of three warehouses on the Public Square — J. C. Thomas’s, the Alliance’s and the Farmers Union’s — with the court hall and fire department, the Fryer Hotel, the post office and a water works and electric light plant beside the Central of Georgia tracks.

On the evening of Thursday 27 September 1917 he met Frank Vinson Jr. in the street at Louisville; the two had words, and Vinson fired twice. One bullet struck him in the back, partly severing his spine and passing into his left lung, and left him partly paralysed. The Clayton Record headlined it “Tom Bell Fatally Shot By Vinson,” but he lived: he was taken to Montgomery and brought home ten days later, “somewhat improved.” Vinson was charged with intent to murder, in what the paper called a case “known thru out Barbour County as the Frank Vinson case,” in which “considerable feeling existed in the county for both sides.” It came to trial in October 1919, and the jury returned a verdict of assault and battery and a fine of a hundred dollars.

He died on 30 August 1921, at forty-five, and was laid at Bethlehem beside those two children. The Clayton Record called him a son of Mr. and Mrs. John Bell Sr., pioneer citizens, buried “where two of his children are buried,” and named the five brothers who survived him — Mack and Will of Louisville, Ben, Ed and John of Clayton. The granite his family set over him afterwards gives dates a year earlier than the county’s own, SEPT. 18, 1874 and AUG. 27, 1920, and the two have never been reconciled.

He left almost nothing to divide. No administration was ever opened in his name; in October 1922 “The Tom Bell Home Place, one mile North of Louisville” — twenty acres, all under cultivation, with a good residence and barns — was advertised for sale in front of the courthouse at Clayton — which is the more striking because his own father had died six years before him worth fifty thousand dollars in lands, cotton, insurance and money. What his children eventually got came out of that estate instead: in April 1925 a Barbour County court split one deceased uncle’s share seven ways among them, naming each in turn — Ellie, Ray, Ruth, William, Ethel, the youngest Juanita, and “Henry Bell, Birmingham.”

The little girl of the 1920 census, Juanita, grew up to fly: taught by her husband, C. Foy Halstead, she earned her pilot’s licence in 1954, helped found the Alabama chapter of the Ninety-Nines, the women pilots’ organisation, and raced fifteen times, the Powder Puff Derby among them, logging more than five thousand hours; in 1967 the Associated Press put her on the wire as one of “Alabama’s Flying Grandmothers.” Alice outlived him by thirty-five years, married again, and was brought home to lie beside him. Their names are cut side by side on one block of grey granite at Bethlehem, under the single word BELL.

17.s:
Alice May Bradley was born on 8 October 1876 in Barbour County, Alabama, the fourth of the five surviving children of Henry Bradley, clerk of the circuit court, and his wife Elvira Loveless. She lost both of them young. Her father died in February 1887, when she was ten, of an old war wound; her mother died of cholera morbus on a Sunday afternoon in June 1891. They lie together at Clayton City Cemetery under two draped marble stones inside one iron rail.

That October a Barbour County court appointed a guardian for Alice, then fourteen, and her younger sister Katie, twelve. The petitioner was a great-aunt, L. M. Bell, and among the seven signers of the four-thousand-dollar bond were two Bradley relations and John T. Bell — the man who would be her father-in-law four years later. Two years after that, a Eufaula paper printed the probate court’s settlement of the earlier guardianship and listed her by name among “the following named minor children of Henry Bradley, deceased”, with her sisters Ida Parker and Annie Fortner and her brother Henry.

She married Thomas Jefferson Bell on 13 August 1895, at eighteen, and bore nine children. In December 1898 her sister Katie eloped to Georgetown and married Tom’s younger brother George, so the two orphaned Bradley girls went into the same farming family at Louisville, and two sons of John T. Bell married two daughters of Henry Bradley.

Widowed in 1921, she married Mack K. Norton — and there is a quiet symmetry in it, because Mack’s first wife had been Katie, who died in 1924. Two Bradley sisters each married a Bell, each was widowed, and the same man married them in turn. They were married by the autumn of 1930, when the Clayton paper reported “Mrs. M. K. Norton and daughter, Juanita Bell, of Eufaula” visiting her married daughter Mrs. W. W. Knight. She and Juanita lived at Eufaula, then briefly at Hurtsboro in 1932, and by the autumn of 1933 at Dothan. By 1935 Alice was living with Mack at 118 East North Street in Dothan, and it was that address her eldest son wrote down in 1942 when a draft board asked who would always know where he was. She had been eighteen at her first marriage and had borne nine children, and she said so to the census-taker in 1940. At Dothan she threw herself into the Woman’s Missionary Society of the Headland Avenue Baptist Church: for years the Dothan Eagle’s Monday church column carried the line “Ann Judson—Mrs. M. K. Norton,” for the circle she led and hosted, and in January 1948 the society made her its white cross chairman, gathering bandages and supplies for the mission hospitals. She kept her vote in Barbour County, and in the spring of 1946 she mailed in an absentee ballot there — the ballot on which a young George C. Wallace was running for the legislature for the first time. Mack died in 1954; his obituary called her children his step-sons and step-daughters and named them as Bells — T. R. Bell of Bessemer, W. W. Bell of Jacksonville, and four married daughters.

She outlived her first husband by thirty-five years and died at Montgomery on 29 December 1956, aged eighty. They brought her home to Bethlehem, in Barbour County, and buried her beside Tom under the name Bell — not Norton. Her dates are cut on the right-hand half of his stone: ALICE, OCT. 8, 1876, DEC. 29, 1956.

18.s:
Andrew Jackson Eaken was born on 1 May 1881 in Lauderdale County, Mississippi, one of the youngest children of Joseph William “Joel W.” Eakins and Sarah Hudson Payne. His people had come to Mississippi out of New Hanover County, North Carolina, and he reckoned both his parents North Carolina born.

About 1907 he married Maggie Dillon Swain, of York and Cuba in Sumter County, Alabama — the next county across the state line. In 1910 the two of them were living at Kosters, in Mobile, with their one-year-old daughter Beatrice and Maggie’s young brother Langford Swain lodging in the house. In 1917 he registered for the draft at Princeton, in Jackson County at the far north-east corner of Alabama. He was a man who crossed the state repeatedly, and the clerks spelled him as they heard him: by 1920 the family name was being written “Eakans.”

He was living at 2716 Avenue F South in Birmingham when he died on the night of 20 March 1922, aged forty. The body was sent down to Cuba the next morning, and the funeral and burial took place there, at Clay Memorial Cemetery in his wife’s home village, among her people. He left Maggie a widow at thirty-five. Their children included Alec’s great-grandmother Margaret Beatrice; Andrew Jackson “Jack” Eaken, who became a colonel; Joseph William “Jo Will” Eaken, who rose to be a vice-president of American Airlines; and Melvin Swain Eaken.

The surname moved under him. “Our name was originally spelled Eakins,” his granddaughter wrote in 2009. “My father’s grandfather stopped dotting the ‘i’ and it became an ‘e’. My father dropped the ‘s’, as did his brothers.” Andrew Jackson was the Eaken in the middle of that sentence.

19.s:
Maggie Dillon Swain was born on 27 September 1886 in Sumter County, Alabama, a daughter of Joseph L. Swain and the woman everyone called Dillon Simmons. Her middle name was her mother’s given name, and it puzzled the family for three generations. She grew up at York, where in 1900 the house held Leila, Patton, Maggie, Kirkland, Pinky and Langford.

She married Andrew Jackson Eaken about 1907. Their daughter Margaret Beatrice was born in 1908, and in 1910 the three of them were at Mobile with her brother Langford boarding in the house. Andrew died on 20 March 1922, and she took him home to Cuba to bury him, twenty miles from where she had been born. She was thirty-five.

On 6 November 1925 she married Thomas J. Bloebaum at Birmingham, and the marriage took her north — to Milton, in DuPage County, Illinois, by 1930, and to Wheaton in the same county in 1940 and 1950. That is the “Chicago area” her descendants remembered without being able to name it. The Bell family came north to join her, and in January 1944 her grandson Thomas Jackson Bell was killed in a car crash at sixteen; she had been going to give him a car for his birthday, and he took the keys a few days early.

Illinois held her for thirty-five years, but she kept coming home. In May 1951 she came down from Wheaton to visit her mother, Mrs. Dillon Swain, and her sisters, Mrs. Geo. McElroy and Mrs. M. C. Cobb. Her mother died in November 1952, and on 6 February 1953 Maggie and her two sisters were granted letters testamentary on the will in the Sumter County probate court, signing the notice to creditors together — Maggie S. Bloebaum, Pinkie S. McElroy, Merle S. Cobb. Her second husband, then eighty, died at Wheaton on 18 July 1962 and was brought down to Clay Memorial at Cuba for burial, so she buried both her husbands in her own village, forty years apart.

She came back to Birmingham in the end, to the house her family still pictures, with a set of rosewood twin beds with beautiful inlay. The family remembers that the beds later went to John Duncan Lammon, the second husband of her grandson Robert’s first wife, Joyce, and no one knows what became of them after that. She died there on Sunday 10 March 1985, aged ninety-eight, after fifteen years back in Alabama, outliving her own daughter by two years. The notices called her Margaret Swain Eaker Bloebaum and listed her sons, Col. Andrew J. and Joseph W. Eaker, and her two surviving sisters, Mrs. G. R. McElroy of Chattanooga — the Pinkie of the old York household — and Mrs. Cliffton Cobb of Meridian, who was Merle. She was buried at Clay Memorial Cemetery in Cuba, where her first husband had lain since 1922 and her second since 1962. In family memory she is “Ms Blevon”: Bloebaum, softened by sixty years.

20.s:
John Willis Stephens was born on 12 March 1876 in Sumter County, Alabama, the son of Caswell Massey Stephens and his first wife, known to her own gravestone only as A. M. and remembered in the family as Ava Marilla Shelton. His mother died when he was fourteen, and his father married again the following spring, near Cuba.

On 4 July 1906 he married Mary Price Williams in Sumter County; she was nineteen and had been born across the state line at State Line, in Greene County, Mississippi. They had four children — Lois Mildred, born 1908, who married Thomas Turnipseed; Rufus D.; Jess Steve Willard, born at York in 1917; and Clara Mae, born 1922, who married Edgar Herndon. In 1920 the family was at Election Precinct 6, York.

Like his father he went by “J. W.” He farmed and kept a dairy, lived his whole life in Sumter County, and was a member of the Baptist church for fifty years. In time he moved the family to Livingston, the county seat — a town of two livery stables still doing business in the middle of it, the court house and jail on Marshall Street, the Everitt Hotel on Spring, the public school, the Methodist church and the public library. He was living there when his father died in February 1935; the Livingston paper offered its sympathy to him by name “in the loss of his father.”

On the last Sunday of July 1939 he and his wife gave the Stephens-Williams reunion at their Livingston house, and the company that day ran from his brother H. R. at Halsell and his sister’s Knight household to his wife’s Williams brothers coming in from Pascagoula, Baton Rouge and Jackson.

He died at home in the night between Sunday 13 and Monday 14 April 1947, aged seventy-one, after a long illness — the paper remembered it as Sunday night, the state record and the stone as the 14th. The funeral was held in the house at half past ten on the Tuesday, Rev. Audrey Granade assisted by Rev. Henry Niles. He lies in Myrtlewood Cemetery at Livingston under a double stone with his wife, who followed him in 1957: his half headed FATHER, hers MOTHER, a stone urn between them and the family name cut across the base.

21.s:
Mary Price Williams was born on 18 March 1887 at State Line, in Greene County, Mississippi — a railroad village that takes its name from sitting flat on the Alabama border — the daughter of Francis R. Williams and Mary J. Lewis. She grew up in a large family a few miles west, in Beat 3 of Clarke County, Mississippi, where in 1900 she was thirteen and at home with her brothers and sister Jesse F., Etta S. and Knox A.

On 4 July 1906, at nineteen, she crossed back over the line to marry J. W. Stephens in Sumter County, Alabama, and she lived the rest of her life on the Alabama side. Her children included Lois Mildred, born in 1908, who married a Turnipseed; Rufus D.; Jess Steve Willard, born at York on 29 April 1917; and Clara Mae, born in 1922, who married a Herndon. She made her home at Livingston for many years and was a faithful member of the Livingston Baptist Church.

Her own people stayed scattered across Mississippi and Louisiana, and she kept up with them. On Sunday 30 July 1939 she and her husband gave the Stephens-Williams reunion at their house, and her brothers and sister came a long way for it — her sister Mrs. L. L. Craig from Gulfport, and H. H. Williams from Pascagoula, K. A. Williams from Baton Rouge and J. F. Williams from Jackson. When her brother Ira died at Laurel, Mississippi, in March 1935 the family he left behind was counted as four sons, four daughters, three brothers and five sisters, and she was one of the sisters: “Mrs. Price Stevens, Livingston, Ala.” The others named that day were Mrs. Billie Barrow and Mrs. Wallace Davis of Meridian, Mrs. L. L. Craig of Gulfport and Mrs. Sophie Childers of Hattiesburg.

She was widowed in April 1947 and outlived her husband by ten years. She died at her home on the Sunday morning of 20 October 1957, aged seventy, after a long illness. The funeral was at the Livingston Baptist Church at three the next afternoon, Rev. Jackson Robertson officiating, Causey Funeral Home directing, and she was buried beside her husband at Myrtlewood Cemetery under the half of their double stone headed MOTHER. Her own paper printed her name out in full: Mrs. Mary Price Williams Stephens.

22.s:
Thomas William Truette was born in September 1893 in Clarke County, Alabama, the son of William Curtis Truett and Amanda Webb, and grew up answering to the family’s own pet name for him, “Tamie.” In June 1900 he was six years old at Clarksville, fifth of six children in a farmhouse full of them: Tela, thirteen; Jane, twelve; Bigy, ten; Lillie, eight; himself; and Bessie, who was one.

He grew up around Clarksville and Coffeeville, the strip of Clarke County where his people had farmed since before the Civil War — his grandfather had enlisted at Coffeeville in 1862, and his father lies at New Prospect. About 1916 he married Sennie Lawrence, a Coffeeville girl six years younger. They were at Coffeeville in 1920 with two small daughters, “Gracie E.” and “Gladis G.”; Grace Estelle, born in January 1917, was Alec’s great-grandmother. A third daughter, Jewel Rae, followed.

He died before 1930, somewhere under thirty-seven years old. Sennie was a widow by then and married again in 1934. Where he lies nobody knows: he is not among the eight Truetts at New Prospect with his father, and of the four generations of Truetts in Clarke County he is the only one whose grave is lost.

23.s:
Sennie E. Lawrence was born at Coffeeville, Clarke County, Alabama, on 5 January 1899 — the date cut on her gravestone; as a small child her age was returned a year or two older, 1897 at one count and 1898 at the next, which is the ordinary drift of a child’s age reported by a parent. She was the fourth of seven children of “Calm” Lawrence, a farmer, and his wife Eliza. The man who called at the house in 1900 wrote her baby brother Alfonso down as nought days old: he had come on the day the child was born.

Her father was gone by 1910, and her mother Eliza kept the house with six children in it and no man. Clerks wrote the family name Lawrence, Larance and Laurence, and her own given name Sennie, Senie, Cenis and Zennie.

About 1916 she married Thomas William Truette. Their daughters Grace Estelle and Gladys were with them at Coffeeville in 1920, and a third, Jewel Rae, followed. Thomas died before 1930 and she was a widow at about thirty. On 24 June 1934 she married again, at Chatom in Washington County: Sol L. James Sr., born 18 April 1891. He died in 1953 and she was widowed a second time.

She died on 13 September 1975, aged seventy-six, and lies beside him at Ulcanush Cemetery, Coffeeville, under a double granite marker with the name JAMES on the base and a cross and spray of flowers cut on each stone. Her own slab reads SENNIE E., JAN. 5, 1899, SEPT. 13, 1975. The graveyard runs out into open field behind a chain-link fence, with a grain silo on the skyline. Her parents lie in the same ground, about forty yards off, under two slabs of rough concrete.

24.s:
Dennis Clark Tuttle was born at Peoria, Illinois, on 25 January 1884. His parents, Richard B. Tuttle and Emma S. Fuerstenberger, had married at Terre Haute two years earlier, and what took them to Peoria nobody now knows; they were home again within the year. On 17 December 1884, before Dennis could walk, his father died of consumption at twenty-six. He was named for his father’s elder brother Dennis and for his grandfather Clark Strong Tuttle, the miller of Otter Creek — so the “Clark” he carried had come down from a Connecticut bride of 1788, and he would pass it on to a grandson.

His mother married twice more, and the man who raised him was her third husband, Gifford H. Spear. Dennis repaid that in the plainest way a man of his time could: he gave his own first son the name Gifford.

On New Year’s Eve 1902, at the house of the bride’s widowed mother on North Sixth Street, he married Leona Marie Alexander of Clinton, Indiana. Terre Haute’s Daily Tribune had told the city four days earlier that “The marriage of Miss Leona Alexander and Mr. Dennis Tuttle will take place Wednesday evening at the home of the bride’s mother on North Sixth street,” and that “Mr. Tuttle is an employe of the Van shops”; the next day’s paper made him “a well known employe of the Van shops.” The Van shops were the Vandalia Railroad’s Terre Haute works, which the Pennsylvania Railroad absorbed in 1917 — so the forty-three years he eventually gave the Pennsylvania as a freight-car repairman began in a railroad town four days before his wedding. He retired onto the road’s Roll of Honor.

Gifford was born nine months and six days after the wedding, and a daughter, Dorothy, followed. Leona’s widowed mother Mary moved in with them and never left, dying in their house in 1934.

What he carried in his pockets survives: his Social Security card, issued on 22 April 1937; a courtesy card from Kerman Grotto, where he was the Grotto’s Prophet; an accident policy from the Terre Haute Tribune-Star dated 7 May 1952; and the card from an Indiana unemployment claim that paid him twenty dollars a week in his sixties. In April 1942 he registered for the “Old Man’s Draft” with Vigo County Board 1. In 1934, from 2626 Fenwood Avenue, he took $1,813 as his late mother’s one-fifth share of a family estate.

By the early 1950s he and Leona were at 2438 North Eleventh Street. On New Year’s Eve 1952 they had been married fifty years, and the Terre Haute Tribune printed their photograph two days beforehand under the heading FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY — a stiff-collared old railroader beside his wife. They issued no invitations; the paper simply told the city that the Tuttles would be at home on New Year’s Day to their friends, and that all were invited. Their son Gifford came down from Evanston with his wife, their daughter Dorothy Stephens was living at home, and their two grandsons sent word, one from Rochester, New York, the other from an army post in Germany.

He and Leona were married sixty-seven years. She died in 1970, his son Gifford in December 1974, and he himself on 22 August 1975, at ninety-one. He lies with Leona at Highland Lawn Cemetery in Terre Haute, in the same ground as the Bavarian shoemaker who was his grandfather.

25.s:
Leona Marie Alexander was born at Clinton, in Vermillion County, Indiana, on 16 February 1883, the only child William L. Alexander and Mary Elizabeth Fletcher ever had. Her father died while she was small. By the summer of 1900 she was seventeen and living with her widowed mother at 314 Mulberry Street in Terre Haute, in a house her mother owned outright and paid for by keeping house for other people.

On New Year’s Eve 1902 she married Dennis Clark Tuttle, a young man out of the Vandalia railroad shops; the wedding was in her mother’s house on North Sixth Street. Their son Gifford arrived nine months and six days later, and a daughter, Dorothy, followed. Her mother moved in with them and stayed until her death in 1934.

She was a member of St. Stephen’s Episcopal Church in Terre Haute — the first Episcopalian in a family that had been Congregational for six generations, and the change may well have come in with her. She was also a life member of the Daughters of Mokanna, Kerman Caldron No. 19, the women’s side of her husband’s Grotto; her 1964 membership card is among the family papers.

On New Year’s Eve 1952 she and Dennis had been married fifty years. The Terre Haute Tribune printed their photograph — Leona in a dark lace-shouldered dress, smiling, her glasses catching the flash — above a caption inviting the whole city to call on them on New Year’s Day. Her daughter Dorothy Stephens was living at home with them that winter; her son Gifford came from Evanston.

She died at three o’clock on the afternoon of Sunday 13 September 1970 at St. Anthony Hospital, aged eighty-seven, out of the house at 501 North Seventh Street she and Dennis had lived in. She left a husband of sixty-seven years, a daughter in Terre Haute, a son at Highland Park, Illinois, two grandsons and seven great-grandchildren. The funeral was at St. Stephen’s, the Rev. Harold Taylor officiating, and she was buried at Highland Lawn, where Dennis joined her five years later.

26.s:
Joseph McGee Knott was born on 5 March 1851 at Lowell, in Washington County, Ohio, on the Muskingum, the son of Benjamin and Margaret Nott. The family spelled the name both ways for a century; he was born a Nott and died a Knott.

He grew up on his father’s farm in Adams Township, with the post office at Lowell: Benjamin and Margaret, both forty-three in 1860, and the boys — P. J. fifteen, William F. thirteen, and “Jos M” eleven. A brother, John A. Nott, born in 1846, died in 1851, the year Joseph was born, and lies in the Mason cemetery near the village. In the summer of 1859 diphtheria went through Adams Township and carried off a houseful of five-year-olds, among them a Thomas H. Nott, aged five. Joseph, then eight, came through it.

By about 1868 he was at work in a steel mill, and he stayed at it: a heater, fifty-seven years in the trade, last working in 1925. The work took him to Terre Haute, Indiana, about 1881, and he was a resident of the city for the next fifty years. About 1897 he married Martha Ellen (Lamb) Ford, a widow with a young son, Percy; their daughters were Mildred and Helen. The family lived at 3500 Wabash Avenue.

He was not only a mill hand. By the summer of 1915 Joseph Knott of 623 North Ninth Street was one of the City of Terre Haute’s four park superintendents, in charge of Steeg Park; on 1 October 1915, with the formal close of the park season, he and the other three superintendents and nine labourers were dropped from the city payroll. Two days later he was in the witness chair. The city council was taking evidence in the great Terre Haute election-fraud inquiry into Mayor Donn M. Gossom, and “Joseph Knott, of 623 North Ninth street, until recently superintendent of Steeg park, was next called.” He testified that the mayor had asked him to wake him on the morning of the election to go down and organise the board, that Gossom then left the precinct in Knott’s charge and drove off saying “he had a lot off ‘hunkies’ he wanted to run in” — to be picked up “around the Malleable works or stamping mill” — and that Gossom told him that night, “I finished up across the river this evening.”

In November 1914 he and his wife, then living on Rose Avenue, announced their elder daughter Mildred’s engagement to Emmet C. Cooper, and in July 1916 their first grandson was born in their house and went onto the front page of the Tribune as the first war baby born in Terre Haute.

On 1 September 1931, at eighty, he left Terre Haute for Cedar Rapids, Iowa, to live with Mildred — Mrs. E. C. Cooper, of 2505 First Avenue. He had been there four and a half months when he died, in her house at 10:40 in the morning on Friday 15 January 1932, of arteriosclerosis, with a cerebral haemorrhage on the 7th and bronchopneumonia on the 14th among the causes; a doctor had been attending him since 24 October. He left a wife, two daughters and four grandchildren. There was no service in Iowa: the family set off for Terre Haute the next day, and on 18 January the Ryan funeral home buried him at Highland Lawn, Section 14, Lot 386. His flat granite marker reads simply Joseph Knott 1851 1932. Thirteen years later his widow was laid in the same grave, of the same cause, by the same undertaker.

27.s:
Martha Ellen Lamb was born on 27 August 1865 at Richmond, in Wayne County, Indiana, the second of the four children of Erwin R. Lamb and his first wife Melissa J. Bailey. She was ten years old when her mother died at Newport, after a few days’ illness, on the evening of 29 November 1875.

Her father married again in May 1879, to Mary Elizabeth (Jackson) Hall, a Civil War widow with five children of her own, and in 1880 the blended household was living on Main Street in Vermillion, Indiana: Erwin forty, his new wife, “Mattie E.” the eldest girl at home, her brother Frank, her sister Bell, and a nine-year-old stepsister, Effie Hall. Her father eventually left Indiana altogether and died at Jonesboro, Arkansas, in 1919.

She married twice. Her first husband was George Ford, and their son was Percy. By May 1890 she was keeping house as Mrs. Mattie Ford on north Third Street in Terre Haute together with her brother Frank, and her father came down from Plainfield to visit the pair of them. Mattie was what the family called her.

About 1897, at Terre Haute, she married Joseph McGee Knott, a steel-mill heater fourteen years her senior, and had two daughters, Mildred and Helen. One small document in her own hand survives: the back of a real-photo postcard of the two girls, pencilled “My too sweet dauters, Mildred and Helen” and signed “Mama.” The spelling is phonetic, and it is the only specimen of her writing anyone has found.

She and Joseph announced Mildred’s engagement to Emmet C. Cooper in November 1914, and in July 1916 her first grandchild was born in her house. Joseph died in January 1932 at Cedar Rapids, in Mildred’s house; Martha was with him, and the family travelled home to Terre Haute together for the funeral.

Widowed, Martha moved in with her daughter Helen and son-in-law Gifford Tuttle, and was still in that household in 1940 — so Alec’s grandfather, Richard Clark Tuttle, then ten, grew up under the same roof as his grandmother. She died on 18 January 1945 at Terre Haute of a cerebral haemorrhage, aged seventy-nine, and two days later the Ryan funeral home buried her in Highland Lawn Cemetery, Section 14, Lot 386 — the same grave as Joseph, under a flat granite marker matching his: Martha E. Knott 1865 1945.

28.s:
Harry B. Frost was born at Macclesfield in Cheshire, the English silk town, about March 1860, the second son of George Frost and Frances W. Bell, and was baptised Harry Bell Frost in the town’s parochial chapel on 11 April. He was four years old when the family crossed: they came to America in 1864 and settled at Paterson, the silk-weaving capital of the country, built on English hands. He went through the Paterson public schools, finishing at the J. Waters school.

He began work with his father in the throwing business — the twisting of raw silk into yarn — while still a boy. At twenty he was living at 309 Straight Street and working in the silk mill, in a house with his father (fifty-eight, silk manufacturer, rheumatism set down against his name), his mother, a sister and three brothers. That same year, 1880, his father took him and his brother Frank into partnership, and George Frost & Sons built the Albion Mill, a hundred feet of frontage on Madison Street; the firm was the first house in Paterson to bring in the celebrated Atwood machinery. The mill he was taken into was, as it stood in 1887, a long brick block on the north side of Madison Street, Nos. 34 to 52, with GEO. FROST & SONS — SILK THROWING lettered along the pavement, three hundred hands at work in it, one engine of 350 horsepower driving the whole of it, and an artesian well sunk in the yard.

On 10 June 1896, aged thirty-six, giving his trade as silk manufacturer and his home as Paterson, he married at Detroit, Michigan. The bride was Kathaline Chalmers, thirty, a schoolteacher living in Detroit but born at Orange, New Jersey. A pastor named John Reed performed the ceremony, with Mary N. Reed and Edith May Reid as witnesses. Why a Paterson man and a New Jersey woman were married in Michigan nobody in the family can now say.

Three children followed: Katherine King, born in September 1898; Harry Bell, born in Pennsylvania in July 1900; and Alan Chalmers, born at Paterson in February 1903. There was a live-in servant in the house all through those years. About 1908 he moved the family out of the city to Wyckoff Avenue, in Wyckoff, Bergen County, and lived there the last twenty-two years of his life. He was in silk for fifty years — George Frost & Sons, then the Frost & Van Riper Co., with mills at Paterson and at Scranton and Pittston in Pennsylvania — at the end of 1903 the Luzerne County papers noted him as proprietor of his own mill, the West Side Silk Mill at West Pittston — and at the end the Special Rayon Throwing Company. He was a Mason of Joppa Lodge and a life member of Mecca Temple of the Mystic Shrine.

He was ill through the second half of 1930 and died at home on the evening of Thursday 18 December, in his seventy-first year. The funeral was held at the house on the Saturday afternoon at half past two, taken by the rector of St. Paul’s Episcopal Church, Paterson, and the minister of the Wyckoff Reformed Church, and he was buried at Cedar Lawn in Paterson, where his father and his brother Frank already lay. “He was of a kindly and generous disposition,” the Wyckoff paper said, “and was always happiest when he had a group of friends around him.” His widow Katharine outlived him by thirteen months.

29.s:
Katharine Chalmers was born in January 1866 at Orange, in Essex County, New Jersey — East Orange, by one later account — one of the four daughters of Mathew Chalmers, a Scot who had retired from dealing in stores, and Ellen King, also a Scot. She became a schoolteacher, and by 1896 she was living in Detroit; it was there, on 10 June that year, that she married Harry B. Frost of Paterson, an English-born silk manufacturer six years her senior.

She named her children from both sides of the house. Katherine King Frost, born in September 1898, carried her own mother’s maiden name; Harry Bell Frost, born in Pennsylvania in July 1900, carried his father’s mother’s; and Alan Chalmers Frost, born at Paterson in February 1903, carried hers. About 1908 the family left the city for Wyckoff Avenue, in Bergen County, and she lived there for the rest of her life, a quarter of a century.

She was a figure in both towns: second vice-president of the Paterson Woman’s Club in 1930 and, until her death, a member of its board of directors and chairman of its reception committee; a charter member and past president of the Wyckoff Woman’s Club, and chairman of its garden committee, which ran the annual flower shows; an active member of the Wyckoff Reformed Church, and for many years before that of the Baptist church at East Orange, her mother’s denomination. A former schoolteacher, she served several terms on the Wyckoff Board of Education, and the local paper credited her with many improvements in the town’s schools.

Harry died at the house on 18 December 1930, and she was a widow for thirteen months. In January 1932 her youngest son came up from Wilmington for a weekend; three weeks after that she went into the Paterson General Hospital with a short illness, underwent a serious operation, and died there at a quarter to eleven on the night of Sunday 31 January. The service was held the following Wednesday afternoon at the house on Wyckoff Avenue, taken by the curate of St. Paul’s, Paterson, and the Paterson Woman’s Club postponed its regular meeting and went to the funeral in a body. She left a daughter and two sons, and two sisters at East Orange — Mrs. Margaret Jordan and Miss Sarah Chalmers. She was buried at Cedar Lawn in Paterson, beside Harry.

30.s:
John G. Roush was born in September, in 1876 or in 1877 — his gravestone and his birth entry disagree by a year, and the family never settled it — the third son of Moses B. Roush, a Union veteran, and Sarah Duckworth, the daughter of a Lancashire collier. In 1880 he was down as a two-year-old in his parents’ house in Sutton Township, Meigs County, Ohio. He was three when his mother died, and his father took the four children across the river into Mason County, West Virginia.

On 22 February 1897 he took out a licence at the Mason County courthouse to marry Bertha Ellen Nease. He gave his age as twenty and hers as eighteen; the man who swore the information was her own father, L. J. Nease. They were married two days later at the Evangelical Lutheran parsonage at New Haven by the Rev. D. W. Files. By June 1900 the young family were at Hartford village in Graham District, a few doors from his father Moses, with two small daughters, Nola and a baby.

He was not only a miner — he had been in the insurance business at Mason — but about September 1907 he moved his family to Broad Run to work in Claude Ryan’s mine below Hartford. A year later, at about seven on the evening of Saturday 12 September 1908, Bertha had been baking and a gallon oil can stood near the hot stove. He set a miner’s lamp on the table where a daughter was ironing, and in trying to fill the lamp from the can touched off an explosion that threw burning oil in every direction. The girl was enveloped in flames and died within a few hours; a second daughter died five days later at New Haven; the house burned with everything in it. His fellow workmen gave up a day’s wages for the family and the mine operator gave fifteen dollars.

He was badly burned, worst about the legs, and nobody expected him to live. He died on 21 October 1908 in Graham District of the effects of the burns, certified by Dr. D. A. Sayre — a married coal miner of thirty-two. The Weekly Register gave him a paragraph two weeks afterwards: “John D. Roush, who was injured several weeks ago at Broad Run, near Hartford, by the explosion of a lamp, died last week from injuries received at that time.” It got his initial wrong, and it said he left “a wife and two children”; in fact three daughters survived him and a fourth was born after his death. In May 1909 his widow qualified in the Mason County court as guardian of “Iva Roush, Florence Roush, Velm Roush and Della Roush, infant children of John G. Roush, deceased,” on a $500 bond, with his father Moses standing surety.

He lies at Broad Run Cemetery under a low granite marker that says only FATHER, and the years 1876 - 1908.

31.s:
Bertha Ellen Nease was born on 12 January 1878 in Mason County, West Virginia, the eldest child of Lewis J. Nease, a farmer, and Martha Jane Love, who had married the April before.

On 22 February 1897, at eighteen, she took out a marriage licence with John G. Roush at the Mason County courthouse, her father giving the clerk her age and birthplace, and two days later they were married at the Evangelical Lutheran parsonage at New Haven. She was marrying back into her own grandmother’s family: her father’s mother had been born a Roush.

By 1900 the couple were keeping house at Hartford village with two small daughters, a few doors from John’s father. In 1907 they moved to Broad Run so that John could go into the mine. On the evening of 12 September 1908 Bertha had been baking when the oil can by the stove took fire; she fought the flames and was burned about the hands and arms. Her eldest daughter died that night, a second five days later, and her husband on 21 October. The house, the furniture and the family’s clothes were all gone, and she was carrying another child.

She did not go back to either set of grandparents. In May 1909 she went to the Mason County court and qualified as guardian of her four daughters on a $500 bond, her father-in-law Moses Roush standing surety. In April 1910 she was the head of her own household at Wagner, Mason County — a widow of thirty-three with Iva Mae, Florence, Velma and the baby Claudia under her roof. On 2 March 1914 she married William L. Knopp at Mason City, he thirty-two and she thirty-four, by the Rev. C. H. Cox of the Church of the United Brethren in Christ. In March 1947, when she was ill at Mason, two of her daughters travelled down from Akron and Indiana to see her.

Bertha Ellen Knopp died on 5 April 1950 at St. Joseph’s Hospital, Parkersburg, aged seventy-one, her home still at Mason, West Virginia. Her daughter Iva buried her at Broad Run on 7 April, under a stone cut MOTHER / BERTHA E. ROUSH KNOPP / 1878 - 1950: she carried both her husbands’ names to the grave.
