32.s:
John T. Bell was born on 10 June 1841 in Barbour County, Alabama, eleven years after his parents came down from South Carolina. As his obituary put it, “his parents moved to Alabama from Darlington, S. C., about 1830, and settled in the neighborhood where he lived at his death” — and he never left that neighbourhood in seventy-four years. He married Sarah Ann “Sallie” Cox in March 1861, weeks before the war, and they raised eleven children, of whom eight outlived him.

He went to war that spring. He joined the Barbour Grays, which became part of the 5th Alabama Infantry, and served in Company A under Captain Eugene Blackford of Lynchburg, Virginia, in Rodes’ brigade, later as a sharpshooter in Jackson’s corps. His first child, his obituary says, was born on the very day he left for the front, “and leaving his young wife and child behind, he went bravely to the call of duty.” He was wounded and sent home in the autumn of 1864, and set out for Virginia again in late March 1865. The sketch his family gave to Thomas Owen’s Dictionary of Alabama Biography tells the war as they remembered it: from First Bull Run to the surrender at Appomattox, through Seven Pines, the Seven Days, South Mountain, Sharpsburg, Fredericksburg, Gettysburg, the Wilderness, Winchester and Strasburg, and nine more battles between 4 May and 9 June 1864. He was, it says, “wounded in the hand about half an hour before Stonewall Jackson met his death, and was taken to the same hospital in which the general died,” wounded in both legs at Strasburg, and at the Wilderness “he and a single comrade were the only ones who broke through the ranks of the surrounding enemy.” After the peace he came home to Barbour County and to farming.

He farmed, and he prospered, on a place six miles south of Clayton that was known on the map simply as Bell’s. On 8 July 1867, with the Reconstruction acts new on the statute book, he came in to Precinct No. 11 and registered as a qualified voter, and the clerk wrote him down White. In April 1888 he and Sallie sold a right of way across their land to the Eufaula & East Alabama Railway. He was a Freemason of thirty-two years’ standing, raised to the sublime degree of Master Mason in Royal White Hart Lodge No. 10 on 16 March 1883; when the lodge met a fortnight after his death to pass resolutions of respect, it regretted that the distance he lived from town and his last illness had kept him from its meetings. The town he traded in had been mapped for the insurance companies in February 1910, five years before he died: three cotton warehouses on the Public Square — J. C. Thomas’s, the Alliance’s and the Farmers Union’s — the court hall and fire department, the Fryer Hotel, the post office, and a water works and electric light plant beside the Central of Georgia tracks.

Sallie died at home in March 1910, and the county paper called him John T. Bell, Sr., for by then his eldest son was a man of standing in Clayton in his own right. By that year he was sixty-nine and living in his son Ben T.’s household, in his son Tom’s own precinct. He died at his house on 6 November 1915. His sons told the court that what he left consisted “chiefly of lands, cotton, insurance and money, all of said real and personal estate being estimated to be worth about fifty thousand dollars” — something like a million and a half in modern money, to be divided among ten children’s and grandchildren’s lines.

His will names his children in his own voice: “I give, devise and bequeath to my beloved children John T. Bell, Jr., Mack Bell, Will A. Bell, Sallie Stallings, Ed Bell, Tom Bell, Mary McPherson and Ben F. Bell.” Letters testamentary were granted on 19 November 1915 by Thomas D. Grubbs, judge of probate, to four of those sons — John T. Jr., Mack, Will A. and Ben F. — who advertised for claims against the estate in the Clayton Record three weeks running that winter. The eldest, John T. Bell Jr., became an undertaker at Clayton and buried a good many of his neighbours, including his own uncle William nine years later. The Tom of that list is Thomas Jefferson Bell, and he is the step in Alec’s own line; he died six years after his father, leaving nothing at all to administer.

He lies at Bethlehem Baptist churchyard inside a low wrought-iron rail, under a marble shaft whose pediment is carved with the square and compasses of the Freemasons. Sallie’s stone stands a few feet from his across the same plot.

33.s:
Sarah Ann Cox — Sallie — was born on 24 August 1841 in Barbour County, Alabama, and married John T. Bell there on 7 March 1861. He was twenty, she was nineteen, and the war began the month after the wedding. Two of the thirteen people who had founded Bethlehem Baptist Church up the road in April 1824 were a William and an Elizabeth Cox, though whether they were hers nobody knows.

She had eleven children and raised them on the farm known as Bell’s, six miles south of Clayton. Eight outlived their father and were named in his will — six sons and two daughters; one of the sons was Thomas Jefferson Bell, and a daughter married in 1886 was named Sallie for her. In April 1888 she put her name beside her husband’s on the deed selling a right of way to the Eufaula & East Alabama Railway, giving up her dower in some forty-six acres of it as a wife had to do. She signed it Sarah A Bell.

Her photograph survives, and it is the oldest likeness of anyone on the Bell side of this family: an oval vignette of an old woman with white hair swept up and a lace jabot at the throat of a dark dress, on an embossed cream cabinet-card mount that somebody in the family labelled in blue ink — “Mrs. John T. Bell. Mother of Sallie Bell Stallings.”

She died on the morning of Friday 11 March 1910, five years before John, at home, after what the county paper called a long and “linquering” illness — a stroke, the Montgomery paper said, that had left her paralysed for more than a year. Her daughter Sallie, Mrs. W. O. Stallings, had come from Montgomery and was at her bedside. The Montgomery paper put her home at Pratt’s Station, on the Eufaula and Ozark road, and said she had reared seven sons and two daughters, all grown and married. Under the headline AGED LADY DIES NEAR CLAYTON it called her “one of the most estimable and widely known women in the county … a lady who has raised a large family and maintained the high respect and goodwill of all who knew her,” and said she was survived by her husband, many children, grandchildren and some great-grandchildren. The funeral was preached at Bethlehem church by her former pastor, the Rev. W. R. Bickerstaff of Florala, and she was buried in the adjoining cemetery. Her headstone stands beside her husband’s inside the Bells’ iron-railed plot — a white marble tablet under a carved egg-and-dart band — and it gives her no surname at all: SALLIE A., WIFE OF J. T. BELL.

36.s:
Joseph William Eakins — “Joel W.” on most of the paper and “William J.” on some of it — was born in December 1838 or 1839 in New Hanover County, North Carolina, a son of John Eakins Sr. and Nancy Costin. In 1850 he was twelve, one of nine children in his father’s house on the Moores Creek land the family had farmed since before the Constitution was ratified.

By the end of the 1850s the family’s reach had extended to Lauderdale County, Mississippi, where an uncle, William Eakins, had already settled, and where four orphaned Eakens boys born in North Carolina were being raised in the household of William Payne. On 13 May 1861, a month after the war began, Joel married Payne’s daughter Sarah Hudson Payne. The marriage happened inside a house that had already fused the two families for a decade.

Two of his North Carolina kin went the other way that same May: his brother John J. B. Eakins and his cousin Owen J. enlisted at Lower Black River in the Moore’s Creek Rifle Guards, Company E of the 18th North Carolina, and both were dead within two years — John at Sharpsburg, Owen at Chancellorsville.

He and Sarah farmed in Lauderdale County and had ten or more children. By 1880 the house held Mary A., Ada J., Jno. N., Minnie, Cassie E., Orgun, Joel P., Nancy and the newborn Andrew J.; a son Sam came later. Two of those names, Orgun and Joel, were Sarah’s own younger brothers’ names, carried over from the Payne household she had grown up in. In 1900, asked for his particulars, he gave his birth as December 1838, his birthplace as North Carolina and his marriage as 1861.

He died in 1902 in Mississippi, probably in Lauderdale County in the June of that year. His other lasting mark on the family was a piece of handwriting: he stopped dotting the “i” in Eakins, and his descendants have been Eakens, and then Eaken, ever since.

37.s:
Sarah Hudson Payne was born on 2 May 1842 in Mississippi, and grew up in Lauderdale County in a crowded house. William Payne, who headed it, was fifty-seven in 1850 and Virginia born; his wife Mary was thirty and born in North Carolina; four boys born in North Carolina and carrying the Eakens name, aged ten to sixteen, the fatherless sons of Andrew Eakin, whose property William Payne managed for them; and four younger children had been born in Mississippi, of whom Sarah was the eldest. Two of the little ones were called Origon and Joel. Whether William Payne was her father or her stepfather has never been settled.

What is certain is the household — and what came of it. On 13 May 1861 she married Joseph William “Joel W.” Eakins, who bore the same surname as the orphaned boys who had grown up under that roof.

They farmed in Lauderdale County for forty years. She bore ten or more children: Mary A., Ada J., John N., Minnie, Cassie, Nancy, a Sam, and two she named Orgun and Joel after the little boys she had been raised with. Her youngest, Andrew Jackson Eaken, born in 1880 or 1881, is the one through whom the line runs down to Alec.

She died on 1 May 1908, one day short of her sixty-sixth birthday. Her stone still stands over her in a fenced Mississippi burying ground, a leaning white marble obelisk behind a chain-link fence: SARAH H. EAKINS, BORN May 2, 1842, DIED May 1, 1908, AGE 65 Yrs 11 Mos & 29 Days. Her middle name, Hudson, has never been explained, and her mother’s name is not known.

38.s:
Joseph Lee Swain was born on 23 December 1861, the eldest child of Joseph Tolbert Swain and Nancy E. Jane, who had married in Lauderdale County, Mississippi, the year before. He was four or five when his parents crossed the state line into Sumter County, Alabama in the first months after the war, and he grew up at Cuba; in 1880, at nineteen, he stood at the head of a row of eight younger brothers and sisters.

He married twice over, and buried a wife in between. On 10 February 1884 he married Eugenia Simmons, with J. M. Patton the minister — and a son of his would be named Patton. A wife called Leila Eugenia died before the end of 1885 and lies in the churchyard at Salem Baptist, across the line in Lauderdale County, Mississippi, under a stone that gives 1861–1885 and calls her “wife of J. L. Swain”; whether she was the bride of 1884 nobody now knows. Then on 23 December 1885, his own twenty-fourth birthday, he married the woman the register enters as Rebecca A. D. Simmons and everyone else called Dillon. The minister that day was D. C. Langford, and they named a son for him too: Joseph Langford Swain.

They farmed at York and Cuba. In 1900 the children at home were Leila, Patton, Maggie, Kirkland, Pinky and Langford, and he gave his years married as sixteen — counting, it seems, from the first wedding rather than the second. In November 1905 he sold a hundred and sixty acres at the post-office door at Cuba as administrator of the estate of J. T. Swain, very probably his own father, dead the year before. He stood for public office as well: at a meeting of the voters of the third commissioners district at Livingston on 28 August 1911 the vote went fifty-seven to twenty-seven in his favour, and in September he announced himself from Cuba as a candidate for county commissioner, “subject to the action of the Democratic party.” The Livingston paper thought he would make a good commissioner.

Five of their children lie in the family burying ground at Salem Baptist, and the dates make a hard chapter of their life: Marvin, dead at two in 1892; Fletcher, dead at two in 1905; and then Patton, dead at nineteen in January 1916, Lucille Kirkland, dead at eighteen in January 1917, and Myrtle, dead at sixteen the following month. Three grown children in thirteen months.

Cuba, as it stood in 1928, was laid out building by building along one street: the Walker-Shaw planing mill and saw mill at one end, a grist mill and feed store, G. W. McElroy’s blacksmith and carpenter shop, the Cuba Mercantile Co., the Southern Railway depot with its covered platform, a Methodist church and two Holiness churches.

He lived out his life on the land three miles west of York, near the old McConnell Station — a six-room house on twenty acres, with running water and a telephone. He died there at a quarter to one on the afternoon of Thursday 21 November 1940, aged seventy-nine, after a long illness, and the funeral was held in the house the next afternoon. He left his widow, “Mrs. Dillon Simmons Swain,” four daughters — Leila Collier of Meridian, Maggie Bloebaum of Wheaton, Illinois, Pinkie McElroy of Fort Knox and Merle Cobb of Geiger — one son, Langford of Cuba, a brother, John M. Swain of York, and two sisters, Mattie Shamburger and Laura McDonald. A week later the widow and all five surviving children signed a card of thanks to their neighbours, styling him Mr. Joe L. Swain, Sr. He was buried at Salem Baptist; his stone gives his name as JOE L. SWAIN and, under the dates, one word: PAPA.

39.s:
Dillon Simmons was born on 1 December 1863 in Sumter County, Alabama, a daughter of Ben and Adeline Simmons of Cuba. At sixteen she was still at home in her father’s house, her name written down “Dellon.”

She married Joseph L. Swain of the same small village on 23 December 1885; the register entered her as Rebecca A. D. Simmons, but Dillon is what she was called all her life. He had been married before, and an earlier wife, Leila Eugenia, had died by the end of that year. The Swains farmed at York and Cuba, three miles out near the old McConnell Station, in a six-room house on twenty acres. In 1900 she had six children at home: Leila, Patton, Maggie, Kirkland, Pinky and Langford.

Five of her children lie in the churchyard at Salem Baptist, across the state line in Lauderdale County, Mississippi: two who died as infants, and Patton, Lucille Kirkland and Myrtle, who died grown within thirteen months of one another in 1916 and 1917. Her husband’s obituary of November 1940 named her in print as “his wife, Mrs. Dillon Simmons Swain,” and when her son Joseph Langford Swain died at New Orleans in 1946 she was named as his mother, Dillon Simmons. In May 1951 her Wheaton daughter came down to visit her, and the county paper called her Mrs. Dillon Swain.

Her daughter Maggie Dillon Swain carried her name forward, and it travelled two more generations as a middle name nobody could explain.

She outlived her husband by twelve years and died on 1 November 1952, aged eighty-eight; her four daughters thanked their neighbours in the Sumter County Journal a fortnight later for their kindness “during the illness and passing of our precious mother.” She left a will, and on 6 February 1953 Judge Wilbur E. Dearman of the Sumter County probate court granted letters testamentary on it to three of her daughters — Maggie S. Bloebaum, Pinkie S. McElroy and Merle S. Cobb — who published the notice to creditors through that February and March. She lies beside her husband at Salem Baptist under a matching stone: DILLON S. SWAIN, DEC. 1, 1863 – NOV. 1, 1952, and beneath the dates, answering his PAPA, the single word MAMA.

40.s:
Caswell Massey Stephens was born on 8 January 1852, in Sumter County, Alabama by the family’s reckoning, though a later hand put his birth in Mississippi. He was the son of Henry H. Stephens, a farmer and Minister of the Gospel, and Sarah Ann Jones. He was named at the very least for a neighbour: in 1850 a twenty-four-year-old North Carolina man called Caswell Massey farmed the dwelling that stood between the Stephens house and the Joneses’, though whether he was kin to either family nobody knows. His mother died before he was three, and his father married her sister Elizabeth in October 1854. By 1860 the family had moved to Newton County, Mississippi, where he was eight.

On the last day of 1869, not yet eighteen, he stood in the Sumter County probate court before Judge J. A. Abrahams, said he was over fourteen, and chose his own father as his guardian: he and his brothers Calvin and John were the “minor heirs of Daniel Jones deceased,” their mother’s father, and his bond was set at $800. There was enough property in it that his father was still filing annual settlements two years later.

In October 1871, aged nineteen, he married a widow thirteen years his senior, and his own father performed the ceremony. The register enters her as “Mrs. A. M. James”; her gravestone never gives her a first name either, calling her only A. M., wife of C. M. Stephens. The family remembers her as Ava Marilla Shelton. Their children included Martha Alice, born 14 April 1874, who married John William Knight, and John Willis, born 12 March 1876; a son Rufus L. belongs to one marriage or the other. She died on 8 January 1891 — his thirty-ninth birthday — and on 19 April that year he married again, near Cuba. The county paper gave the whole of it in eleven words: “Married — Near Cuba, on the 19th, Mr C M Stephens and Mrs I Dearman.” The bride was Isabella, a Britt by birth and a Dearman by her first marriage, and she was about forty-five. She died in 1917.

He farmed all his life. At twenty-three he registered to vote in Precinct No. 5 of Sumter County on 19 June 1875, entry 67, signing “C M Stephens” in his own hand and giving his occupation, like almost every man on the page, as farmer. In old age he was at Halsell, in Choctaw County, just over the Sumter line. In May 1928 his son Rufus died at Livingston without a will, leaving about a thousand dollars, and the only heir was “The Father Caswell M Stephens of Livingston Ala., age 76 years,” who declined to administer it.

A photograph kept in the family as him shows a bearded old man in wire spectacles and a dark coat, sitting on a huge heap of split firewood with a small fair-haired child in a white dress leaning against his knee — said to be his granddaughter Clara Mae.

He died a widower at eight o’clock on the morning of Sunday 10 February 1935, aged eighty-three, after a short illness, at the home of his daughter Mrs. Alice Knight; his stone was cut a week out, with the 17th. The Sumter County Journal ran the notice on its front page. Funeral services were at eleven on the Monday at Siloam Church, Revs. Ezell and Dearman officiating, and he was buried in the church cemetery at Siloam, where his first wife had lain forty-four years. He left two sons, J. W. of Livingston and H. R. of Halsell, one daughter, two brothers — Bob Stephens of Kewanee and Bill Stephens of Cuba — and thirteen grandchildren and fifteen great-grandchildren.

41.s:
The woman the family remembers as Ava Marilla Shelton was born on 21 November 1839, in Mississippi or Alabama, and in her own lifetime the records give her only initials: her gravestone calls her A. M., and the marriage register Mrs. A. M. James. The name comes back half a century later, when her son John Willis died in 1947 and his death record named his mother as Rilla Shelton — Rilla for Marilla.

She came to Caswell Massey Stephens a widow with a child. The family’s account is that her first husband was Isaac James, born about 1839 in Franklin County, Alabama, who went to the war in Company C of the 27th Mississippi Infantry and seems not to have come home, leaving her a daughter, Dartha, born about 1863.

On 2 October 1871, at thirty-one, she married again — to a farmer’s son of nineteen, thirteen years her junior, whose own father performed the ceremony. The Sumter County register entered it in a line: “C. M. Stephens · A. M. James · Married by H. H. Stephens, Minister.” With Caswell she had Martha Alice, born 14 April 1874, and John Willis, born 12 March 1876, and probably others.

She died on 8 January 1891, her husband’s thirty-ninth birthday, aged fifty-one. He remarried near Cuba fifteen weeks later. She lies at Siloam Cemetery in Sumter County under a marble headstone carved with a dove above a spray of flowers — In memory of A. M., wife of C. M. Stephens, born Nov. 21, 1839, died Jan. 8, 1891 — and below the dates four lines of verse, now so weathered that they can only be guessed at: Sleep on dear one in Jesus’ arms / Secure from all the world’s alarms / Sweet be thy rest in mansions above / Safe in the arms of his infinite love. Her husband’s flat granite marker lies in the grass beside her.

42.s:
Francis R. Williams lived on the Mississippi side of the Alabama line, in the strip of pine country where Greene and Clarke Counties meet. The family’s account gives his name in full as Francis Roundtree Williams, born in February 1840 and dead in April 1907. He told the 1900 census-taker that he was born in Alabama, to a father from Georgia and a mother from North Carolina.

He married Mary J. Lewis, and they raised a large family in that border country. Ira J. was born in 1870; their daughter Mary Price was born at State Line, in Greene County, on 18 March 1887 — a railroad village that takes its name from sitting flat on the Alabama border. In 1900 he was keeping house in Beat 3 of Clarke County, Mississippi, with Mary J. and four of the children still at home: Mary Price, Jesse F., Etta S. and Knox A. Others were Lizzie, who married L. L. Craig, and H. H. Williams.

His children scattered across the Gulf South as they grew — Gulfport, Pascagoula, Laurel, Hattiesburg, Meridian, Jackson, Baton Rouge, Washington — and in 1906 Mary Price crossed the line into Sumter County, Alabama, to marry J. W. Stephens. His own parents are not known.

43.s:
Mary J. Lewis married Francis R. Williams and spent her life with him in Greene and Clarke Counties, Mississippi, on the Alabama line. The family’s account calls her Mary Lucy Jane Lewis and gives her birth in 1848 and her death on 2 February 1934; in 1900 she gave July 1851, in Alabama, with both her parents born in Georgia.

She bore a large family. Ira J. came in 1870; Mary Price was born at State Line, in Greene County, on 18 March 1887 and carried her mother’s maiden name into her own records all her life. In 1900 she was “Mary J. Williams,” keeping house in Beat 3 of Clarke County with her husband and four children — Mary Price, Jesse F., Etta S. and Knox A. Lizzie, who married L. L. Craig, and H. H. Williams were hers too, and her grown children ended up spread from Gulfport and Pascagoula to Baton Rouge and Washington. Her own parents are not known.

She outlived her husband by twenty-seven years. She died on 2 February 1934, aged eighty-two, at the home of her daughter Mrs. M. C. Childress on Tenth Avenue in Hattiesburg, and the pastor of the Fifth Avenue Baptist church buried her in the city’s Old City cemetery. Nine of her children survived her — from Livingston, Alabama, and Gulfport to Meridian, Laurel and Baton Rouge — with thirty-three grandchildren and forty-six great-grandchildren.

44.s:
William Curtis Truett was born on 25 July 1867, the son of John Wesley Truett and Emily Caroline Ward, and grew up at Chilton in Clarke County, Alabama, in a house that held three generations at once: his father, a Confederate veteran who could not write his own name; his mother; his brothers and his sister; and his grandmother Alcey, the widow of the preacher William Hampton Truett, who was sixty-seven in 1880 and living under her son’s roof.

On 17 June 1886, not yet nineteen, he married Amanda Webb in Clarke County. They farmed at Clarksville, and by the summer of 1900 there were six children in the house — Tela, Jane, Bigy, Lillie, Tamie and the baby Bessie. Bessie and Jane were still living in 1960, when his second wife’s obituary named them as her step-daughters — Mrs. Bessie Shewmake of Satsuma and Mrs. Jane Hutchinson of Juniper, Georgia. He and Amanda could both read and write, which neither his father nor his grandmother could do: the first literate generation on this line. Thomas William, the “Tamie” of that household, was Alec’s great-grandfather.

Amanda was alive in that house in June 1900 and dead or gone not long after, and he married a second time, to Zella Shewmake, born 1 June 1878.

He farmed at New Prospect, a settlement whose little Baptist church had been constituted about 1860 by an Elder C. J. Miles, who for his trouble was paid “one dollar per day while in active service.” When the county’s thirty-four Baptist churches were apportioned in 1892, New Prospect was asked for sixteen dollars — near the smallest sum in the county. All the places of his life sat within a few miles of one another: Chilton, where he grew up; Clarksville, where he farmed in middle life; and New Prospect, with Harris Creek running between them.

Two Truett brothers married two Webb sisters — he took Amanda, and his younger brother John Wesley took Valley. That brother died at his home in Coffeeville on a Wednesday morning in February 1936, of pneumonia after a few days’ illness, and was buried at Prospect church, the Rev. T. C. Paul of Grove Hill officiating. By then the family had scattered: a brother George and a sister, Sarah Giger, were both in Florida, where their mother had gone as an old woman.

He died at New Prospect on 21 December 1925, aged fifty-eight, and is buried in the church graveyard under a low double marker of pale granite, TRUETT across the top, his own name on the right and Zella’s on the left. She outlived him by thirty-five years, and the stone was almost certainly cut when she joined him in 1960. Amanda, the mother of his eldest son, is not on it, and is not buried there.

45.s:
Amanda Webb was born in July 1868 in Alabama and married William Curtis Truett in Clarke County on 17 June 1886, when she was not quite eighteen and he not quite nineteen.

They farmed at Clarksville. By the summer of 1900 she was thirty-one and fourteen years married, and had borne six children, all six living and all six in the house with her: Tela, thirteen; Jane, twelve; Bigy, ten; Lillie, eight; Tamie, six; and Bessie, one. Tamie — Thomas William, born that September of 1893 — is the one Alec descends from. She and her husband could both read and write, which neither his father nor his grandmother could do.

She was alive in that house in June 1900, and after that nothing of her survives: no death date, and no grave anywhere. Her husband married again, to Zella Shewmake, and it is Zella’s name, not hers, on the other half of his gravestone at New Prospect.

The Webbs were old Clarke County people. A William Webb came into the county about 1812 and died at his home there in February 1853 at about seventy-eight; the Webb mill on the Tallahatta was built about 1836; and Webbs were among the families forted up at McGrew’s Fort in the Indian troubles of 1810. Whether Amanda belonged to them is not known.

46.s:
Sennie Lawrence’s father was born in Alabama in September 1860, to a father from North Carolina and a mother from South Carolina. His given name has never been settled. The hand that wrote it down in 1900 reads “Calm,” and what it was meant to be nobody knows.

He married Eliza about 1888 — they had been married twelve years when they were counted in 1900 — and they farmed at Coffeeville in Clarke County. Five children were in the house that year: Tomas N., eleven; Sallie E., nine; Mary E., six; Senie E., three; and Alfonso, entered as nought days old, because the enumerator had called on the day the baby was born. Two more followed, Lucy about 1905 among them.

He was not an old Clarke County man. The county’s history of 1882 names hundreds of its families across seven hundred and eighty pages and has no Lawrences in it at all, so his people must have come in from somewhere nearby — Washington or Choctaw or Marengo — recently enough to be strangers; the name is written Larance as readily as Lawrence.

By 1910 he was gone from the household: Eliza was head of the house with six children and no husband in it. A C. J. Lawrence who was very probably him died near Jackson, in Clarke County, in February 1929 — a widower, seventy-two years old by the clerk’s reckoning, born in Monroe County, Alabama — and was buried at Coffeeville.

He is very probably buried at Ulcanush Cemetery in Coffeeville, the same ground as his daughter Sennie and his infant son Alphonso, under one of two home-made markers that stand side by side there: slabs of rough concrete with the lettering scratched into them with a nail while the cement was still wet. His gives only initials, C J Lawrence. The other gives no name at all, only Mrs Lawrence, and a birth year that is his wife’s to the year.

Eliza was born in Alabama about 1863 or 1864 and married, about 1888, a Clarke County farmer named Lawrence whose given name nobody has been able to read — the hand that wrote it in 1900 gives “Calm.” They farmed at Coffeeville, and in 1900 she was thirty-six with five children in the house: Tomas N., Sallie E., Mary E., Senie E., and a baby, Alfonso, who was nought days old when the enumerator called. Two more followed, Lucy about 1905 among them — seven children in all.

By 1910 her husband had gone, and she was head of the household: “Elizon A. Larance,” with six children under her roof and no man in it. She kept them together for at least another decade.

She died in 1927, in her early sixties. At Ulcanush Cemetery in Coffeeville — the ground where her son Alphonso and her daughter Sennie lie — stands a marker that is very probably hers: a slab of rough concrete, the lettering scratched in by hand while it was still wet, reading Mrs Lawrence · Born 1864 · Died 1927. The 1864 is the year her own age gives. The stone does not give her name. What is written on it, and has been for a hundred years, is the word Mrs.

The index of the Clarke County death register gives her maiden name as Shoemake and names her mother as a woman called Polly Hutto; it records that she died at Coffeeville on 29 January 1927 and was buried at Ulcanush Church the next day. That comes from the index, not from the certificate itself, which has not been read.

The censuses fit that record. In 1870 a girl called E. A. C. Shoemake, eight years old, was living at Webbs Mill in Clarke County with J. M. and Mary A. Shoemake. In 1880, in Choctaw County, “Eliza A. C.,” nineteen and still at school, is entered as the daughter of Jefferson M. Shoemake and his wife Mary A.

48.s:
Richard B. Tuttle was born on 24 March 1858 at Tuttle’s Mills, in Otter Creek Township, Vigo County, Indiana, the fourth child of Clark Strong Tuttle and his second wife Nancy A. Harbert. He grew up in a prosperous miller’s house, with three hired hands and a servant living in, and with an older brother named Dennis — the name he would one day give his own son.

He followed his father’s trade and was a miller himself, but by the time he was grown the mill had gone: his father sold the 117-acre mill tract in July 1870, dissolved the firm a fortnight later, and was out of the township altogether by the autumn.

On 12 October 1881, at twenty-three, he married Emma S. Fuerstenberger, the daughter of a Bavarian shoemaker in Terre Haute. Some time in the next two years the young couple went to Peoria, Illinois, where their son Dennis Clark Tuttle was born on 25 January 1884; why they were there is not known. The Terre Haute they came home to is the city of the bird’s-eye view drawn in 1880 — the grid of streets running back from the Wabash, the bridges, the mills along the river and the Normal School on its square.

He was dead before the year was out. Consumption took him on the morning of Wednesday 17 December 1884, at twenty-six, and the funeral was held at ten the next morning from his father-in-law Frank Fuerstenberger’s house at 521 South Third Street. No gravestone for him is known.

49.s:
Emma S. Fuerstenberger was born at Terre Haute, Indiana, in July 1863, the fifth of the eight children of Francis Fuerstenberger, a Bavarian shoemaker, and his Pennsylvania-born wife Sophia. She grew up in the one house her father occupied for forty years, 521 South Third Street, and was still at home there at seventeen.

On 12 October 1881, at eighteen, she married Richard B. Tuttle, a young miller. Their son Dennis Clark Tuttle was born at Peoria, Illinois, on 25 January 1884, and in December of that year Richard died of consumption in her father’s house. She was twenty-one, with a baby.

She married twice more: Hamilton B. Martin on 24 May 1891, and then, on 20 December 1894 at Charleston in Coles County, Illinois, Gifford H. Spear. It was Spear who finished raising her son, and the son repaid him by naming his own firstborn Gifford. In September 1916 she and Gifford Spear were living at 512 North Eighth Street in Terre Haute and had just come home from a month’s holiday in California.

Her elder sister Anna had married James H. Jumper at Terre Haute on 11 October 1876, before H. E. Wulzen, pastor of the German Methodist Episcopal church, with John Fuerstenberger signing as witness — the Fuerstenbergers were a German Methodist family five years before Emma’s own wedding. The Bible the Jumpers kept held what families keep: a slip of receipt paper noting which minister had baptised which child and, in a small white paper bag, some of young Elmer’s hair.

She died on 9 April 1926 as Emma S. Spear. The family Bible enters the death under that name, with “Tuttle” pencilled faintly above it — somebody wanting the record to remember which husband she belonged to. Eight years later her son stood in her place when a Fuerstenberger estate was divided five ways among her brothers’ and sisters’ lines.

51.s:
Mary Elizabeth Fletcher was born in Indiana on 21 September 1858, the daughter of John Fletcher and Sarah Wallace. Where the family lived while she was growing up is not known.

She surfaces at Clinton, in Vermillion County, in 1880, aged twenty-three, single, and living in another family’s house as a “houseworker” — a domestic servant. A year later, on 16 June 1881, she married William L. Alexander of the same small town, and in February 1883 their daughter Leona was born. She bore one child and one only.

She was a widow by 1900, and she had not gone under. That June she was at 314 Mulberry Street in Terre Haute, forty years old, head of her own household, working as a housekeeper and owning the house — with her seventeen-year-old daughter beside her. By December 1902 she had moved to North Sixth Street, and it was in her house that her only child was married. After that she moved in with Leona and Dennis Tuttle and stayed for the rest of her life, more than thirty years under her daughter’s roof. She was still travelling with them in 1914, going out to West Terre Haute for the weekend in August and again in September.

In October 1910 her grandson Gifford’s seventh-birthday cake was a present from the boy’s grandmother, and she, living in the house, is the likelier of his two grandmothers to have baked it.

She died just after four o’clock on the afternoon of 16 April 1934, at the Tuttles’ place on the rural route out of Terre Haute at East Glenn, in Lost Creek Township, aged seventy-five. Her heart had been failing for twenty years. It was Leona who gave the particulars for the certificate — her mother’s birthday, and the names of the grandparents she had never known, John Fletcher and Sarah Wallace. She was buried at Highland Lawn two days later. The family Bible records it simply: “Mary Elizabeth Alexander (1934).”

56.s:
George Frost was born at Macclesfield in Cheshire in the spring of 1822 and baptised there that July, the son of George Frost, a silkman, and his wife Sarah, a Somerset woman from Bridgwater — a family “engaged largely in the silk manufacture.” He entered the trade himself in 1838, while still in his early boyhood, and his department from the first was throwing — the twisting of raw silk into yarn.

By March 1851, at twenty-eight, he was already a widower, a journeyman silk throwster living in his mother’s house in Oxford Road with three small children of the family, Eliza Ann, Mary Elizabeth and George Thomas Hatton. He was still a widower, with a son and a daughter, when on 10 June 1857, at thirty-five, he married Frances Wright Bell, twenty-five, in Prestbury parish church, after banns. Both gave their residence as Macclesfield; he was a silk throwster like his father, George Frost, and her father, Nathaniel Bell, a silk manufacturer, stood witness and signed the register. Their children included Mary; Frank, born at 6 Lord Street, Macclesfield, on 4 April 1858 and baptised at the Wesleyan chapel on Park Green; Harry Bell, baptised at Macclesfield in April 1860; Maurice and Charlie, baptised together in July 1863, by which time George had become a trimming manufacturer. Charlie lived only five months and was buried at Christ Church that December; a later son, born in America, was given his name, and was Charles, the youngest, in the Paterson census of 1880. The family came over in 1864 and settled at Paterson, and he commenced business in this country about 1870 with but four hands.

By June 1880 he was at 309 Straight Street, Paterson, fifty-eight years old, a silk manufacturer with rheumatism, and two of his sons were working in the mill. That year he took Frank and Harry B. into partnership, and George Frost & Sons built the Albion Mill, with a frontage of a hundred feet on Madison Street and, as one visitor put it, “an air of taste too rarely seen in factory buildings.” They threw yarn exclusively on commission, and were the first house in Paterson to install the celebrated Atwood machinery. By the middle eighties the firm was advertising from 36 to 52 Madison Street as makers of “Organzine, Tram, Floss, etc. On Commission,” and in September 1885 a fire in Straight Street singed the back of a new mill they were putting up.

The Albion Mill in 1887 was a long brick block on the north side of Madison Street, running from No. 34 to No. 52, with GEO. FROST & SONS — SILK THROWING lettered along the pavement. Reeling was done on the first floor, spinning on the first and second, winding and doubling on the third, winding on the fourth, and there was a carpenter’s repair shop in the basement. One engine of 350 horsepower drove the whole of it, an artesian well was sunk in the yard, and about three hundred hands worked there. His neighbours were the rest of the trade — Wm. Strange & Co. and Doherty & Wadsworth across the street, Jno. Dunlop’s silk twist mill and Naef Bros. & Co. round the corner, Benj. Eastwood making silk machinery a block away.

In February 1887, when the Paterson silk dyers struck and the whole trade seized up, George Frost & Sons told their four hundred hands that the Albion Mills would not reopen until the strike was settled. The news went out on the wire and was reprinted as far away as Topeka, Grand Island and Victoria, British Columbia. It is the one day his name travelled.

He had made his will in October 1878, leaving a dollar apiece to the three children of his Macclesfield first marriage — Eliza Ann, by then Mrs Galation, Mary Elizabeth and George Thomas — and everything else to “my wife Frances Wright Frost” for her life, and after her to their four sons, Frank, Harry Bell, Morris and Charlie. He named John C. Ryle, the patriarch of the Paterson silk trade, among his executors, then in 1881 struck Ryle out and left the whole estate in Frances’s hands alone.

He died at Paterson — on 27 June 1887 by his memorial, though his will was not proved until July 1889, and the year is not yet settled — in his sixties, and was buried — all but certainly — at Cedar Lawn Cemetery, remembered there in the terms he would have chosen: “senior member of the firm, George Frost & Sons, silk manufacturers; native of Macclesfield, England.”

57.s:
Frances Wright Bell was born at Macclesfield in Cheshire about 1832, the daughter of Nathaniel Bell, a silk weaver who rose to be a silk manufacturer. Almost certainly she is the Frances, born 1832, whom a Nathaniel Bell, silk weaver of Sutton, brought to St George’s, Sutton, to be baptised at five on 30 June 1837, on the same day as her brother James — though no record yet carries a second member of that family through to the Chestergate house of 1851. By 1851 her mother was dead, and Frances, nineteen, was living in her widowed father’s house on Chestergate, Macclesfield’s main street, with a younger brother and sister and a servant. On 10 June 1857, at twenty-five, she married George Frost, a widowed Macclesfield silk throwster, in Prestbury parish church, with her father as witness — thirty-nine years to the day before her son Harry married. She bore the sons who carried the firm on — Frank, born at 6 Lord Street, Macclesfield, on 4 April 1858 and baptised at the Wesleyan chapel on Park Green, where the minister wrote her out in full as Frances Wright Frost; Harry Bell, baptised at Macclesfield in April 1860; Maurice and Charlie, baptised together there in July 1863, when the clerk wrote her name in full as Frances Wright Frost. Charlie died at five months and was buried at Christ Church, Macclesfield, a week before Christmas; the son born to her in America was named Charles after him, the youngest in the Paterson census of 1880. The family crossed in 1864 and settled at Paterson.

In June 1880 she was at 309 Straight Street, Paterson, keeping house for a household of seven: her husband, his grown daughter Mary, and three sons, the two eldest boys already working in the family’s silk mill. Her maiden name went forward into the generation after her children’s: her grandson, born in Pennsylvania in July 1900, was christened Harry Bell Frost. It was that boy’s father, Harry B., who had married a Detroit schoolteacher in 1896.

She was not George’s first wife: he had a son George and a daughter by an earlier marriage, and the daughter went home to England. Frances outlived him by a dozen years. Her last home was 189 Tyler Street, Paterson, and she died there of cancer at nine on the morning of 5 January 1899, leaving her four sons, Frank, Harry, Maurice and Charles, and her two stepchildren; in all likelihood she was buried beside George at Cedar Lawn.

60.s:
Moses B. Roush was born on 30 January 1842 in Meigs County, Ohio, in the riverside settlement the Roushes and the Neases had founded together and called the Nease Settlement. He was a son of Benjamin “Bennie” Roush and Sophia Altman, and grew up on their farm in Sutton Township — seven years old in 1850, eighteen in 1860, one of twelve children.

He went to the war late. He entered service on 23 July 1864, aged twenty-two, as a private in Company A — and afterwards Company B — of the 28th Ohio Volunteer Infantry, Ohio’s “2nd German Regiment,” raised at Camp Dennison from German-speaking volunteers and by 1864 taking whatever recruits the state had left. He served the last twelve months of the war, from the Atlanta summer through to three months after Appomattox, and was discharged on 6 July 1865.

On 1 September 1870 he married Sarah Duckworth, the daughter of a Lancashire collier, at Orange Township in Meigs County; her brother Adam married in the same township eight days later. They had Sarah Ann in 1871, Charles Benjamin in 1874, John G. in 1877 and Richard in 1880. In March 1880 he applied for an invalid pension on his war service; eleven months later, on 4 March 1881, Sarah died, leaving him four children under ten. He married Lydia E. in Mason County in August 1883 and took the family across the Ohio into Graham District, where he lived about twenty years and had five more children.

In May 1883 the Grand Army of the Republic mustered in Washington Post No. 13 at New Haven, Mason County, with fourteen charter members, and its Officer of the Guard was a Moses Roush — very probably him. In the first weeks of 1887 he was called before the United States Board of Examining Surgeons, which sat every Wednesday at Dr. Hoy’s office at Point Pleasant. The county paper ran the summons three weeks over, under the heading “ATTENTION! — The boys who wore the blue,” and listed him as “Moses Roush, Co. A. 28th Ohio Vols.”; he had to be re-examined before the quarter closed on 31 March or lose his place on the pension pay roll. In 1900 he and his son John were neighbours at Hartford village. He was still doing road work with a team for the county in his sixties, and the Graham District road accounts of 1907 and 1910 pay him for team and labour.

Lydia died in 1906. In 1908 he buried his son John and two granddaughters, and in May 1909 he stood surety on his widowed daughter-in-law’s $500 bond to be guardian of the four orphaned girls — the grandfather behind the orphans’ bond. He married a third time, to Margaret A. Zerkle, in 1911. From 1920 the government paid his invalid pension at an increased rate, and raised it again in 1923.

He died at six in the evening on 23 August 1925 at New Haven, aged eighty-three years six months and twenty-three days, of general arteriosclerosis with senility, after Dr. R. S. Bryant had attended him for three days. It was his son Charles who gave the county his parents’ names — “Bennie” Roush of Graham Station and Sophia Aultman of Portsmouth, Ohio. He was buried at Broad Run under a barrel-topped stone of the same pattern as his parents’, reading FATHER & MOTHER / MOSES B. ROUSH / BORN JAN. 30, 1842; no death date was ever cut on it, and it has since come off its base and lies tilted. His widow filed her pension claim eight days after he died, and the money that paid for the end of his life had been granted for a war that ended sixty years before.

61.s:
Sarah Mary Duckworth was born in June 1851 in Pennsylvania, the fourth child and the first American child of James Duckworth, a Lancashire collier, and his wife Ann Collins. Her three elder brothers and sisters were born in England and her two younger brothers in Pennsylvania and Ohio, so hers is the birth that marks the family’s crossing: they were still in Lancashire when Adam came in March 1847, and in the Pennsylvania coalfield by the time she arrived.

By 1860 the Duckworths had moved on to the Ohio Valley coalfield at Syracuse, Meigs County, where the family name was as often written “Deckworth” as not, and where she was nine. She was still at home in the summer of 1870, aged nineteen, and on 1 September that year she married Moses B. Roush at Orange Township in the same county — a Union veteran nine years her senior. Her brother Adam married eight days later in the same township. It was a busy fortnight for the family.

They had four children: Sarah Ann in 1871, Charles Benjamin in 1874, John G. in 1877 and Richard, born at Syracuse in 1880 and named for her own brother. In June 1880 the little household was in Sutton Township, with her widowed mother Ann keeping house five doors away.

Sarah died on 4 March 1881, aged twenty-nine, leaving four children under ten and the youngest still a baby. Her mother was living at the end of the row when it happened. She is buried at Broad Run Cemetery in Mason County — which the neighbourhood also called the Nease Cemetery, and which is the same ground her husband, her son John and her grandchildren would come to — under a stone giving June 1851 to 4 March 1881.

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ THIS NODE WAS “J. W. NEASE” UNTIL 7 AUGUST 2026. IT IS NOW SETTLED [ROUSH-53]. Two threads had closed this slot with two different men and both closures were still on disk. Three record images were read at native resolution and the answer is Lewis J. Nease.

The decider — his daughter’s own marriage licence, Mason County, 22 February 1897 (WV VRR marriage Id 12211313): “The name of the party giving the foregoing information is L. J. NEASE of Mason County, State of West Virginia.” The looping capital L is unmistakable beside the J of “John Roush” written three lines above in the same hand — and the party who gives a bride’s age and birthplace to the clerk is her father.

And his own death register entry dates him exactly. WV VRR death Id 5286043, Register of Deaths p. 120 line 6: “Nease, Lewis — Waggener — married — 62 [yrs] 2 [mos] 28 [days] — Laborer — Heart trouble.” Work the age backwards and it lands on 20 November 1854 — to the day, the birth date the 1928 Roush genealogy gives Lewis Nease. An age in days on a register and a date in a book, agreeing exactly.

Corroborated four more ways: the 1900 census (Lewis Nease, married 23 years ⇒ 1877, wife Martha born Ohio, one page from Bertha’s own household); the county birth index for 1891 and 1895, both naming Lewis Nease and Martha as parents; and the 1928 Roush genealogy pp. 416–417, whose child list matches the 1900 census nine names out of ten.

⚠ The 1878 birth register really does read “J. W. Nease”, and so does the county’s later typed copy of it — but those are ONE source recorded twice, not two witnesses. Why the assessor wrote the wrong initials is left open rather than smoothed over.

⛔ James W. Nease (1852–1906) is retired as a candidate [ROUSH-53]: no death record anywhere in the West Virginia index for Mason County 1901–1911, and no James Nease anywhere in the 1928 Roush genealogy — a book that reconstructs these very households.

62.s:
Lewis J. Nease was born on 20 November 1854 in Mason County, then still Virginia, the second child of George Nease and Nancy Roush, who had married six years before. He was six years old on the family’s farm in 1860, in a household the enumerator wrote down as “Neoce.”

On 12 April 1877, aged twenty-two, he married Martha J. Love, seventeen, who had been born across the river in Athens County, Ohio. Their eldest, Bertha, was born the following January, and Lewis reported the birth himself as a farmer of Mason County. At least nine more children followed over the next twenty years, down to births registered in 1891 and 1895. By 1900 he and Martha had been married twenty-three years and were living close by their married daughter Bertha.

Twenty years after his own wedding he stood at the same courthouse counter for his daughter’s: on 22 February 1897 it was he who gave the clerk Bertha’s age and birthplace when she married John G. Roush. He went by his initials all his life, and L. J. is the name on his gravestone.

By the end he was a labourer. He died on 17 February 1917 in the Waggener District of Mason County, of heart trouble, aged sixty-two years two months and twenty-eight days. He lies at Broad Run — the Nease burying ground, as the neighbourhood called it in print as early as 1899 — under a small obelisk carved with a gate or lattice, and the inscription reads L. J. NEASE, 1854 - 1917. Nobody at his death could give the county his own parents’ names; both columns were left unfilled.

72.s:
John Eakins was born about 1795 in New Hanover County, North Carolina, the eldest son of Joseph Eakins and the woman who was probably Elizabeth Pigford. He was about ten when his father died in the first months of 1805, leaving a widow, a houseful of small children, four hundred acres on Moores Creek, and an estate the county court had to superintend for the next fourteen years.

That estate paid for his upbringing. In February 1816 it was charged $3.83 for schooling Joseph and William Eakins and $10.50 for boarding them; his sisters Sarah and Deborah were put into calico and cambric and a pair of shoes. Part of the money came from hiring out the three people the estate held in slavery — Simon, Rachel and Cesar — who were still in the administrator Edward Pigford’s hands in 1817.

At the February term of 1819, aged twenty-four, he took over from Timothy Pigford as guardian of his own younger brothers and sisters, and on 22 March that year he rendered his first account to the court and signed it “John Eakins, Guard’n.” One of the securities named in that return was Stephen Coston.

He married Nancy Costin — of that same Coston family — probably about 1828 or 1829. In 1850 he was fifty-five, a farmer with $800 in real estate, Nancy was forty-three, and nine children were at home: Margaret, Ella, John, Andrew, Joseph, Susan, Presilla, Cornelia and Sarah. His younger brother Joseph lived in the next house; the two brothers’ tracts adjoined on the east side of Moores Creek, where their father had bought in 1790.

The war took two of the family. In May 1861 his son John J. B. Eakins and his nephew Owen J. enlisted at Lower Black River in Company E of the 18th North Carolina — the Moore’s Creek Rifle Guards, a company named for the water the Eakinses had farmed since before the Constitution was ratified. John J. B. was killed at Sharpsburg; Owen at Chancellorsville. On 29 January 1863, in New Hanover County, John Eakins Sr. swore before a justice of the peace that he was the father of the dead soldier and claimed the $100.23 owed on his account. Daniel McAlister, who had known the boy for twenty-five years, witnessed it. The government paid in November 1864.

He was still living after 1880. He has no marked grave in the Eakins family burying ground on the creek.

73.s:
Nancy Costin was born in 1807 in North Carolina and married John Eakins Sr. of New Hanover County, probably about 1828 or 1829 — not in 1819, as the family long had it, for in 1819 she was twelve.

She bore at least nine children between about 1830 and 1848: Margaret, Ella, John J. B., Andrew, Joseph William, Susan, Presilla, Cornelia and Sarah. They farmed the Moores Creek land her husband’s father had bought in 1790, and in 1850 all nine were under the one roof.

Two of her sons went into the 18th North Carolina in 1861, and one of them, John J. B., was killed at Sharpsburg in September 1862; she was alive to know it, and her husband swore the affidavit that claimed the dead boy’s pay.

Her own people were Costins or Costons — one family spread across two counties, rooted on Stump Sound in Onslow and moving down into New Hanover in the 1790s. A Stephen Coston of that family stood security on her husband’s guardian bond in 1819. Her father’s name is not known. She died in 1870, and like her husband she has no marked grave in the Eakins burying ground.

76.s:
Joseph Tolbert Swain was born on 24 May 1838 in Wilcox County, Alabama. By his early twenties he had moved west into Lauderdale County, Mississippi, where on 6 February 1860 he married Nancy E. Jane Phillips; their first child, Joseph Lee, was born there that December.

He enlisted on 8 March 1862 at Lauderdale Station, a private in Company C of the regiment that ended the war as the 2nd Mississippi Cavalry, bringing his own horse. The army described him then: twenty-four, five feet eight, dark complexion, black eyes, black hair, a farmer born in Wilcox County, Alabama. Within five months he was discharged with consumption — “phthisis pulmonalis” — and paid off at Columbus in August 1862, having already signed his claim to the back pay over to another man. In September 1863 he enlisted again, at Enterprise; he was sick in the recruiting camp in the summer of 1864, and in October 1864 he was discharged by order of General Hood. A portrait of him survives — a man in a dark coat and a hard round hat, with a heavy beard down his chest and a direct, unsmiling stare.

When the war was over he did not wait. His two eldest children were born in Mississippi, in 1861 and 1864; every child from 1866 onward was born in Alabama. He moved his wife and two small children across the state line into Sumter County in the first months after the surrender, when he was about twenty-seven, and settled at Cuba. By 1880 the house there held him and Nancy, both forty-two, with seven children at home, from Joseph L. at nineteen down to John M. at six.

On 3 July 1875 he walked into the registrar's office at Cuba, in Precinct No. 18 of Sumter County, and took the registration oath ahead of that August's referendum on a new state constitution. The printed oath he swore made him promise that he would “never countenance or aid in the secession of this State from the United States” and that he “accept[ed] the civil and political equality of all men” — ten years after he had ridden with the 2nd Mississippi Cavalry. The registrar W. H. Lewis wrote his name for him and he made his mark: he could not write. Against his name the registrar put down his living in a word: farmer, near Cuba. Two lines below him on the same page, registering the same day, was B. A. Simmons, the miller and farmer whose daughters his son Joseph Lee would marry nine and ten years later.

Two more babies, Jesse and Hassiel, were born and died in 1876–79. Nine children in all are known, and four of them were still living in 1940: Joseph Lee, John M. Swain of York, Mattie Shamburger and Laura McDonald. Joseph Tolbert Swain died on 14 January 1904, aged sixty-five, in Sumter County; his son William T. followed him four months later. In November 1905 his eldest son, acting “as the administrator of the estate of J. T. Swain, deceased,” cried a hundred and sixty acres of his land for sale at the post-office door at Cuba, to be divided among the heirs. He lies in Clay Memorial Cemetery at Cuba under a marble marker reading JOSEPH TOLBERT SWAIN, PVT CO C 2 MISS CAV, CONFEDERATE STATES ARMY. Someone left a line over him in 2013: “Here rests one who so bravely fought for the land he could not save.”

77.s:
Nancy E. Jane was born in Mississippi in the last days of 1837 — 26 December is the date carried from her grave, though all her life she gave her age as if she had been born in 1838. Her people were probably Phillipses; the family has long held her father to be Robert Phillips and her mother Nancy White. She married Joseph Tolbert Swain in Lauderdale County on 6 February 1860, when she was twenty-two, and their first child was born that December.

She bore at least nine children. The two eldest, Joseph Lee and Alice Jane, were born in Mississippi; from 1866, after the family crossed into Sumter County, Alabama, the rest were born there — Martha Ann, Laura, Minnie Lou, William T., John M., and two who did not live, Jesse in 1878 and Hassiel in 1879. She kept house at Cuba, and in 1880 seven of the children were still under her roof. Two of her daughters, Alice Jane and Minnie Lou, married Phillips men in their turn.

She was widowed in January 1904 and lost her grown son William T. that May. Four of her children outlived their father by decades — her eldest, Joseph Lee, and John M. Swain, Mattie Shamburger and Laura McDonald, all three of the others still at York in 1940. She died at Cuba on Monday 1 June 1908, about seventy years old, and was buried the next day beside her husband in Clay Memorial Cemetery at Cuba. Her stone does not give her own name. It reads only “Wife of J. T. Swain.”

80.s:
Henry H. Stephens was born on 8 August 1822 in North Carolina, in Orange County by the family’s account, the son of Moore Stephens and Rebecca Moize. He was a small child when the family left for Alabama — they were in Greene County by 1824 — and he grew up on the Alabama side of the Tombigbee country, moving on with his father into Sumter County.

On 4 June 1846, at twenty-three, he married Sarah Ann Jones, born in North Carolina about 1833, whose family lived a few doors from his own. In the summer of 1850 the whole arrangement sat on one page of the census: in the “Intercourse” division of Sumter County, enumerated on 7 June, Henry was twenty-seven and farming at dwelling 1184 with Sarah, seventeen, and a son Calvin, aged one, and a boarder in the house, Redden Marshall, twenty-three and North Carolina-born. Two dwellings along lived Daniel Jones, Sarah’s father; six houses away, at dwelling 1190, lived Henry’s own father Moore. A son, Caswell Massey Stephens, was born on 8 January 1852.

Sarah died young, and nothing records her death. On 21 October 1854 Henry married again, to Elizabeth Jones — almost certainly his first wife’s younger sister — before Jesse B. Thorne, Justice of the Peace. He was a Minister of the Gospel as well as a farmer, and the Sumter County marriage registers have him performing weddings through the 1860s and seventies, his own son Caswell’s among them in October 1871.

By 1860 the family had followed Moore Stephens west into Newton County, Mississippi, where Henry was listed with Elizabeth, twenty-one, and the children Caroline, Caswell, James and William. He was forty when the war reached him, with a second wife and small children at home and no exemption — he was liable to Confederate conscription from September 1862. He served, and the company he most likely marched in was the Newton County company of the 5th Regiment, Mississippi Infantry (State Troops) — the Minute Men — where an H. H. Stephens appears as a private in 1863, with a W. Stephens and a Z. Stephens beside him on the roll and a cluster of Joneses: Daniel, Samuel, William, Riley, H. D., A. and W., the surname he had married into twice. The 5th mustered from 31 July to 1 October 1862 and again from 17 July to 21 September 1863, and it was at Vicksburg: the regiment’s papers afterwards count the men paroled there on 5 August 1863, with the killed, the dead of wounds and the dead of disease through the siege beside them. A service file for an H. H. Stephens of that regiment, very probably his, survives: a private of Company A who enlisted at Decatur, the Newton County seat, on 5 February 1863, joined in May, was taken when Vicksburg surrendered on 4 July 1863, and signed his parole there on 10 July, swearing not to take up arms again until exchanged. His widow, swearing to his service forty years later, remembered it differently — 2nd Lieutenant in Company I of the 4th Mississippi Infantry Volunteers — but that company was the Benela Sharpshooters of Calhoun County, two hundred miles from anywhere this family lived, and no Stephens of his initials is on its roll.

He came home. By 1870 the family was back at Cuba, in Township 17 of Sumter County, Alabama — the third leg of one continuous migration. On 31 December 1869 he stood in the Probate Court at a special term before Judge J. A. Abrahams and was appointed guardian of three of his own sons, Caswell M., Calvin D. and John M., each over fourteen and each described as “a minor heir of Daniel Jones deceased,” posting bonds of $800, $800 and $1,000; the property was real enough that he was filing annual settlements two years later. On 22 June 1875 he registered to vote at Thornville, Precinct No. 3 of Sumter County, entry 25, writing “H. H. Stephens,” farmer, in his own hand. Two lines down the same page a D. C. Stephens registered the same day, and immediately above him A. J. Shelton, “Farmer & Blk Smith.”

He died on 20 October 1879 at Gaston, in Sumter County. His gravestone reckons his life to the day — born 8 August 1822, died 20 October 1879, aged 57 years, 2 months and 12 days — and carries a Masonic square and compasses inside a carved wreath. The carver spelled the family name STEAVENS.

What the war and his death left behind shows in one document, sworn a quarter of a century later. On 4 July 1904, in Sumter County, Elizabeth Stephens went before the county pension examiner R. H. Hale and swore that she was “the widow of H. H. Stevens, who served as a 2[nd] Lieutenant in company I of the 4th Regiment Miss Infantry Volunteers,” that her husband “died on the 29 day of Oct, 1879,” and “that he did not desert the service of the State of Alabama, nor of the Confederate States.” Two men of the neighbourhood swore the same day that they had known him personally and that “the services set forth in the application were rendered by said H. H. Stephens” — W. H. Stephens, very probably one of his own family, and T. J. Tucker. 81.s:
Sarah Ann Jones was born about 1833 in North Carolina, the eldest daughter of Daniel Jones. Her younger brothers and sisters were all Alabama-born from about 1837, which puts the family’s move south in the middle thirties, with Sarah born just before it.

On 4 June 1846, at about thirteen — fourteen or fifteen if her recorded age runs light — she married Henry H. Stephens in Sumter County, Alabama. She had her first child, Calvin, at about sixteen. In 1850 she was “Sarah Stephens, 17,” keeping house at dwelling 1184 in the Intercourse division of Sumter County with her husband, their one-year-old son and a boarder. Her father’s house stood two doors away and her husband’s father’s six houses off; the whole connection fitted into one short row. Caswell Massey Stephens was born to her on 8 January 1852, and a son John M. probably followed.

She died somewhere between then and October 1854, when Henry remarried — the new wife, Elizabeth Jones, in all likelihood her own younger sister. Nothing records her death, her age at it, or where she lies. What survives instead is an inheritance: in December 1869 her three sons were bonded in the Sumter County probate court as “minor heirs of Daniel Jones deceased,” a share that could only reach grandsons through a parent already dead. That is the nearest thing she has to an epitaph.

88.s:
John Wesley Truett was born on 20 October 1833, the son of the Reverend William Hampton Truett and Alcey Wiggins.

On 2 November 1854, at twenty-one, he married Emily Caroline Ward in Henry County, Alabama. She was seventeen, so her father had to consent, and five days before the wedding W. H. Ward wrote it out for the clerk to copy into the marriage book: “license should issue for the marriage of John Truett with my daughter Emily C.” His father-in-law wrote a firm, practised hand. The bridegroom could not write at all.

They moved three hundred miles west to Clarke County, and the children came — Sarah Ann in 1858, William Curtis in 1867, George in 1872, John Wesley in 1875, Elisha Dozier in 1877, Carrie in 1878 — and he farmed at Chilton.

He enlisted on 15 October 1862 at Coffeeville, his own village, signing on “for the War” with Colonel Alexander McKinstry: Private, Company D, 32nd Alabama Infantry, under Captain Cox — George W. Cox, one of the two captains the county furnished to that regiment. He was twenty-eight. Four weeks later he was in the Confederate post hospital at Dalton, Georgia, with chronic rheumatism, and he never really came back. He was sent on to Tullahoma in February 1863, drew clothing at Dalton that April and signed the receipt with an X, and was furloughed for thirty days at the end of May. Every muster roll says the same word, absent. Then the rolls stop, in the summer of 1863, with no discharge, no capture and no parole; fifty-seven years later his widow, asked on a state form when he had quit the service, left the line blank. The family did not know either.

In 1880 the house at Chilton held him at forty-six, “Emlie C.”, the children — William Curtis among them — and his mother Alecey, the preacher’s widow, at sixty-seven. In 1907 the state counted him among its surviving old soldiers at Coffeeville, aged seventy-three.

On 9 July 1909, at Grove Hill, he went in person before the county pension board. What he owned, sworn on the schedule: thirty-six acres at $150, a “Small Frame Box House one Room” at $25, and one cow and calf at $10. The other eleven categories — horses, hogs, guns, watches, furniture, tools — all say None. Asked what made him unable to make a living, the board wrote three words: catarrh of the head. It wrote to the State Auditor at Montgomery that “he has some head trouble, is unable to do but little work, has no income except what little work he can do himself, no one to look to for support,” and the form says he had no children upon whom he could depend, though six of them were living. Two neighbours swore to his service, Elijah Brown and J. H. Geiger senior, and both signed with a mark, as he did — John his X mark Truett, the same mark he had made at Dalton forty-six years before. The application also has him enlisting at Murfreesboro in Tennessee and honourably discharged in May 1865, neither of which matches the rolls of his own company; whoever filled it in for him was working from an old man’s memory. The county board put him in Class 4, the state board at Montgomery agreed, and he drew pension number 27126 in Clarke County until he died.

Another Truett lies at New Prospect under a Confederate government marker reading G. W. Truett, Corporal, Company D, 32nd Alabama Infantry — his own company — and how the two of them were kin has never been worked out.

He died on 17 April 1914, aged eighty, and lies at Oak Grove Cemetery, Chilton, under a rounded marble headstone with clasped hands carved at the top and the words GONE BUT NOT FORGOTTEN. Caroline outlived him by eight years and lies three hundred miles away in Florida. A studio photograph of the two of them survives, with their son George standing behind.

89.s:
Emily Caroline Ward was born on Christmas Day 1836 at Abbeville in Henry County, Alabama, the second daughter of William H. Ward, a South Carolina-born farmer with four hundred dollars of land at Rowville. Who her mother was is not known: the Syntha who kept her father’s house married him only in December 1844, eight years after Caroline was born, and was very probably her stepmother. In 1850 she was twelve, one of eight children at home.

She married at seventeen. Because she was under twenty-one her father had to consent, and the clerk copied his words into the Henry County marriage book above the licence: “I give my free and unqualified consent that license should issue for the marriage of John Truett with my daughter Emily C.” The licence issued on 28 October 1854, and she and John Wesley Truett married five days later. Neither bride nor groom could write.

They moved west to Clarke County, and the children came — Sarah Ann in 1858, William Curtis in 1867, George in 1872, John Wesley in 1875, Elisha Dozier in 1877, Carrie in 1878. In 1880 she was “Emlie C.” at Chilton, keeping house for her husband, four children and her mother-in-law Alcey. Sarah married William Green Geiger on 12 December 1878, a match that would decide where Caroline spent her last years.

When her father’s Henry County estate was broken up in 1870 she was so far away that the administrators left her off the petition altogether; six weeks later a neighbour, Abijah Wiggins, swore her back into it — among the heirs of full age, he said, was “the wife of JOHN TRUETT.” Her husband went back to Abbeville in person on 26 December 1871 and collected three hundred dollars of her share.

She was widowed on 17 April 1914 and applied for her Confederate widow’s pension three months later. In April 1915, at Coffeeville, she swore that she had been born at Abbeville on the 25th day of December 1836, and signed with her mark. Then, in 1917, at eighty, she left Alabama for good: Sarah and William Green Geiger moved the household to Hardeetown in Levy County, Florida, and the old woman went with them. On 13 December 1920 she put her X on an Alabama pension form with the word ALABAMA struck out and “Florida” written in, gave her address as Hardeetown and her income as “NONE.”

Two likenesses of her survive: the family group with her husband and their son George standing behind, and a head-and-shoulders portrait of a dark-haired woman with her hair parted in the middle, kept in a cousin’s scrapbook and copied so many times that the face has gone to patches of black and white.

She died at Chiefland at six in the evening on 30 November 1922, of what the doctor called paralysis of the bowels after a fortnight, with old age contributing. She was eighty-five. The informant was simply “Son,” who gave her father’s name as John Ward and answered the next three questions with a question mark. She is buried at Hardeetown Methodist Cemetery in plot S5, the only Truett in the ground, with her daughter Sarah on one side and Sarah’s mother-in-law on the other: three old women in a row. Her stone reads CAROLINE W. TRUETT — the W for Ward, her maiden name cut into her own marker — over a birth year, 1829, that is seven years wrong and came from the son standing at the registrar’s desk two days after she died.

96.s:
Clark Strong Tuttle was born in Jefferson County, New York, on 27 April 1811 — that is his family Bible’s date; the printed Tuttle genealogy says the 28th. His father, Colonel Gershom Tuttle, kept a farm and a famous tavern outside Watertown; his mother was Pamelia Strong Clark, and he carried both of her surnames and used them in full, unusually enough that a United States land officer wrote him down in 1837 as Clark Strong Tuttle.

He was six when the family crossed to Indiana in the autumn of 1817 and took up land near Fort Harrison on the Wabash, and he grew up there. His father died in September 1823, when Clark was twelve, leaving an estate that proved insolvent and took nine years to close. In 1830, aged nineteen, he had no Tuttle household in the county to live in: he was counted in the house of Henry Markle, who had married his sister Amanda.

He came of age in April 1832 and married Harriet M. Sweany two weeks later, on 11 May. Their children, in the Bible’s hand, were Gersham, Aula, Hannah, Chester, Josephine, Frank and a second Aula — and four of the first five died as infants or small children and lie together under “C.S. & H. TUTTLE” stones at Otter Creek Union Cemetery. The second Aula was named for the sister who had died four years before she was born. Harriet herself died on 3 June 1851, aged thirty-seven; five weeks later, on 10 July, Clark married Nancy A. Harbert, and by her he had Edward, Emma, Dennis, Richard B., Harriet B. and Dollie A.

He was a miller, and a rich one: $9,500 in land in 1850, and in 1860 $14,000 in land and $9,215 besides, with three hired hands and a servant living in and every school-age child in the house at school. He took United States patents on four parcels in 1839 and 1841, became a county commissioner in October 1858, and was postmaster at Ellsworth — which was the post office at his own Tuttle’s Mills. The 1874 county atlas gave the mill a plate of its own: a four-storey frame mill under a smoking stack with box cars on the siding, captioned C. S. TUTTLE & CO., MILLERS & DEALERS IN GRAIN, FLOUR, MEAL &c., ELSWORTH, VIGO CO., IND., with his name, his son Frank’s and a partner’s beneath it; the township plat in the same atlas is lettered “C. S. Tuttle · Mill · ELSWORTH STA.” The mill was the town.

Not everything went well. In October 1869 a postal detective charged his son Frank, who ran the office under him, with robbing the mail, and the Terre Haute paper reported that “Mr. Clark Tuttle, the father of young Frank, is terribly distressed at the result of this unfortunate affair.” The following summer he sold out: the 117-acre mill tract on 12 July 1870 for $6,000, the partnership of C. S. Tuttle & Co. dissolved on the 26th, the home parcels gone by 24 October. By 1878 the mill “has been standing idle for four years.”

He was still alive and still public-spirited in June 1876, when the committee for the Centennial Fourth of July listed him among its vice-presidents as “Clark Tuttle, Otter Creek.” He was dead before May 1880, when his daughter was being described in print as the daughter of “the late C. S. Tuttle.” His widow Nancy was buried from Union Church in Otter Creek in April 1883. No stone marks either of them.

97.s:
Nancy A. Harbert — the Vigo County clerk wrote it Herbert — was born in Ohio about 1826 or 1827. Nothing is known of her parents, or of how she came to Indiana.

On 10 July 1851 she married Clark Strong Tuttle, the miller of Otter Creek Township, before Harvey W. Allen, justice of the peace. His first wife Harriet had died five weeks earlier and had left him young children and a mill to run, and four of Harriet’s children were already buried in the Otter Creek ground. Nancy had six children of her own by him — Edward, Emma, Dennis, Richard B., Harriet B. and Dollie A. — and this family descends from her.

The house she kept in 1860 was a prosperous one: her husband a miller worth $14,000 in land, three hired hands and a servant living in, and every school-age child at school. She was thirty-three that summer.

She outlived her husband by several years. She died on 25 April 1883 and was buried the next day out of Union Church in Otter Creek Township, the church attached to the cemetery where her stepchildren lay. The notice gave her no name of her own — Mrs. Clark S. Tuttle, widow of the late Clark S. Tuttle, the miller. No stone survives for her.

98.s:
Francis Fuerstenberger — Frank, to Terre Haute — was born on 17 August 1826 and baptised the next day, at Wiesloch, in Baden, a few miles south of Heidelberg — the son of Daniel Fürstenberger and his wife Veronika. In America he told the 1870 census-taker he was from Bavaria, but every other record says Baden, and so does the register of his baptism. He is the immigrant on this line, and the ship he came on is lost.

On 26 February 1852, in Clark County, Illinois, he married a young widow, Sophia Flint. The county clerk, J. Stockwell, licensed “Francis Fiestenburgen” and Sophia Flint, “now both of this County,” and the minister certified that he had joined them “according to the usual custom and laws of the State of Illinois.” Their first child was born at Marshall, in that county, the following November.

About 1854 they came to Terre Haute, and from that year until the day he died he lived in one house: 521 South Third Street. He was a shoemaker, and by 1870 he owned $2,000 of real estate; a few doors away lived another Bavarian in the leather trade — the immigrant quarter of a river city in miniature. In October 1864 the Terre Haute post office advertised the letters nobody had called for, and there in the gentlemen’s column, between Foulke and Fort, stood “Fuerstenberger F.”

Eight children were born to him and Sophia. In October 1881 his daughter Emma married Richard B. Tuttle, a young miller; three years later, in December 1884, Richard died of consumption, and the funeral was held at ten in the morning from Frank’s own house on South Third Street. The widow and the baby stayed.

On the Wednesday before 1 March 1890 he and Sophia kept their fortieth wedding anniversary at the South Third Street house, “very delightfully,” afternoon and evening. She was dead within four months.

He died in September 1894, aged sixty-eight. The Saturday Evening Mail gave him a paragraph on its front page as “an old and well known citizen” and noted the thing he was known for: forty years in Terre Haute, and all of them in the one house. He lies at Highland Lawn Cemetery, Section 3, Lot 162, under a shared obelisk with Sophia, the inscription recording his age to the day — sixty-eight years and twenty-four days, which counts back to the very day of the Baden baptism entry. Forty years after his death an inheritance suit was still naming the heirs of five of his eight children.
