99.s:
Sophia was born in Pennsylvania in 1828. She had been married once before: when she stood up with Francis Fuerstenberger in Clark County, Illinois, on 26 February 1852, she was Sophia Flint.

She and Francis had eight children between 1852 and 1870 — John Fredrick, James W., Anna, Clara Rebecca, Emma, Daniel, George and Eliza. The family came to Terre Haute about 1854 and lived at 521 South Third Street, where Francis made shoes and where, in December 1884, her daughter Emma’s young husband was buried out of the front room.

In February 1890 she and Francis kept their fortieth wedding anniversary in that house. Four months later she was dead: pleuro-pneumonia took her on 14 June 1890, aged sixty-two years, three months and two days, and she was interred the next day at Highland Lawn. She lies with Francis in Section 3, Lot 162, under a stone that records her age but not her birth.

120.s:
Benjamin Roush was born on 30 August 1816 at Graham Station, in Mason County, Virginia, the fifth child of John “Blackbird John” Roush and his wife Regina. He was the last of them born on the Virginia bank: his sister Hannah arrived in May 1820 in the Nease Settlement across the river in Meigs County, Ohio, so the family crossed in the years between, and he grew up on the Ohio side.

On 23 May 1839 he married Sophia Altman at Orange Township, Meigs County. She was not yet sixteen. The justice of the peace who joined them did not get round to filing his return until the following July, when he certified two weddings at once in a single sentence. Twelve children were born to them, nine of them still in the house in 1860.

He farmed in Sutton Township. In 1850 he was thirty-four, with seven children under his roof and an older Virginia-born woman, Mary Roush, thirty-six, living with them; four dwellings up the road was his father John, sixty-six. In August 1849 John Roush — a man who could not write and signed every deed with a mark — sold him sixty-nine acres and twenty poles in the north-east corner of Section 25, Town 3, Range 12 for five hundred dollars; on the same day, before the same justice and the same two witnesses, the rest of that same strip went to John Roush Junior. Neither deed says a word about why, or that the men were kin.

By 1870 Benjamin and Sophia were at Syracuse, the salt and coal village on the river, in the same year and the same place as the English Duckworth family whose daughter their son Moses would marry that September. By 1880 they had crossed back into West Virginia, to Waggener District in Mason County.

He died on 5 March 1897. Sophia outlived him by sixteen months. They lie together at Broad Run Cemetery under a barrel-topped stone on a rough-faced plinth: FATHER & MOTHER / BENJAMIN ROUSH / BORN AUG. 30, 1816 / DIED MAR. 5, 1897. To his son Moses, giving the names to a county clerk in 1925, he was always “Bennie.”

121.s:
Sophia Altman was born on 1 June 1823 in Ohio, and her family remembered her as coming from Portsmouth, in Scioto County, sixty miles down the same river.

She married Benjamin Roush at Orange Township, Meigs County, on 23 May 1839, at fifteen years and eleven months — nine days short of her sixteenth birthday. Ohio required a parent’s consent for a bride that young, so a paper naming her father was filed at the Meigs County courthouse that May; it has never turned up, and who her parents were is still an open question.

Twelve children were born to the marriage, and nine of them were still under the Sutton Township roof in 1860: Moses, Joseph, Sarah, Livina, Zillah, Hannah, Maria and the rest. Six are known by name and fate — Moses B., Sarah Elizabeth Kauff, Mary Lovina Findley, Maria Ann Goodnite, Serepta Ann, and Dillia McDaniel — and four of her daughters lived long enough for Ohio and West Virginia to register their deaths, each of them naming her as their mother, spelled Altman by some clerks and Aultman by others.

The family farmed Sutton Township through the 1850s and 1860s, were at Syracuse in 1870, and by 1880 had crossed into Waggener District, Mason County, West Virginia. Sophia died back in Meigs County, Ohio, on Independence Day 1898, sixteen months after Benjamin. She was buried beside him at Broad Run, under a stone that calls her only SOPHIA, HIS WIFE — the granite does not give her maiden name at all.

122.s:
James Duckworth was born in Lancashire about 1813 to 1818, the son of George Duckworth, a hatter of the Bury district. He went down the pit instead. On 21 January 1839, “of full age, Bachelor, Collier, of Wood Head Hill,” he married Ann Collins of Freetown at the parish church of St Mary, Bury, after banns, by the curate J. F. Amos. Neither of them could write; both signed with a mark, and so did one of the witnesses, Richard Duckworth.

Three children were born to them in England — Mary about 1842, William about 1844, Adam in March 1847 — and the family spoke of themselves ever after as coming from Manchester, nine miles south of Bury and the name a Lancashire family abroad would naturally use. They crossed the Atlantic about 1850 or 1851: Sarah was born in Pennsylvania in 1851, Ralph there about 1856, and by about 1859, when Richard came, they had moved on to Ohio. It is the classic path of an English mining family — the Pennsylvania coalfield first, then the Ohio Valley pits.

At Syracuse, Meigs County, in 1860 he was forty-seven with Ann and six children in the house, the name written down as “Deckworth,” and he was still the head of his own household at fifty-six in 1870. Sarah married Moses Roush that September.

On 24 April 1874 the Meigs County probate court heard a case headed “In the Matter of the Insanity of James Duckworth.” James was present. On the sworn testimony of Wm Duckworth — almost certainly his own son William — and of Henry and August Bartels and David Thomas, the court found him insane, of less than two years’ duration, with a legal settlement in Sutton Township, and entitled to admission to the Lunatic Asylum of the State of Ohio at Athens, which had opened only three months before. Dr. Isaac Irwin was ordered to file his medical certificate; in the meantime the court directed that the patient be held in the county jail “separate and apart from those who are charged with crime.”

He was dead by June 1880, when Ann was a widow. Where he died, and where he lies, nobody knows; a man sent to a state asylum leaves behind him no will and no inventory.

123.s:
Ann Collins was born in Lancashire about 1818, the daughter of Adam Collins of Freetown, in Bury. She was still under twenty-one, and needed her father’s consent, when she married James Duckworth, a collier of Wood Head Hill, at St Mary’s, Bury, on 21 January 1839. Neither of them could write; both made their mark.

Three children came in England — Mary about 1842, William about 1844 and Adam in March 1847, named for her father. Then the family crossed to America, most likely in 1850 or 1851, and Sarah was born in Pennsylvania, Ralph about 1856, and Richard in Ohio about 1859.

In 1860 she was forty-three and keeping a house of eight at Syracuse, Meigs County, in the Ohio Valley coalfield. Her children married into the English and Cornish mining families around them: Mary to John W. Treadwell, himself a Manchester man; William to Sarah Pascoe, a Cornish name; Sarah to Moses Roush, and Adam eight days after Sarah, in the same township, in September 1870.

In April 1874 her husband was committed to the state asylum at Athens, and by June 1880 he was dead. Ann, sixty-two and widowed, kept her own house in Sutton Township, five households from her daughter Sarah, who had four children under ten. Sarah died the following March, and her mother was right there when it happened. After that nothing more is known of her — when and where she died, and where she is buried, are lost.

144.s:
Joseph Eakins came into New Hanover County, North Carolina about 1788 or 1790, a man of some twenty-four years with money in his pocket and no kin of his name anywhere in the county. Where he came from, nobody knows; it is the oldest unanswered question on this side of the family. On 11 June 1790 James Fleming, a Wilmington merchant, conveyed to “Joseph Eakins of the same place, Gentleman,” for fifteen pounds currency, two tracts: a hundred acres beginning at a black oak below the old track path, and three hundred acres on the east side of Moores Creek.

He worked that land for fifteen years. In December 1793 he sold a parcel to Jacob Moore, calling himself “planter” this time rather than gentleman. In 1796 he went to the state land office and took out a patent of his own — grant No. 482, two hundred and ten acres on the east side of the Widow Moore's Branch, beginning at a pine on the east side of the New Road in the meadow, signed at Raleigh by Samuel Ashe, Governor, Captain General and Commander in Chief. By then the surveyors' boundary calls were running past “a pine, Parker's corner, now Eakins.”

He married, almost certainly, Elizabeth Pigford, and they had six children: John, born about 1795, Sarah, Joseph, William, Deborah and Andrew.

He died in the first months of 1805, leaving children too young to act for themselves. At the March term the county court sent three men out to set aside his widow's year's provision, and they wrote down what they left in the yard to keep the household alive for twelve months: the corn in hand with the bacon, four cows and calves, one four-year-old steer, and the mark or right of hogs. On 11 April the rest went under the hammer — cattle, hogs, sheep, plantation tools, household furniture — and made $1,657.57. Edward and Jacob Pigford administered the estate, Timothy Pigford took the children, and Solomon Pigford stood security on its notes. He also left three people he had held in slavery, Simon, Rachel and Cesar, whose hired-out labour went on paying the estate's bills for years afterwards, including the schooling of his own sons.

The family never moved off that ground. His son Joseph bought the adjoining 138 acres in 1834, the deed running from “Joseph Eakins's own corner” along “Eakins's line”; and the Eakins Family Cemetery still stands on the Moores Creek land, in what is now Pender County. That son, born in 1797 and eight years old when his father died, lived to ninety-three; his is the oldest grave in it, and the newest is from 2019.

145.s:
Elizabeth Pigford was, in all probability, the wife of Joseph Eakins of Moores Creek and the mother of his six children — John, Sarah, Joseph, William, Deborah and Andrew. No record of the marriage survives, and so the “probably” stays in front of her name.

Her father was probably William “Lost Billie” Pigford of Sill's Creek, the shipwrecked orphan who ended a landowner on both banks of it, and whose 1801 will left a shilling each to a list of children that included “my daughter Elizabeth Aiken” — Aiken and Eakins being one name in the hands of New Hanover clerks.

What is beyond doubt is what happened when her husband died in the first months of 1805: the Pigfords closed around his family. Edward and Jacob Pigford administered the estate and ran the April auction. Solomon Pigford stood security on its notes. Timothy Pigford was guardian of the minor children for fourteen years, until the eldest, John, was old enough to take over at the February term of 1819. Four Pigfords in one court file is not neighbourliness; it is kin. And a Pigford was still selling Eakins land to an Eakins in 1834.

She is the “Widow Eakins” to whom the county court allotted a year's provision in March 1805 — the corn and the bacon, four cows and calves, a four-year-old steer and the mark or right of hogs that would keep her children fed while the estate was settled — and very likely the “Elizabeth Eakens” who was still holding a note of $220.76 against the estate in 1819. She is a woman the surviving papers keep pointing at and never quite name.

160.s:
Moore Stephens was born about 1796 in North Carolina, one of at least ten children of a Stephens household in Orange County whose father’s name has not survived. On 3 September 1817 he and his brother Charles bound themselves to the Governor in five hundred pounds that there was no lawful cause to obstruct his marriage to Rebecca Moize, with Joseph A. Woods witnessing. Both men signed the bond with a mark: Moore could not write his own name.

Within a few years the whole family picked up and went to Alabama — they were in Greene County by 1824 — and Moore worked his way west again into Sumter County. On 12 October 1846 the Greene County Orphans’ Court divided the estate of Mary Thorn among ten heirs at law in equal shares, and he was one of them, due $107.50 and receipting $95. The nine others were his brothers and sisters: William, Lewis, Charles and James Stephens, Nancy Barnett, Mary Barnett, Lucinda Ball, Elizabeth Beavers and Esther Hitt. He bought nothing at the sale, because by then he no longer lived in the county; the clerk’s cost bill files him under “Heirs of Sumter Co., Ala.” Two-thirds of what he inherited was the price of a human being — the sale raised $1,075.86 and $700 of it was paid for a woman named Jane, so about $70 of Moore’s share was her price.

In 1850 his house at dwelling 1190 in Sumter County held Moore, fifty-four, Rebecca, fifty, and the children Benjamin W. 21, James M. 18, John F. 16, Mary A. R. 13, Charles L. 12, Easter C. 10 and William K. 6 — and two more, Rebecca J. and Richard Hitt, both ten, the orphans of his dead sister Esther, being raised alongside his own. He had named a daughter Easter for that sister. His son Henry farmed six houses up the road. He himself held one enslaved person that year, a Black girl of about seven, born around 1843, whose name was never written down.

He was a man the county put its trust in. In 1853 and 1854 he stood surety three times alongside his neighbour Daniel Jones — twice on the administration of Thomas Fowler’s estate, for $1,200 and $2,800, and once on a $5,000 guardianship of Willis Thomas’s small children.

By 1860 he had moved on again: “Moore Stevens, 66, born North Carolina,” in Newton County, Mississippi, with Rebeca 55 and five children still at home. Henry brought his family to the same county. When Moore died is not known. The Newton County courthouse burned in September 1876, “supposed to have been of incendiary origin,” and the records that would have dated his death burned with it.

161.s:
Rebecca Moize was born about 1800 to 1805 in North Carolina, into a Moize family that had held the same few square miles of Orange County for generations and would still be in Lebanon Township there in 1880. Her parents are not known for certain; a family account names them Frederick Moize and Anne Ragland, and Frederick was buying land on Ellerbe Creek within three months of her wedding.

On 3 September 1817, at about seventeen, she married Moore Stephens in Orange County. Within seven years the couple were in Greene County, Alabama, and by the 1840s in Sumter County. She bore a large family — in 1850 seven of her children were still at home, from Benjamin W. at twenty-one down to William K. at six — and when Moore’s sister Esther Hitt died she took in Esther’s two orphaned children as well, Rebecca J. and Richard, both ten years old and listed in the household between her own.

She was still beside her husband at the next census, in Newton County, Mississippi, in 1860: “Rebeca Stevens, 55, born North Carolina” — forty-three years and two states from an Orange County wedding at seventeen. She was alive after that; when and where she died is not recorded.

176.s:
William Hampton Truett was born in 1806 in Sumter District, South Carolina, and became a preacher. His was the generation that carried the family out of the Carolina low country and onto the Alabama frontier — Darlington and Sumter districts to Henry County, in the south-eastern corner of Alabama, and from there west again.

On 10 October 1831, in Henry County, Wiley Peebles, a justice of the peace, married him to Alcey Wiggins and entered it as number 191 in the county book. She was a daughter of the Daniel Wiggins family, who had made the same journey out of Darlington. The Truetts and the Wigginses went on marrying each other in Alabama for another hundred years.

Their son John Wesley was born on 20 October 1833. A daughter, Winnie, married a Joshua Johnson, and the Johnsons’ son James Lafayette “Fate” Johnson was born in Clarke County in 1861.

He died in 1870 in Henry County, Alabama. For a preacher he left remarkably little behind him: no grave that anyone has found, no place in the register of the state’s Baptist ministers, and not a line in the history of the county where his widow and his son ended up. An Elige Truitt, who died in 1864 and is said to have been his brother, lies in the same Oak Grove graveyard at Chilton where his son John Wesley was buried fifty years later.

177.s:
Alcey Wiggins was born about 1813, almost certainly in Darlington District, South Carolina, and was very probably one of the two small girls in Daniel Wiggins’s house when the family was counted in Sumter District in 1820. Her parents, Daniel Wiggins and Susannah Truitt, had married at Darlington in 1800 and would end their lives in Henry County, Alabama.

She married at eighteen: on 10 October 1831, in Henry County, Wiley Peebles, a justice of the peace, married her to William Hampton Truett, a preacher. Their son John Wesley was born on 20 October 1833. A daughter, Winnie, married Joshua Johnson, and another daughter, Martha, became Martha Powers.

Widowed in 1870, she went to live with her son. In 1880 she was in John Wesley Truett’s household at Chilton in Clarke County, about sixty-seven years old — three generations of the family under one roof: the old preacher’s widow, her son the Confederate veteran who could not write, and her grandson William Curtis, Alec’s great-great-grandfather. She died that same year.

The Truetts and the Wigginses kept marrying each other. Her husband’s brother married her sister; Truett–Wiggins matches run on in the Alabama records into the twentieth century; and the neighbour who swore at Abbeville in 1870 that her daughter-in-law was an heir of the Ward estate was an Abijah Wiggins — very probably her own brother.

Syntha Ward — profile as it stood:

Syntha Ward — the clerks also wrote Cyntha, Cynthia and Cintha — was born in South Carolina about 1813, and both her own parents came from North Carolina. In October 1844 the Henry County clerk issued a licence to William H. Ward and “Syntha Armstrong,” and a justice of the peace, Wm. R. Kelly, married them on 18 December 1844. She was about thirty, and Armstrong may well be a first husband’s name rather than her own; a Wade Armstrong had married a Cynthia Bright in the same county in 1837. Since the marriage came eight years after her husband’s daughter Emily Caroline was born, she was probably that girl’s stepmother rather than her mother, and who Caroline’s mother was is an open question.

She kept his house at Rowville, where there were at least ten children between his and theirs. In 1850 she is “Syntha, 35” on the Henry County schedule beside her husband and eight children; in 1860 she is “Cyntha, 47” at Rowville, Beat 5. Her youngest son was given the unusual name Caraway — or Conway; it is written both ways — which is exactly the way a mother’s maiden surname usually travels, and the best clue anyone has to hers.

Her husband died without a will in February 1869, and on the 18th of September the court appointed a day to hear her application for dower, with notice to be published in the Henry County Register and J. H. Simonton named guardian ad litem for the minor heirs. Her dower was eighty acres, measured off by five freeholders on 23 November 1869 and chosen, the writ insisted, by men not connected to any of the parties by blood or by marriage. She took property at the estate sale against her own share, and rented the estate land for 1870 jointly with her son William, signing both papers with a mark.

In 1880 she was still at Rowville, sixty-six, widowed, keeping house, entered as MOTHER in the household of her youngest son Isaiah. She died sometime between 1880 and 1900, before Alabama began registering deaths. In every paper of her husband’s estate — the dower petition, the writ, the commissioners’ return, the sale petition, the depositions, her own receipts — she is Mrs Cynthia Ward, widow of the deceased, and nothing else; whatever family name she was born with has not survived.

178.s:
William H. Ward was born about 1806 in South Carolina and came west to the south-eastern corner of Alabama, to Henry County. He married at least twice. His first wife, the mother of Elizabeth, Emily Caroline, Sarah and John, is not named in any record that survives; she was living about 1842 and dead by the autumn of 1844. On 11 October 1844 the clerk issued a licence to him and Syntha Armstrong, very probably a widow, whom Wm. R. Kelly, a justice of the peace, married to him on 18 December that year.

In 1850 he was farming with four hundred dollars of land — “W. H. WARD, 44, m, Farmer, $400, S.C.” — with Syntha, thirty-five and South Carolina-born like himself, and eight children, every one of them born in Alabama. By 1860 he was at Rowville, Beat 5, aged fifty-three, with Cyntha and the younger children.

On 28 October 1854 he put his name to the best document he left behind. His daughter Emily Caroline was seventeen and wanted to marry John Truett, and Alabama required a parent’s consent for a bride under twenty-one, so the clerk copied his words straight into the marriage book: “I give my free and unqualified consent that license should issue for the marriage of John Truett with my daughter Emily C.” It is signed Wm. H. Ward in a firm, practised, unmistakably literate hand — which is worth noticing, because the bridegroom and the bride both signed their own papers with an X for the rest of their lives.

He died on 6 February 1869, without a will. Six weeks later his eldest son John E. Ward and his son-in-law C. J. Hutto swore to the date and asked the Probate Court at Abbeville for letters, and on 18 September the court set a day to hear his widow’s claim for dower, with notice ordered published for thirty days in the Henry County Register.

He left about a thousand dollars of land and twenty-five hundred dollars of personal estate, and most of the personal estate was other men’s promises: a hundred and thirty-nine dollars and ninety-seven cents in specie, thirty dollars and thirty cents in greenbacks, and eleven notes running from twenty-four dollars to three hundred and thirty, several of them marked doubtfull. The rest of the inventory is a working farm, counted down to the last tool: seven weeding hoes at three dollars, three grubbing hoes at two, four plough stocks, two iron wedges, an ox ring and staple. The family’s lawyers were Oates & Cowan of Abbeville, and W. C. Oates himself signed the receipt for their hundred and five dollars.

His land — three hundred and twenty acres, the north-west quarter of Section 5 and the north-east quarter of Section 6 in Township 6, Range 27 — could not be divided, so it was sold at the courthouse door at Abbeville on 12 December 1870 to his own son William H. Ward, named for him, for twelve hundred and sixty dollars on twelve months’ credit; the sale was confirmed on 11 December 1872. The petition for it, sworn on 28 September 1870, names every heir: the widow Cynthia; Ann Elizabeth Hutto; John E. Ward; Mary Nichols; Martha Driggers; William H. 192.s:
Gershom Tuttle was born on 11 June 1769 at Bristol, Connecticut — the third Gershom Tuttle in a row in this family, and almost certainly the son of the second, the Revolutionary conductor of teams, though that one link has never been put beyond doubt.

He married Pamelia Strong Clark at Farmington on 8 July 1788, when he was nineteen. In 1791 he and Joseph Tuttle, then of Wardsborough in Vermont, bought a fifty-acre lot at Wilmington in that state; by the mid-nineties the family had moved west to Paris, in Oneida County, New York, where he was the junior of two Gershom Tuttles in one small town. About 1800 he went north again into the new Black River country and opened a farm of 275 acres some five miles from the site of Watertown, in the town of Rutland.

He was there from the beginning. When Rutland held its first town meeting in March 1803, in David Coffeen’s house, he was one of the three men chosen highway commissioner — the same meeting that set a ten-dollar bounty on wolves. In 1806, with Seth Bailey, he built the first grist mill on that stretch of the Black River. He was a charter member of the Masonic lodge warranted at Watertown on 17 June 1806, entered on its roll as “Gershom Tuttle, Jr.” From 1808 he was one of the county’s commissioners for loaning the moneys of the state, and in 1810 he took five shares at ten dollars in the Black River Navigation Company. He traded, made potash, and kept a tavern on the great highway to the lake country.

The tavern is what his neighbours remembered. About 1803 a hundred men of Rutland and Watertown assembled there, by appointment, to settle a bet about which town could out-wrestle the other, the winners promised all they could eat and drink. The first Congregational church of Watertown, organised in 1803, met in his ball-room when it had nowhere else, and he was one of its original members. In June 1809 the county court fined him and Jabez Foster eight dollars each for not turning up as grand jurors. His family’s book remembered him as “a man of excellent character, genial temper, very fond of a joke, a capital story teller,” and that is the man everything else about him shows.

He was commissioned second major of the Jefferson County militia on 5 April 1805 and, on 4 April 1808, lieutenant-colonel of the 76th Regiment — the regiment the county histories simply call Tuttle’s. In the War of 1812 the Watertown militia belonged to it and were turned out en masse whenever invasion threatened; at the Battle of Sackets Harbor on 29 May 1813 they stood “in the edge of the woods, back of the clearing,” under Colonel Gershom Tuttle. He resigned his commission in 1814. (A second and quite unrelated Colonel Gershom Tuttle, of Massachusetts and of the regular army, died at that same post during the war and lies under the monument there.)

In 1816 he took the family on to Vigo County, Indiana, and settled in Otter Creek Township; a federal land clerk entered him in November 1817 first as “Gershom Tuttle, Jeff’n Co N.Y.” and, three weeks later, as “Gershom Tuttle, Fort Harrison.” He became a county commissioner in 1820. The last summer of his life a sheriff was advertising a half-quarter section, “the property of Gersham and Chester Tuttle,” for sale on execution at the suit of John F. King, and his patent for eighty acres came through under James Monroe’s hand on 15 July 1823, seven weeks before he died. On 29 August he made a will leaving everything to Pamelia for life and naming no child at all.

He died on the Friday night of 5 September 1823 in Otter Creek Township, in the fifty-fourth year of his age. Terre Haute’s first newspaper reported that “on Sunday last his remains were consigned to the earth, accompanied with Masonic honors by the Terre Haute Lodge of which he was a member” — which is how a Watertown lodge roll of 1806 came to matter eight hundred miles away. The estate turned out to be insolvent and was still in court nine years later. His grave has never been located.

193.s:
Pamelia Strong Clark was born at Farmington, Connecticut, on 4 November 1770. Clark was her surname; Strong was a middle name, and it descended four more generations — Clark Strong Tuttle, Dennis Clark, Richard Clark — long after anyone remembered where it had come from. Her brother was an officer of the United States Army and died while in charge of the federal arsenal at Troy, New York. On 8 July 1788, aged seventeen, she married Gershom Tuttle of Bristol.

She spent the next twenty-eight years moving west with him: Wilmington in Vermont, Paris in Oneida County, and about 1800 the new Black River country of Jefferson County, New York, where her husband farmed 275 acres, built a mill and kept the tavern whose ball-room served the neighbourhood for a church. Her son Chester was born at Sackets Harbor in 1796, Cynthia at Watertown in 1803, Amanda in 1810, Clark Strong in April 1811, Asa in 1813. In 1816 the family went on to Vigo County, Indiana.

Her husband died on 5 September 1823, leaving a will that gave her everything for life, with power to provide “for any of our children for whom she may think necessary to provide.” Three weeks later she gave bond as executrix, with Abraham and Henry Markle as her securities, and the inventory of the whole estate came to a little over six hundred dollars. It was insolvent, and her co-executor Nathaniel Huntington was out of the sheriff’s reach by 1829 and dead by 1831.

What followed is the hardest stretch of any life on this chart. The probate court cited her in January 1829, again in November 1829, and summoned her once more on 2 November 1830 to show cause “why she has not made a final settlement of the estate of Gursham Tuttle deceased, of which she is the executrix.” In March 1831 she petitioned, through a solicitor, to be let out of it, in words that are still painful to read: the estate’s business was “long since closed,” but “the papers of said Estate were left in the possession of Nathaniel Huntington Esq. who is dead, and they are now in so confused and mutilated a situation that no accurate statement of the condition of the Estate could be made from them.” On 29 December 1831 the court issued a writ of attachment for her body for contempt. The sheriff executed it on 2 February 1832 and charged eighty-three and a half cents in fees. Bail was set at ten dollars.

She outlived her husband by twenty-eight years, and in old age she followed one of her children ninety miles south into the hills of Brown County. She died on 22 April 1851, in her eighty-first year, and her stone at Southview Cemetery in Nashville reads: In Memory of PAMELIA TUTTLE DIED April 22 1851 Aged 80 Y’s, 5 M’s, 18 D’s — an age that counts back to the day she was born, 4 November 1770.

240.s:
John Roush was born on 22 November 1785 in Shenandoah County, Virginia, a son of George Roush and Catharine Zerkel, and was baptised into the Lutheran faith on 5 January 1786, with another John Roush and his wife Susannah standing as witnesses.

On 18 May 1808 Francis Watkins, a justice of the peace, married him to his own cousin Regina Roush, the daughter of Jonas Roush — a Roush marrying a Roush, both of them grandchildren of the same Shenandoah Valley family, and the name still written Rausch in that neighbourhood. Eleven children were born to them, and all of them, by the family’s own account, were baptised in the Lutheran church at New Haven.

Benjamin, the fifth, was born at Graham Station on the Virginia side in August 1816; Hannah was born in the Nease Settlement, in Sutton Township, Meigs County, Ohio, in May 1820. Between those two births John and Regina crossed the river for good, into the few square miles where the Roush and Nease families who later intermarried were founding neighbours — the same ground where their great-great-grandson John G. Roush would be born more than fifty years on. He was known in the family as “Blackbird John.”

He could not write. Every deed he made he signed “John his + mark Roush.” In the twenty months between July 1848 and March 1850 he settled land on four Roush men — Abel, James, John Junior and Benjamin. On 9 August 1849 he cut the east strip of Section 25, Town 3, Range 12 in two on a single day, before one justice and the same two witnesses: seventy acres running north from the south-east corner to John Roush Junior, and sixty-nine acres and twenty poles running south from the north-east corner to Benjamin, each for five hundred dollars. He was a widower by then; no wife joined in any of those deeds to release her dower.

He was sixty-six in 1850, living four doors up the road from Benjamin in Sutton Township. He died on 21 January 1861. Regina’s father Jonas had spent his last years in her house and lies in the same ground. For most of a century John’s and Regina’s graves went unmarked, though the neighbours could still point out the two of them, just north of Jonas’s. Today a granite stone at Gilmore Cemetery in Minersville carries the name ROUSH, and underneath, JOHN 1785 – 1861 and REGINA 1788 – 18. Whoever ordered it still could not supply her death year, and the cutter left the last two figures off.

241.s:
Regina Roush was born on 30 November 1788, the second child of Jonas Roush — a private of the Virginia line who was at the siege of Yorktown and saw Cornwallis surrender — and his wife Barbara Fox.

On 18 May 1808, at nineteen, she married her cousin John Roush before Francis Watkins, a justice of the peace. A Roush had married a Roush: both of them grandchildren of the same Shenandoah Valley family. Eleven children were born to them. Benjamin, the fifth, arrived at Graham Station on the Virginia bank in August 1816; Hannah, in May 1820, was born after the move across the Ohio into the Nease Settlement in Sutton Township, Meigs County.

Her father came to live with her. In June 1837 Jonas, by then an old pensioner of the Revolution, removed to Meigs County to be with a daughter, and he spent his last years in her house in the Nease Settlement, near where he now lies buried. He died there on 14 December 1850.

When she died is not known, and it was already beyond recovery within a lifetime of it. She had very probably gone before the summer of 1848: her husband was a widower by the time he began deeding his land away to his sons and kinsmen, with no wife to join in and release her dower.

She lies at Gilmore Cemetery in Minersville, beside her husband and near her father. The granite over the two of them reads JOHN 1785 – 1861 and REGINA 1788 – 18, and there the inscription stops.

In 1850 he was sixty-two, with a thousand dollars of land, keeping house with Margaret, fifty-six, also Pennsylvania-born, and four Ohio-born children at home: Jacob, twenty-three, and Solomon, nineteen, both farming with him, Mary, fourteen, and Samuel, twelve. A John Altman of about thirty-one, born in Ohio, kept a second Altman household in the same township, with a wife and four sons.

He was very probably the father of Sophia Altman, who was born in Ohio on 1 June 1823 and married Benjamin Roush in Meigs County in 1839 — she falls exactly into the gap between John, born about 1819, and Jacob, born about 1827, and she had married out of the house eleven years before his family was last counted — though nothing yet says so outright.

He was dead, or gone from Meigs County, by 1870.

Margaret Altman was born about 1794 in Pennsylvania, and was the wife of David Altman, a farmer of Sutton Township, Meigs County, Ohio. In 1850 she was fifty-six and he was sixty-two, with four of their children still at home: Jacob, twenty-three, Solomon, nineteen, Mary, fourteen, and Samuel, twelve.

Both she and her husband were Pennsylvania-born, and every one of their children was born in Ohio, the eldest of them so far traced being John, about 1819. So she came west over the mountains as a young woman, some time after 1815, and raised her family on the Ohio side of the river. Sophia Altman, born in Ohio in June 1823 and married to Benjamin Roush in Meigs County in 1839, was very probably her daughter, though nothing yet proves it.

Her own family name has not come down.

244.s:
George Duckworth was a hatter in the Bury district of Lancashire. Hatting was Bury’s trade beside cotton and coal, and a skilled one, but his son James went down the pit instead: when James married Ann Collins at the parish church of St Mary, Bury, on 21 January 1839, he was a collier of Wood Head Hill, and he signed for himself with a mark because he could not write. A Richard Duckworth was one of the witnesses that day and made his mark too — very likely George’s brother, or another son of his.

Whether George lived to see his son and daughter-in-law take their children across the Atlantic about 1850 is not known. Nothing else of his life has come down.

246.s:
Adam Collins was a crofter of Bury, Lancashire — very likely a worker at one of the bleaching crofts where the district’s cloth was laid out to whiten. In July 1820 he and his wife Betty, then living at Elton, west of the town, had their daughter Ann baptised at St Mary’s; by 1839 he was at Freetown, on the other side of Bury.

His daughter Ann was still under twenty-one in January 1839, so when she married James Duckworth, a collier of Wood Head Hill, at St Mary’s church on the 21st of that month, it was with her father’s consent. Neither bride nor groom could write; both of them made their mark.

Eight years later, and an ocean away from Bury, Ann and James named a son Adam. He was born on 14 March 1847, the only Adam among the Duckworths, was carried to America as a small boy, and died a miner in Sutton Township, Meigs County, Ohio, in 1919.

321.s:
Mary Thorn died in Greene County, Alabama, shortly before 23 January 1844. She was the widow of James Thorn, who had made his will on 12 June 1837 and whose estate was proved there in October 1839. His will names his own children but no wife at all, so she was probably his second wife and not the mother of his family; when his estate was finally settled on 14 October 1844 his sons Jesse W. and William H. Thorn released every claim against hers.

Her own next of kin were Stephenses. The court that opened her estate on 23 January 1844 cited Moore, James, Lewis and William Stephens, Esther Hitt, Lucinda Ball and Elizabeth Bevers as her nearest relations; James Stephens was appointed administrator; and when the estate was divided on 12 October 1846 it went in ten equal shares to that same set of brothers and married sisters, with the share of Esther Hitt — by then dead — going to her “Representatives,” the way a court treats a predeceased child. In all likelihood Stephens was her first married name and Thorn her second, which would make those ten her children; nothing says so outright, and she may equally have been their sister or their aunt.

Her inventory, taken on 27 April 1844, catalogues her entire world down to an eighteen-cent umbrella and a woman’s saddle — and then one line worth more than all the rest together: “1 Negro woman Jane — 475.00.” Jane had very likely come to her as part of her widow’s share of James Thorn’s estate. She had been hired out for seventeen months, and she was sold at the estate sale on 29 April 1844 to the administrator, James Stephens, for $700. The whole sale raised $1,075.86, so Jane was sixty-five per cent of everything Mary Thorn owned, and roughly $70 of Moore Stephens’s $107 share was her price.

Mary had also been lending money to the men around her: her papers include promissory notes on Charles Stephens for $15.13 and $32.40 and on Lewis Stephens for $100 — she was banking her sons. Her land was sold at the ordinary sale to Andrew Norwood for $127.09.

352.s:
The Reverend William Hampton Truett’s father is not known. Two men stand in the slot, and there is nothing to choose between them on paper: Elisha Truitt, given as 1786–1864, and Noel Truett, given as 1769–1850.

Elisha is the likelier of the two, and the reason is the names and the neighbourhood. John Wesley Truett called a son Elisha Dozier Truett in 1877, and men of that generation named children for their grandfathers almost as a rule. An Elige Truitt, who died in 1864, lies in the little Oak Grove graveyard at Chilton in Clarke County, the same ground as John Wesley Truett, and the family has long held him to be William Hampton’s brother, with a third brother, Curtis Forby. An Elijah Truett served as a private in a Clarke County company in 1861. If that reconstruction holds, Elisha is the man who brought the family out of Darlington District, South Carolina, into Alabama.

Noel Truett leaves almost no footprint of his own. The one place the name turns up in this family is as the supposed father of Suzanna Truitt, the woman who married Daniel Wiggins in 1800 — a different person in a different generation, which may well be how it came to be attached here at all.

384.s:
Gershom Tuttle was born on 22 August 1738 at Farmington, Connecticut — in the parish of New Cambridge, which later became the town of Bristol. His father was Ensign Gershom Tuttle and his mother was Lois Allis.

On 22 December 1757, at Deerfield in Massachusetts, he married Tabitha Mitchell, and he married inside his mother’s family: Tabitha’s mother Mary Allis and his own mother Lois were sisters, so bride and groom were first cousins. The wedding was at Deerfield because that was where the bride was at home; the clerk styled him “of New Cambridge”, the outsider of the two.

His father died in 1777, leaving a will made that May which gave the widow Lois a third for life and divided the rest among “my Three Sons Gershom, Oliver and Samuel Tuttle,” and appointed “my Son Gershom Tuttle whole and sole Executor.” The account of “Gershom Tuttel Executor” was allowed in January 1779.

He is a patriot of the Revolution, and his war was logistics rather than battle — which in Connecticut in 1780 mattered as much. He was a conductor of teams: he ran wagon trains of provisions out of Connecticut into New York State, some three thousand barrels, about five hundred tons, averaging a hundred and fifteen miles a haul. On 23 May 1780 the Connecticut General Assembly paid him £285.13.8 in wages and £60.13.11 for forage in advance, and still owed him £200.2.8; he stands first of the nine conductors on the list. The Daughters of the American Revolution honour him as ancestor A131791, rank teamster — “Conductor of teams transporting supplies for the army.”

After the war he moved north to Claremont, New Hampshire, where his father had died, and on 17 December 1789 he signed a town recommendation of Ambrose Cossitt as justice of the peace, with his brother Oliver and his son Solomon; in 1790 he was keeping house there. About 1790 he went on to Clinton in Oneida County, New York, and afterwards joined the settlement at Watertown in Jefferson County. His family’s book made him the first deacon of Watertown’s first church, organised in 1803, although the deaconship of 1808 may really have belonged to his son. He lived to see that son become a colonel of militia there.

He died on 5 January 1818, in his eightieth year. Where he died, and where he lies, nobody now knows.

Full dates: b. 9 Feb 1736/7 – m. 22 Dec 1757, Deerfield; daughter of Joseph Mitchell and Mary Allis

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ THE DAR DOES NOT KNOW HER GIVEN NAME — AND WE DO [TUTTLE-46, 7 August 2026]. On DAR ancestor record A131791 the patriot’s wife is listed only as “X MITCHEL” — surname, no more. This project has her as Tabitha Mitchell, married at Deerfield 22 December 1757, with her parents Joseph Mitchell and Mary Allis and her grandfather Michael Mitchell of Wallingford, all from records. Alec is in a position to give the DAR something it does not have — worth saying to the registrar when the application goes in.

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ HER PARENTS FOUND — AND GERSHOM II MARRIED HIS FIRST COUSIN [TUTTLE-41]. History of the Town of Sunderland, image 567: “MITCHELL, Joseph, m. Nov. 2, 1726, MARY, dau. WILLIAM ALLIS.” And from the Allis side, image 355: “Ch.: MARY, b. Feb. 18, 1705; m. Joseph Mitchell. … LOIS, b. Jan. 13, 1708; m. Oct. 17, 1737, Gershom Tuttle.” ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ MARY ALLIS AND LOIS ALLIS WERE SISTERS. Lois married Gershom Tuttle I. Her sister Mary married Joseph Mitchell. Twenty years later Lois’s son married Mary’s daughter. TABITHA MITCHELL WAS GERSHOM II’S FIRST COUSIN, and the 1757 Deerfield marriage stops being a mystery entirely — he married inside his mother’s family. ⭐ It also explains the Deerfield venue: the bride was local and the groom was styled “of New Cambridge” [TUTTLE-26] — the DEERFIELD hypothesis, preferred over the Farmington one in TUTTLE-24, is confirmed. ⛔⛔ AND IT HALF-CLOSES THE MAYFLOWER DOOR [MAYFLOWER-01]. Her MOTHER’S line is the ALLIS line already on this chart — Braintree freeman 1640, Massachusetts Bay, not Plymouth. The Mayflower question now rests on her FATHER Joseph Mitchell alone, whose origin the Sunderland book does not give. ——— Earlier note: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ HER BIRTH AND HER FAMILY FOUND — 6 Aug 2026 [TUTTLE-40]. Sheldon, History of Deerfield vol. 2, image 505, in the MITCHELL genealogy: “Ch.: Joseph, Mar. 3, 1726-7, in SUND[ERLAND]. TABITHA, Feb. 9, 1736-7; m. Dec. 22…” The marriage day and month match ours exactly — 22 December 1757 — and the birth of 9 February 1736/7 sits inside the c.1735–40 window TUTTLE-24 predicted for her when the Farmington Mitchel hypothesis was killed. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ AND THE FAMILY WAS AT SUNDERLAND. Her brother was born there in 1726-7. Sunderland is the town where the groom’s own parents married in 1737 [node 769]. Father and son married women from the same small Connecticut Valley town, twenty years apart. That is not coincidence; that is a family that kept its Massachusetts ties. ⚠ Her father is almost certainly JOSEPH MITCHELL of Deerfield — Sheldon has daughters Hannah (m. Zadock King 1751), Thankful, Mary (m. Samuel — of Ashfield, 1753) and Lydia all styled “dau. Joseph Mitchell”, plus the son Joseph. Recorded as a strong identification, not yet a proved one — the head-of-family paragraph has not been read. ⭐⭐⭐⭐ AND THIS IS THE ONE PLACE A MAYFLOWER LINE COULD ENTER THIS TREE [MAYFLOWER-01]. The Plymouth Colony Mitchells descend from EXPERIENCE MITCHELL, who came on the ANNE in 1623 and married JANE COOKE, daughter of FRANCIS COOKE, MAYFLOWER PASSENGER, 1620. ⭐ And Sheldon’s own pages carry the tell: “FULLER, John; m. July 12, 1774, EXPERIENCE MITCHELL of Ash[field]” — the given name “Experience” running in this very Mitchell family in this very valley is the classic marker of descent from him. ⚠⚠ A MARKER IS NOT A DESCENT. Mitchell is a common name and no link is shown. Nothing about the Mayflower goes on this chart until Joseph Mitchell’s own father is documented. ——— Earlier note: Married at Deerfield, Massachusetts — “TUTTLE, Gershom of New Cambridge, C[onn.] … Mitchel, Dec. 22, 1757.” ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 6 Aug 2026 — THE FIRST CHECKABLE LEAD ON HER FAMILY [TUTTLE-23]: the complete signer list of the October 1742 New Cambridge petition — the one GERSHOM TUTTLE SR. signed — includes “Joel mitchel.” A MITCHEL was living in that small Connecticut parish fifteen years before the groom’s son married a Tabitha Mitchell.

Outstanding: ⚠⚠ A LEAD, NOT A PROOF — Joel is not shown to be her father. ⚠ And it cuts both ways: the Deerfield entry styles the GROOM “of New Cambridge” but gives the bride no parish, which is what a clerk does for a LOCAL bride. Test both hypotheses in parallel: ① a TABITHA MITCHELL born at Farmington c.1735–1740 (cheapest test; would give her parents for the first time); ② Joel Mitchel’s own family; ③ the Deerfield/Hampshire Co. Mitchells. ⚠⚠ TESTED ONE TURN LATER AND LARGELY FAILED [TUTTLE-24]. Joel Mitchel is confirmed real and really at Farmington — his eldest child Mary was born there 2 Sept 1743, eleven months after the petition — but his first recorded child is 1743, AFTER Tabitha’s c.1735–40 birth window, no Tabitha appears among his seven children, and he moved to WETHERSFIELD from 1746 onward. ⛔ By the 1757 marriage the Mitchels had left New Cambridge. ⛔ And no Connecticut or Massachusetts birth for a Tabitha Mitchell 1730–1742 exists in the FS index at all — 3,822 results, and the only New England hit is the 1757 marriage itself. At that point she still had no parent, no birth date and no place. ⛔ SUPERSEDED WITHIN THE WEEK — self-correction #385, 10 Sep 2026. [TUTTLE-40] and [TUTTLE-41], at the top of this node, gave all three: born 9 February 1736/7, father Joseph Mitchell, mother Mary Allis, the family at Sunderland. This sentence is retained only to show what the search looked like before it landed — it is not the current state of the question. ⭐ The DEERFIELD hypothesis is now the stronger one — the entry styles the GROOM “of New Cambridge” (an outsider) and gives the bride no parish (a local). NEXT: the Deerfield and Hampshire Co. Mitchells, and the 1757 entry read AT THE IMAGE — the printed abstract may drop a father or a parish the register carries.

⭐⭐⭐⭐ HER FATHER’S WILL, read at the page 13 Sep 2026 [TUTTLE-147 §⑤]: the will of Joseph Mitchell of Deerfield, dated 14 April 1792 and proved 25 Nov 1794 (Hampshire Co., Mass. Probate Records vol. 19–20, entry 91): “I give to my Daughter Tabitha Wife of Gersham Tuttle Twelve Pounds,” beside her sisters Mary Belding and Hannah Bigelow and the children of “my late Son Joseph.” This documents Tabitha’s parentage and her marriage by record, and shows her ALIVE in April 1792 — the unsourced “1737–1782” is refuted. It contradicts SAR’s Patriot Research System entry for P-308288, which gives the patriot’s spouse as “Catherine Stevens” from a 2002 index. The Joel Mitchel lead above is superseded.

⭐ 27 Oct 2026 — bio-and-photo sweep. Find a Grave's memorial for her husband carries, from a contributor, exactly the parentage this project proved from records — confirmation from an independent compiler, not a new fact. [TUTTLE-215]

⭐ 28 Oct 2026 — moved from the bio. Out of the story: “and the match was not the mystery it looked like for years” and “the Deerfield venue needs no explaining” — both about the search, not about her; and the three-part evidence sentence on her father’s will, “That one clause does three things: it documents her parentage from a record, it documents her marriage, and it shows her alive in the spring of 1792 — which refutes the unsourced ‘1737–1782’ that followed her around” [TUTTLE-147 §④]. The bio keeps the will’s own words and the fact that she was alive in 1792. Also moved: “This family knows her first name, her birthday, her parents and her grandfather, all from records, and the national society that honours her husband does not” [TUTTLE-46] — the bio keeps the wry fact of the ‘X Mitchel’ entry without the comparison.
385.s:
Tabitha Mitchell was born on 9 February 1736/7, the daughter of Joseph Mitchell and Mary Allis. The family was at Sunderland, in the Connecticut valley of Massachusetts, where her brother Joseph had been born in 1726/7, and afterwards at Deerfield.

On 22 December 1757, at Deerfield, she married Gershom Tuttle of New Cambridge in Connecticut — her own first cousin. Her mother Mary Allis and his mother Lois Allis were sisters: Lois had married the elder Gershom Tuttle in 1737, and twenty years later Lois’s son married Mary’s daughter. The wedding was at Deerfield because the bride was at home there.

She went with him through Connecticut, through the Revolution, north to New Hampshire and on into New York. Her father’s will, made on 14 April 1792 and proved in November 1794, gives “to my Daughter Tabitha Wife of Gersham Tuttle Twelve Pounds,” beside her sisters Mary Belding and Hannah Bigelow and the children of “my late Son Joseph” — so she was still living in the spring of 1792, in her middle fifties.

Her name very nearly did not survive at all. On the Daughters of the American Revolution’s own file for her husband she is “X Mitchel” — a surname and nothing else.

ph.w: NAMED BUILDING of the event that destroyed this family's Deerfield branch. HABS: 'The "Old Indian House" was built in Deerfield about 1698 for Capt. John Sheldon. John Catlin and his daughter Alice (wife of Samuel Allis) were killed in that raid; Sarah Catlin, who married Michael Mitchell, survived it. This is the house they would all have known, not the Catlins' own.

480.s:
George Roush was born in July 1761 in Frederick County, Virginia — the part of it that became Shenandoah County eleven years later — one of the younger sons of the German immigrant John Adam Roush and his wife Susannah. He grew up on Mill Creek in a house where the Bible was printed in German, and he was eighteen when the Revolution reached him.

He enlisted in the autumn of 1779 and served two months under his own brother, Captain John Roush, “both of Shenandoah County Virginia.” He was drafted again in the spring of 1780 under Captain Joseph Pugh, and a third time in 1781 for three months — that tour, his brother Jonas later swore, as a substitute for another brother, Jacob. The family always told that he was at Yorktown and saw Cornwallis hand over his sword; his brother Jonas certainly was. He applied for a pension from Ohio in 1832 and it was allowed as claim S18579, and the Daughters of the American Revolution carry him as Patriot Ancestor A098975.

About 1781, in Shenandoah County, he married Catharine Zerkel, the eldest daughter of Michael and Catharine Zerckel of Forestville. Their children, born over more than twenty years, included Michael, Magdalena, John — who in 1808 married his cousin Regina, Jonas Roush’s daughter — Daniel, Lewis, Catherine, Samuel, Susannah, Jacob, Mary and a second Jonas.

He went down the Ohio ahead of his family about 1798, taking up land in Mason County with his brother Captain John, in whose name the purchase was made; his son Jacob was still born and baptised back in Shenandoah County in 1799. In 1807 he crossed to Sutton Township, Meigs County, Ohio, bought a level tract from Edward W. Tupper west of the hamlet of Dorcas, near Racine, and lived on it for the rest of his life. He was a mechanic by trade — “a very good one, we are told,” the family said — and a farmer, and when Meigs County organised itself in 1819 he sat among its first jurors. He had been a citizen of three counties at the moment each was created.

Catharine died in Virginia, after a journey home she had pined for; her burial place was never written down. On 13 August 1815, at Gallipolis, George married a widow, Catherine “Kitty” Wolfe, and they had one daughter, Hannah.

One Sunday morning a schoolmaster boarding in the Roush house — one of the Henkels, the Lutheran printing family of New Market, the family believed — asked to sketch him. After “considerable reluctance” George gave in, put on the coat of his uniform, and sat. The small sketch stayed in the family at Racine for a century, kept by Elizabeth Wilcoxin and then by James L. Wilcoxin, and was carried out to Meigs County pioneer meetings to be looked at. Of the nine Roush brothers who went to that war, he is the only one whose face is known.

In his last illness he talked about charging the British, and told his comrades to get ready, they were coming over the hill. He died on 31 May 1845 and lies in Weldon Cemetery, on the third terrace above the Ohio at Racine, Meigs County. His small marble stone is still legible: “GEORGE ROUSH … DIED May 31, 1845 AGED 84 years.” On 19 August 1933, before about a thousand descendants, the Sons of the American Revolution dedicated a grave marker there; the flat marker lying at the foot of his headstone today reads “GEORGE ROUSH / CONTINENTAL LINE / REVOLUTIONARY WAR / JUL 1761 – MAY 1845,” and it gets his war wrong — all three of his terms were Virginia militia, not the Continental Line. His German Bible, said to have come from his father out of Germany, was still in the family in 1928, in the hands of a great-granddaughter at Racine.

481.s:
Catharine Zerkel was born on 14 August 1763 in Shenandoah County, Virginia — so the family’s own reckoning has it — the eldest of the fourteen children of Michael and Catharine Zerckel of Forestville, with Henry Brock and his wife Magdalene standing as her baptismal sponsors. She was a married woman at seventeen, sponsoring a baptism herself in October 1780, and she married George Roush in Shenandoah County about 1781.

Her first child was born in January 1783, and there were a dozen more over the next twenty years, among them John, born 22 November 1785, who married his cousin Regina Roush. She went west with her husband — to Mason County about 1798, then across the Ohio into Meigs County in 1807.

The one story the family kept about her is a homesick one. In declining health she pined for the Virginia home, and at last George set out with her, more than three hundred miles over the mountains on horseback and on foot. They came up the Shenandoah and stood the horses in the door yard of the old plantation. “The joy was too great, she was overwhelmed and wept as a child.” She did not live long after, and was buried somewhere in Virginia; nobody wrote down where. A later Zirkle family historian guessed the old Nease–Zirkle graveyard on Holman’s Creek, where her father and mother lie, but he was guessing. Her husband married again in August 1815, so she was dead by then; the year itself has never been recovered.

482.s:
Jonas Roush was born in September 1763 at Holman’s Fort in Frederick County, Virginia — soon to be Shenandoah County — the youngest of the sons of John Adam and Susannah Roush. He was seventeen when his turn came in the Revolution, and he told the story himself, on oath, before the court at Mason County, Virginia, on 6 November 1832.

He “entered the service as a substitute for his Brother Henry Roush who was drafted for a tour of three months in the summer of 1781,” served under Captain All in Colonel Bird’s regiment at Falmouth near Fredericksburg, and went out again on a second three-month tour. That tour took him to the siege of Yorktown, and he was there on 19 October 1781 when Cornwallis’s army surrendered. He fell ill near Fredericksburg while escorting prisoners. His pension was allowed at twenty dollars a year from 4 March 1831 as claim S4785, and the Daughters of the American Revolution carry him as Patriot Ancestor A098985.

He married Barbara Fox, of a Shenandoah County family settled near Forestville. Their daughter Regina, born 30 November 1788, married her cousin John Roush in 1808 — the marriage that doubles back through Alec’s tree, so that Jonas and his brother George both stand as his ancestors. Their other children were Abraham, John, Adam and Philip.

Like his brothers he came down the Ohio, and he was living in Mason County, Virginia when he applied for his pension. That same year, 1832, his brother Daniel made him executor of a will leaving the residue of the estate “equally divided among the children of my brothers Jonas, George, Henry, Philip and Jacob.” Barbara died in the mid-1830s, and in 1837 he gave up his own household, moved his pension across to Meigs County, Ohio, and spent his last years in his daughter Regina’s house in the Nease Settlement, in Sutton Township. Whether he died on the Ohio bank or back on the Virginia one has never been settled; the two places are opposite sides of the same water.

He died on 14 December 1850, aged eighty-seven, and lies in Gilmore Cemetery at Minersville, Meigs County, Ohio, the burying ground of that settlement. John and Regina were laid beside him in graves that were never marked. His own stone is still there, worn but standing, and two later Revolutionary War markers have been set by it: an upright government headstone, “JONAS ROUSH / PVT / VA TROOPS / REV WAR / 1763 1850,” and a flat bronze, “JONAS ROUSH / PVT VA REGIMENT / REVOLUTIONARY WAR.”

483.s:
Barbara Fox was born about 1766 into a Fox family — Fuchs, in the older spelling — settled near Forestville in Shenandoah County, Virginia, prominent enough in the neighbourhood to stand among the leading names of the district in the first federal census. She married Jonas Roush, probably in Shenandoah County, in the 1780s.

Her daughter Regina, born 30 November 1788, married her cousin John Roush in 1808, and is Alec’s ancestor twice over; there were other children — Abraham, John, Adam and Philip — and the family moved down the Ohio with the rest of the Roush connection into Mason County, Virginia.

She died on 21 October 1836, aged seventy, by the stone that stands over her in Gilmore Cemetery at Minersville, Meigs County, Ohio: “BARBARA / WIFE OF / JONAS ROUSH / DIED / OCT 21 1836 / AGED / 70 YEARS.” It is very probably hers, though it carries no maiden name. Her husband’s pension papers put her death a few months later, in February 1837, and nobody has reconciled the two. Either way she was dead before Jonas gave up his household and crossed the river to live with Regina, and he was buried in the same ground fourteen years after her.

768.s:
Gershom Tuttle was born at Wallingford, Connecticut, on 11 August 1714, the fifth child of Timothy Tuttle — the deacon who had cleared his own farm west of the river — and Thankful Doolittle. He grew up in the Cheshire parish, and as a young man he left Connecticut altogether for the Massachusetts frontier above Northfield, where his father held a proprietor’s right in one of the new townships. He lodged for a time at Northfield with his mother’s brother, the Reverend Benjamin Doolittle, who was minister there. In 1736, when he was already settled up in Hampshire County, his father signed the whole of that right over to him — given, the deed said, for “love, good will and fatherly affection.”

A year later, on 17 October 1737, he married Lois Allis in her own family’s town of Sunderland. By 1739–40 he was buying land back at Farmington, Connecticut. He had gone home with a whole colony of Cheshire people who settled on Chippen’s Hill in the remote parish of New Cambridge — the place that is now Bristol — and there he was prominent in church and town affairs. In October 1742 he put his name to the petition of the inhabitants of New Cambridge asking for a winter preacher; it went down as “Gerfhum Tuttle.” His children came in a steady file: Gershom in 1738, Oliver in 1739, Eunice in 1743, Hannah in 1745, Samuel in 1747, Huldah in 1749, and a daughter Lois about 1751.

He served in the French and Indian Wars, and the rank he carried out of them stayed with him for the rest of his life: he was Ensign Gershom Tuttle at Bristol in 1761 and still Ensign in 1770, and that is how his daughter Lois’s gravestone names him when she died on 5 January 1769 in her eighteenth year — “Lois Daugtr of En[s]n Garshum & Mrs Lois Tutle.”

After that he moved the family north a second time, to Claremont, New Hampshire, and this time he stayed. The spring of 1777 took his small grandson Daniel, Oliver’s boy, buried at four years old on 2 March. On 9 May Gershom made his will. He left his “wellbeloved Wife Lois” the use of a third of his estate, half his household goods to his daughter Eunice, wife of Abner Matthews, and the other half to his “Four motherless Grandchildren Hannah Gurdon Asa and Louisa Johnson,” and divided everything else between his three sons, Gershom, Oliver and Samuel, with his son Gershom as sole executor. He died on 13 August 1777, two days after his sixty-third birthday, in the second summer of the Revolution, while that son was away conducting provision teams for the Connecticut Assembly; the will was proved at Farmington on 27 September. He lies in Union Cemetery at Claremont, section B, lot 106, under a slate stone cut with a winged soul effigy: “In Memory of En[sig]n Gershom Tuttle … A Man of Sober Life, Who Lived beloved & Lamented died.”

769.s:
Lois Allis was born at Hatfield, Massachusetts, on 13 January 1707/8, the second daughter of William Allis and his wife Elizabeth. While she was small the family moved up the Connecticut River to Sunderland, and it was there, in her father’s own parish, that she married on 17 October 1737. She was twenty-nine. Her husband, Gershom Tuttle, was a Connecticut man who had come north to take up land his father held in one of the new frontier townships.

They went back to Connecticut together, to the New Cambridge parish of Farmington on Chippen’s Hill, and the next twelve years were given over to children: Gershom in 1738, Oliver in 1739, Eunice in 1743, Hannah in 1745, Samuel in 1747, Huldah in 1749. A daughter born about 1751 was given her mother’s name. That younger Lois died on 5 January 1769, in her eighteenth year, and the stone raised over her at Bristol names both her parents — “Lois Daugtr of En[s]n Garshum & Mrs Lois Tutle.”

The Allis tie held across two generations. Her elder sister Mary had married Joseph Mitchell of the same valley, and in 1757 Mary’s daughter Tabitha married Lois’s son Gershom — the cousins married, and the same Massachusetts grandparents stand twice in this family.

She was still living in May 1777, when her husband made his will at Farmington and left “my wellbeloved Wife Lois” the use of a third of his estate for life. Where she died, and when, is not known. She is not buried beside him at Claremont, New Hampshire, and she is not in the Bristol burying ground that holds her daughter.

770.s:
Joseph Mitchell was born in 1705, the third son of Michael Mitchell and Sarah Catlin, into a household that had come through the Deerfield raid of the year before untouched while his mother’s family was all but destroyed. He was bred a weaver, not a farmer.

On 2 November 1726 he married Mary Allis, daughter of William Allis of Sunderland; their first child, a son Joseph, was born at Sunderland four months later. Then came daughters — Hannah, who married Zadock King in 1751; Mary, married in 1753; Thankful; Lydia; and, on 9 February 1736/7, Tabitha, who in 1757 married Gershom Tuttle of Farmington and so carried this line forward. There was a son Abner as well. The family lived a few years at Sunderland, then moved to Deerfield, and after that up into the hills to the west, to Ashfield.

At Ashfield he kept the first house of public entertainment in the town — or his son of the same name did; nothing in that town’s books ever says which Joseph Mitchell is meant. From about 1763 the inn stood on the east side of Bellows Hill, and it was to “the house of Joseph Mitchell, innholder” that the voters were summoned for Ashfield’s first legal town meeting on 6 January 1766. At that meeting Joseph Mitchell was chosen constable, and the town went on meeting in his tavern until the meeting house was partly finished in January 1771. He was also one of the handful of men who signed the covenant when the church there was gathered. His daughter Mary’s husband, Samuel Belding, was the town’s first selectman and the man who carried the warrant round. Long afterwards people in Ashfield said the old Deacon Ziba Smith house was the Mitchell tavern, moved.

Mary died on 8 November 1783. Nine years later, on 14 April 1792, describing himself as of Deerfield, Joseph made his will. He gave twelve pounds each to his daughters Mary, wife of Samuel Belding, Hannah Bigelow, and “my Daughter Tabitha Wife of Gersham Tuttle”; eight shillings each to five grandchildren, the children of “my late Son Joseph”; and the land and the residue to his son Abner. He died on 16 September 1794 at Ashfield, and the will was proved at Northampton on 25 November.

771.s:
Mary Allis was born at Hatfield, Massachusetts, on 18 February 1705, the eldest child of William Allis and Elizabeth his wife, and three years older than her sister Lois. The family moved upriver to Sunderland while the girls were small.

On 2 November 1726 she married Joseph Mitchell, a weaver of the Deerfield Mitchells; their first son was born at Sunderland four months after the wedding. Six more children followed — Hannah, Mary, Thankful, Lydia, Abner, and Tabitha, born 9 February 1736/7 — and the household moved from Sunderland to Deerfield and in the end to Ashfield, where her husband kept the tavern the town was born in. She died on 8 November 1783, at seventy-eight.

She joins this family’s tree twice over. In 1757 her daughter Tabitha married Gershom Tuttle, the son of her sister Lois — first cousins marrying — so the two Allis sisters are ancestors of the same descendants, and their own parents stand in two places on one pedigree.

960.s:
John Adam Roush — Johannes Adam Rausch — was born in 1711 in the Palatinate, and the family has always said Darmstadt. He crossed to Philadelphia in the closing months of 1736 and took the oath of fidelity there. The tradition carried down into the twentieth century was that he and two companions, forbidden to emigrate, were hidden inside hogsheads by a friendly cooper, loaded aboard, and let out at sea. He landed too poor to pay his passage, hired himself out near Philadelphia, stayed on past his term because he was paid unusually well, and then married and went down the Shenandoah Valley.

He settled on Mill Creek in what was then Frederick County — later Dunmore, then Shenandoah — and farmed it; the family says he kept a mill and a tannery as well, and more than thirty land transactions stand in his name or his sons’. In 1773 a grant of four hundred acres on Mill Creek was made “to him and his wife Susannah.” By then he had been in the valley more than thirty years and had raised a large family: the sons Philip, John, Jacob, Henry, Daniel, George and Jonas, and the daughters Mary Magdalene, Eleanor and Elizabeth. The family has always said that nine sons went out of that house.

Every one of those sons went into the Revolution, and so, in his sixties, did he: he furnished supplies to the army between 1780 and 1783 and took a Shenandoah County claim certificate, number 2453, for the property impressed from him. The Daughters of the American Revolution carry him for it as Patriot Ancestor A098982. One son was a captain with two of his brothers in the ranks; two of them substituted for each other; one of them witnessed another’s pension application fifty years later.

He was a Lutheran, and the family were tanners and builders of churches. He died on 19 October 1786 near New Market in Shenandoah County and was buried at the Old Pine Church. His gravestone survives — a rough slab cut in German by someone who spelled by ear: ANO 1711 GEBOHREN JOHANNES RAUSCH GESTORBEN DEN 19 OCTOBER 1786. The Adam had already dropped out of his name. When the old burying ground’s stones were moved to St Mary’s Pine Church Cemetery at Mount Jackson in 1868 his went with them, and it is kept upright there under glass with a Sons of the American Revolution patriot star beside it. Susannah outlived him by ten years and lies beside him in a grave that was never marked. In 1936, two hundred years after his crossing, the Roush and Allied Families Association raised a monument over the two of them that names their children one by one and reckons their descendants, living and dead, at about forty thousand American citizens.

Alec’s descent reaches him three times over, because two of his grandchildren married each other. This is the first of the three paths, and it runs through his son George, the Revolutionary soldier who lies at Weldon Cemetery in Ohio — a son by the family’s own settled account rather than by the word of any surviving record.

The tradition carried down into the twentieth century was that he and two companions, forbidden to emigrate, were hidden inside hogsheads by a friendly cooper, loaded aboard, and let out at sea. He landed too poor to pay his passage, hired himself out near Philadelphia, stayed on past his term because he was paid unusually well, and then married and went down the Shenandoah Valley.

He settled on Mill Creek in what was then Frederick County — later Dunmore, then Shenandoah — and farmed it; the family says he kept a mill and a tannery as well, and more than thirty land transactions stand in his name or his sons’. In 1773 a grant of four hundred acres on Mill Creek was made “to him and his wife Susannah.” By then he had been in the valley more than thirty years and had raised a large family: the sons Philip, John, Jacob, Henry, Daniel, George and Jonas, and the daughters Mary Magdalene, Eleanor and Elizabeth. The family has always said that nine sons went out of that house.

Every one of those sons went into the Revolution, and so, in his sixties, did he: he furnished supplies to the army between 1780 and 1783 and took a Shenandoah County claim certificate, number 2453, for the property impressed from him. The Daughters of the American Revolution carry him for it as Patriot Ancestor A098982. One son was a captain with two of his brothers in the ranks; two of them substituted for each other; one of them witnessed another’s pension application fifty years later.

He was a Lutheran, and the family were tanners and builders of churches. He died on 19 October 1786 near New Market in Shenandoah County and was buried at the Old Pine Church. His gravestone survives — a rough slab cut in German by someone who spelled by ear: ANO 1711 GEBOHREN JOHANNES RAUSCH GESTORBEN DEN 19 OCTOBER 1786. The Adam had already dropped out of his name. When the old burying ground’s stones were moved to St Mary’s Pine Church Cemetery at Mount Jackson in 1868 his went with them, and it is kept upright there under glass with a Sons of the American Revolution patriot star beside it. Susannah outlived him by ten years and lies beside him in a grave that was never marked. In 1936, two hundred years after his crossing, the Roush and Allied Families Association raised a monument over the two of them that names their children one by one and reckons their descendants, living and dead, at about forty thousand American citizens.

Alec’s descent reaches him three times over, because two of his grandchildren married each other. This is the second of the three paths, and it runs through his youngest son Jonas, who stood at Yorktown and watched Cornwallis’s army surrender — a son by the family’s own settled account rather than by the word of any surviving record.

1536.s:
Timothy Tuttle was born about 1682, probably at New Haven, by the family genealogy of 1883 the son of Simon Tuttle, a cooper, and his wife Abigail, a descent very probably right but not yet proved from a record. He was about three when the family removed to Wallingford, soon after his grandmother’s death. He grew up there, and as a young man he went out west of the river to look for land, chose a spot, and cleared it with his own hands — staying out through the week because it was too far to walk home each night, and finding his way back on Saturdays along a line of trees he had blazed through the woods. The place was about a mile east of what became the centre of Cheshire.

He put up a house there about 1706, the same season he married: on 2 November 1706 he took Thankful Doolittle to wife at Wallingford. The family called it the first frame house in Cheshire, and it was at the least the second; under its roof, as one neighbour wrote, were born the builder’s children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren and great-great-grandchildren. Late in the nineteenth century, standing empty, it was burned by an incendiary.

His children by Thankful were Ephraim in 1710, Mary in 1712, Gershom in 1714, Timothy in 1716, Simeon in 1721 and Moses in 1723. That genealogy records a gift of nine and a half acres from Simon on 10 July 1711. He was one of the farmers on the west side of the river who petitioned in December 1715 for a parish of their own — the bounds they asked for ran “west from ye rever as high as Timothy tuttle & timothy Beach’s” — and when the new Cheshire society held its first meeting, on 16 September 1723, he was chosen moderator. He sat on the committee that managed the ordination; he was “Sergeant Tuttle” of the school-house committee in 1729 and society moderator again in 1732; and by 1 December 1741 he is “decon Timothy Tuttle” on the committee to petition for town privileges. He lived near the west end of the road to the south of Broad Swamp, four miles west of the river.

Thankful died in November 1728. He married again in June 1729, Mary, widow of Stephen Rowe, who died in January 1747/8; and last, on 28 June 1749, Sarah (Atwater) Humiston, widow of James Humiston. He had also taken a proprietor’s share in one of the new townships granted up in Hampshire County, Massachusetts, and in 1736 he signed the whole of that right over to his second son — “for divers good causes and considerations and perticularly for love, good will and fatherly affection that I have and [bear] to my son Gershom Tuttle.” It is the deed that sent the next generation north.

He made his will on 1 December 1753, “being in ye 71st Year of my age.” Sarah was to have the bay mare, whichever half of the dwelling house she chose, gardens, the young orchard and her firewood from the farm, “for such term of time only as she remains to be my Widow.” His eldest son Ephraim took the house and barn, “he not disturbing his Mother in her use of the same.” To Gershom he left six acres at the Swamp Pasture and thirty pounds old tenor; to Timothy ten pounds and to Simeon twenty; to Moses land and the Great Swamp. The moveable estate went to his daughters Mary, Abigail and Mehitabel and to the children of his dead daughter Rachel. And he set aside twenty pounds old tenor to go into the hands of the minister and deacons, the interest “to be for ye poor of sd Parish as they judge best.”

He died on 15 April 1756 and lies in Hillside Cemetery at Cheshire, in the parish he had helped to found, under a brownstone carved with a winged soul effigy: “Here Lies ye Body of Deacon Timothy Tuttle he died April 15th 1756 in ye 75th year of his Age.”

John Doolittle (1655–1746)”, both errors withdrawn at #17 — the rank is his father Abraham’s and the 1746 death a son’s] and Mary Peck (1666–1710). Find a Grave memorial 139363422. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ THE CHRONOLOGY IS EXACT, AND IT WAS PREDICTED. This node was created empty a few hours earlier with the reasoning: “two of Timothy’s four wives are named — Mary Peck m.1729 and Sarah Atwater m.1749 — and BOTH married him after the children of 1712–1721 were born, so the mother is one of the first two wives and the book does not name her.” Thankful died 23 November 1728. Timothy remarried in 1729. THIRTEEN MONTHS. The deduction was right, and she sits exactly in the gap it pointed at. ⭐ She married at 18 and bore children across at least seventeen years — Ephraim 1710, Mary 1712, GERSHOM 1714, Timothy 1716, Simon 1721, Moses 1723 — and died at forty, with the youngest five years old. ⭐ Her 1706 marriage is also the cleanest proof yet that her husband was born c.1682 and not 1652.

Thankful DOOLITTLE, Nov. 2, 1706, by Justice Hall” (2/0) and “Thankfull, w. Timothy, d.
