1537.s:
Thankful Doolittle was born about 1688, probably at Wallingford, Connecticut — the family’s genealogists say in the spring, a daughter of John Doolittle and Mary Peck — and a granddaughter, on her father’s side, of Abraham Doolittle, one of the men who founded the town. She married young, at about eighteen: on 2 November 1706 Justice Hall married her to Timothy Tuttle, who built his house out west of the river that same season.

The town book enters ten children of Timothy and Thankful across twenty years: Rachel (her birth is written 1706, months before the wedding, most likely a clerk’s slip), Ebenezer in 1708, Ephraim in 1710, Mary in 1712, Gershom in 1714, Timothy in 1716, Abigail in 1719, Simon in 1721, Moses in 1723 and a last daughter, Thankfull, in November 1726. In March 1725 the new church at Cheshire received her into membership, entered on the roll not under her own name but as “wife of Timothy Tuttle”; her husband was not admitted until January 1738/9, ten years after she was dead.

If the family’s genealogists have her parents right — and the two oldest Wallingford genealogies leave her out of John Doolittle’s family, giving a Susannah on the birthday later writers gave her — then her brother was the Reverend Benjamin Doolittle, who took his degree at Yale in 1716 and was settled from 1718 as minister at Northfield, out on the Massachusetts frontier. When her son Gershom went north as a young man to take up his father’s land above Northfield, it was his uncle’s house he lodged in. Her family is the reason the Tuttles knew that country at all.

She died on 23 November 1728, aged forty, when her youngest, the daughter who carried her name, had just turned two. Where she is buried nobody knows. Her husband married again thirteen months later. Wallingford’s books, as they were copied in the 1920s, record her marriage and her death, but not her birth: the town’s page of Doolittle children has every other Thankful and not her, and her wedding entry names no parents. So the link to the Doolittles rests on the family’s genealogists, and it stays probable rather than settled.
1537.gl: Probable — the IDENTIFICATION or the LINK rests on one source, or is in conflict

1538.s:
William Allis was born at Hatfield, Massachusetts, a grandson of the first William Allis of Braintree and Hatfield. Which of that man’s sons was his father is not settled. Hatfield had two cousins named William Allis of nearly the same age. One was born on 19 October 1680 to Samuel Allis, the carpenter and builder of Hatfield street, and his wife Alice. The other was born on 16 May 1684 to Captain John Allis and his wife Mary. Both were alive in 1712, when Captain John’s children signed a family agreement that names their own brother William and, separately, “Cousin William Allis”. In 1729 a “William Allis of Sunderland” sold land together with Captain John’s children, which now points to Captain John’s son, though no record yet settles it. If he was Samuel’s son, he was ten when his father died, and twenty-three on the morning of 29 February 1704 when his mother, remarried and living at Deerfield, was killed in the French and Indian raid, along with his brother Samuel. If he was Captain John’s son, Alice was his aunt.

He had married Elizabeth Davis of Northampton in 1703 or 1704. Their children were Mary, born 18 February 1705, and Lois, born 13 January 1707/8, both at Hatfield; Eliphalet in 1710, also at Hatfield; then Zebediah in 1713 and Elizabeth in 1716, both at Sunderland — so the household moved upriver between the end of 1710 and the autumn of 1713. At Sunderland he appraised a neighbour’s estate in 1739 and deeded land to his son Zebadiah. On 18 August 1748 he made over to Zebadiah the homestead itself: a house lot of twenty-two and a half acres on the Sawmill River, “including a House and a barn orcharding and fence”, with his son Eliphalet’s land on one side and his son-in-law Joseph Mitchell’s on the other. He added all his land in Sunderland not already conveyed, and his clothing, horse furniture and household goods “found after my Decease”. He was still able to ride in and acknowledge the deed before a justice in March 1755. Later the whole family moved again, across the river to Montague, where he was “Mr. William Allis”, a title of standing in a New England town. His wife died there on 1 May 1758. Montague could be a hard place to live: in January 1759 his son Eliphalet and his wife Mary buried four of their children in nine days — Mary on the 7th, Jonathan on the 10th, Samuel on the 12th, David on the 15th.

William Allis died at Montague on 20 February 1763, aged eighty-two. 1539.s:
Elizabeth was of Northampton, Massachusetts, and married William Allis of Hatfield in 1703 or 1704. She bore five children: Mary in 1705, Lois in 1707/8 and Eliphalet in 1710 at Hatfield, and then, after the family moved upriver to Sunderland, Zebediah in 1713 and Elizabeth in 1716.

In later life she and her husband moved again, across the river to Montague, and there she died on 1 May 1758. The town set it down in a single line: “Allis. May first 1758, Elizabeth Allis wife to Mr. William Allis, died in Montague.” Her husband outlived her by five years. Two of her daughters, Lois and Mary, married into the Tuttle and the Mitchell families, and their children then married one another, so she is an ancestor of this family along two lines at once.

Her maiden name was Davis, of Northampton — though that comes down on the family’s word rather than from anything written in her own girlhood, and the Montague book that records her death calls her only “Elizabeth Allis wife to Mr. William Allis.”

1540.s:
Michael Mitchell was a Wallingford, Connecticut man — a proprietor of the town, casting lots with the other townsmen in 1695–6 and still there in 1706. Where he came from before that nobody has ever been able to say. About 1694 he married Sarah, daughter of John Catlin of Deerfield.

He moved his family to Deerfield, the most exposed town on the Massachusetts frontier. On the morning of 29 February 1704, when the French and their allies came over the stockade, his whole family escaped unharmed — which in that town, on that morning, was the exception. His wife’s father and brother were burned in their own house a few hundred yards away.

His children were William, born 1697; Michael, born 8 March 1700/1, afterwards a soldier in Father Rasle’s war and later of Wethersfield, Connecticut; Joseph, born 1705, the weaver, through whom this family descends; and Samuel, born 7 March 1712, very probably the Samuel Mitchell granted land at Sunderland in 1737 on condition that he stayed five years. Sarah died on 30 December 1736.

His Wallingford years matter more than they look. The Tuttles were farming west of the river at Wallingford in exactly those years, and Gershom Tuttle was born there in 1714 — so when Michael’s granddaughter Tabitha married Gershom’s son at Deerfield in 1757, it was not a chance meeting a hundred miles from home. It was two Wallingford families who had both gone north, marrying each other.

1541.s:
Sarah Catlin was a daughter of John Catlin — a Wethersfield man who taught school at Newark in New Jersey, served as that town’s attorney and five years its selectman, and then brought his family to Deerfield about 1683, where he was dignified with the title of “Mr.” — and of his wife Mary Baldwin. About 1694 she married Michael Mitchell, and her eldest child was born in 1697.

That marriage is probably why she lived. On 29 February 1704, when the raid came, she was under her own husband’s roof, and the Mitchell household came through untouched. Her father’s did not. His buildings were all burned and he and his son Jonathan were consumed with them; another son was killed in the Meadow Fight later the same morning; a son and three daughters were carried off toward Canada. Two of those daughters were her sisters — Elizabeth, wife of James Corse, and Mary, wife of Thomas Wells — and both were killed on the march. In a town where a hundred and twelve people were marched away in a single morning, it was said of her father that “no family suffered more than his.”

She bore at least four sons — William, Michael, Joseph and Samuel — and died on 30 December 1736, about two months before her granddaughter Tabitha was born. She lies in the Old Burying Ground at Deerfield, in the same ground as the common grave of the dead of 1704, her father and her brother among them; time and weather have taken the place of her own grave.

The 1883 book does not merely assert his parentage — it abstracts three separate conveyances in which Simon calls William Tuttle his father: 1677-8, to Benjamin Brockett, cordwainer, “a part of land my father, Mr. William Tuttle, bought of John Punderson”; 1686, to Isaac Turner, six acres “formerly belonging to my father, Mr. William Tuttle”; 1705, to cousin Joshua, “all my right in Branford division set to my father, Mr. William Tuttle”. Three deeds, three decades apart, in the grantor’s own words. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ AND A DEED TO HIS SON: “July 10, 1711, he gives to son, TIMOTHY, the land, 9½ acres, ‘I bought of Roger Tyler.’” (and 23 June 1715 a 14-acre house lot to son Daniel). The father-to-son conveyance is the classic proof of descent, and it links node 3072 to node 1536 by a record rather than by a numbering scheme. ⭐ A life, from the same pages: “Simon Tuttle of Wallingford, COOPER” (1685); on the New Haven proprietors’ list of 1680, drawing his share in the third division as “two heads, showing that at that date he had a wife but no children”; a 1673 right-of-way agreement signed by six Tuttle brothers, of which the original paper survived to 1883 and his signature was traced from it; Wallingford lots drawn 1686 (No. 52, 104 acres) and 1690 (No. 14); rated £79 on the 1701 Wallingford grand list; town gauger and packer from 1708-9. He died 16 April 1719; his widow ABIGAIL died 11 August 1722. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ AND HE SETTLES THE 1682 QUESTION INDEPENDENTLY. The deeds show him of New Haven through 1683 and “of Wallingford” from 1685 — “from these records it follows that he removed to Wall’d about 1685”. His son Timothy moved with the family “when about 3 years of age” — so Timothy was born c.1682, and the book’s own printed “1652” is refuted for the fifth time, now by land records. ——— Earlier note: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ NEW NODE, 6 Aug 2026 — GENERATION 13 ON THE TUTTLE SIDE [TUTTLE-30]. Entry 9 of the 1883 genealogy, image 560, in full: “9. Simon Tuttle, bap. in New Haven, March 28, 1647. He appears in the list of proprietors of Wallingford in 1670, and had lot No. 13 with 8 acres of out land assigned to him. Dr. Savage (Gen. Dict.) says he did not stay long. He did not, in fact, take up his allotment and probably continued in New Haven until after the death of his mother, Dec., 1684.” ⭐⭐ THE BARE ENTRY NUMBER 9 IS THE WHOLE POINT: he is the NINTH CHILD OF WILLIAM TUTTLE, and that is why the ladder 92514 → 9251 → 925 → 92 → 9 lands on the immigrant. ⭐ He also dates the family’s move. 3072.s:
Simon Tuttle was baptised at New Haven on 28 March 1647, reckoned the ninth child of William Tuttle, the immigrant, and his wife Elizabeth, on good grounds that no record yet read has proved. He was bred a cooper. When Wallingford was laid out in 1670 he put his name on the proprietors’ list and was assigned lot No. 13 with eight acres of out-land, but he never took the allotment up; he stayed on at New Haven, where he was still drawing his share in the third division in 1680. That list credits him with “two heads” — a wife, and no children yet — so he had married Abigail about 1679 or 1680. He was of New Haven through 1683 and of Wallingford from 1685, moving, it seems, after his mother died in December 1684.

At Wallingford he did well. He drew lot No. 52 with a hundred and four acres in 1686 and lot No. 14 in 1690, was rated at £79 on the grand list of 1701, and from 1708–9 served the town as gauger and packer, the officer who inspects goods sold by weight and measure. He spent thirty years selling off what his father had left at New Haven, and the family genealogy of 1883 quotes him naming him in those papers: in 1677–8, land sold to a cordwainer that “my father, Mr. William Tuttle, bought of John Punderson”; in 1686, six acres “formerly belonging to my father, Mr. William Tuttle”; in 1705, to his cousin Joshua, all his right in the Branford division “set to my father, Mr. William Tuttle.” In 1673 he and five of his brothers signed a right-of-way agreement; the paper, with his signature on it, was still in existence two hundred years later.

He had dealings at Branford too. On 5 August 1685 the town meeting there gave Christopher Tod liberty to sell his house and land to Simon Tuttle, and on 5 November 1687, styled “Simon Tuttle of Wallingford … Cooper,” he sold Richard Rosewell of New Haven a Branford house with a three-acre home lot, twenty-three acres adjoining, half of Wheadon’s Swamp and eighteen acres of farm land yet to be laid out, for thirty-eight pounds.

He gave land to his sons in his own lifetime, as his son Timothy would in turn: nine and a half acres to Timothy on 10 July 1711, land “I bought of Roger Tyler,” and a fourteen-acre house lot to Daniel on 23 June 1715. Simon Tuttle died on 16 April 1719 at Wallingford, and is said to lie in the Center Street burying ground there. His widow Abigail outlived him by three years and died on 11 August 1722.

3073.s:
Abigail married Simon Tuttle, the New Haven cooper, about 1679 or 1680 — in 1680 the New Haven proprietors counted his household at “two heads” in the third division, a wife and as yet no children. Her son Timothy, afterwards the deacon at Cheshire, was born about 1682, and about 1685 she moved with her husband up to Wallingford and brought up his family there.

She outlived him. Simon died on 16 April 1719; Abigail died on 11 August 1722.

Her own family is lost. An old tradition made her a daughter of Richard Beach, and Beach is the right sort of name for that neighbourhood — the Tuttles’ nearest neighbour on the west side of Wallingford was a Timothy Beach, and a Thomas Beach witnessed a Tuttle bond. But the Beach family’s own historian at Cheshire would not have it: Richard Beach’s daughter Abigail is nowhere in the settlement of her father’s estate, and “the point remains in uncertainty.” That she was Simon’s wife and Timothy’s mother is not in doubt; her surname simply did not survive.

3074.s:
John Doolittle was born at New Haven on 14 June 1655, a son of Abraham Doolittle — who had come to New Haven from Boston in 1644, took the freeman’s oath there, served as the county’s chief executive officer, and was one of the founders of Wallingford. His mother was Abraham’s first wife, Joan Alling: no record of the time names her as such, but her father’s will of January 1657 left ten pounds to “her children”, and John and his three older siblings were then Abraham’s only children. His father is not in doubt: in 1681 his childless uncle John Doolittle of Rumney Marsh, near Boston, left fifty pounds “unto John Dowlettell the Son of my Brother Abraham” and a piece of Lynn saltmarsh to Abraham for life and then “to his son John for ever”; in 1687 father and son sold that marsh together, signing as “Abraham Doolittle & John Doolittle, father and Son”; and in 1690 Abraham’s will gave “my son John” ten acres at Wharton’s Brook. On 13 February 1682/3 John married Mary Peck, and settled at Wallingford, the town his father had helped to lay out.

Their children included Esther, born 24 January 1683, who also married a Tuttle; Samuel in 1685; Thankful, who the family’s genealogists say was born in April 1688 (the town’s copied register does not have her birth), and who married Timothy Tuttle in 1706; and Benjamin, born 1695, who took his degree at Yale in 1716, married Lydia Todd the next year, and was settled as the minister of Northfield, up on the Massachusetts frontier, from 1718 until he died suddenly in January 1748. It was to that uncle’s house that Thankful’s son Gershom went when he first travelled north as a young man — which is how a Wallingford family came to have a foothold a hundred miles up the Connecticut River.

Mary died on 1 September 1710. John married again on 29 January 1717, to Grace Blakeslee, and after that he disappears from view; he was sixty-one then, and the year of his death is not known.

3075.s:
Mary Peck was born at New Haven on 4 March 1665/6, a daughter of John Peck and his wife Mary Moss. The Pecks, the Mosses and the Doolittles were three of the families who founded Wallingford between 1668 and 1670 and whose children married across all three, and on 13 February 1682/3 Mary married John Doolittle, Abraham Doolittle’s son.

Her children included Esther, born January 1683; Samuel in 1685; Thankful, who the family’s genealogists say was born in April 1688 (the town’s copied register does not have her birth), and who married Timothy Tuttle, afterwards deacon at Cheshire; and Benjamin, born 1695, afterwards minister at Northfield. Mary died at Wallingford on 1 September 1710, at forty-four. Her husband remarried seven years later.

There was a second Mary Peck in the same town, no relation — daughter of Joseph and Sarah (Alling) Peck, and widow of Stephen Rowe — and it was she whom Thankful’s widowed husband Timothy Tuttle married in 1729. This Mary Peck had been nineteen years dead by then.

3076.s:
Samuel Allis was born at Braintree, Massachusetts, on 24 February 1647, the son of William Allis and Mary his wife. Braintree wrote him down under the year 1646, the year then beginning in March and February being counted the twelfth month: “Samuel, sonne of William Alyes & Mary his wife was Borne the 24th. of ye 12 month.” His father was a Braintree freeman of 1640 who removed about 1661 up the Connecticut River to the new town of Hatfield.

Samuel followed him there and took his own home lot as a young man of twenty-two. On 4 February 1669 the town granted him a house lot sixteen rods wide next to Samuel Marsh’s, with land in the Plain above the great meadow and ten acres in the swamp by the Mill river — “provided he build a sufficient dwelling house upon his lot by or before the last of May in the year 1671, otherwise to forfeit his land.” Daniel Belden had the lot on the other side. He built, and he stayed: a carpenter and builder, living on the east side of Hatfield street.

About 1675–6 he married a woman named Alice, whose surname nobody ever wrote down. Seven children followed: Mehitable on 2 July 1677; Samuel on 20 February 1679; William on 19 October 1680, who may be the William from whom this family descends (his cousin of the same name, Captain John’s son, is the other candidate); Mary on 6 July 1682; Thomas on 12 March 1684; Sarah about 1685; and Rebecca on 29 November 1687.

Samuel Allis died at Hatfield on 9 March 1691, aged forty-four, leaving Alice with seven children all under fifteen. She remarried in 1696 and was killed in the raid on Deerfield of 29 February 1704; their son Samuel was killed in the same attack, and their daughter Mary was carried to Canada and lived to come home.

3077.s:
Alice married Samuel Allis, the Hatfield carpenter, about 1675–6, and bore him seven children between 1677 and 1687 — Mehitable, Samuel, William, Mary, Thomas, Sarah and Rebecca. When he died on 9 March 1691 she was left with all of them under fifteen.

On 20 November 1696 she married again, to Sergeant John Hawks of Deerfield: a soldier of King Philip’s war who had been in the Falls Fight and was wounded going to the relief of Hatfield on 30 May 1676, and who had become a permanent settler at Deerfield in 1683. She had a daughter by him, Elizabeth, born about 1697.

On the morning of 29 February 1704 the French and their allies came over the Deerfield stockade. Alice was killed in the village. Her son Samuel Allis, twenty-five years old, was killed in the meadow. Her little daughter Elizabeth Hawks, six or seven, was taken and died on the march to Canada. Her daughter Mary Allis, twenty-one, was carried off too, survived the march, was redeemed, and came home to marry another survivor of the same raid, Nathaniel Brooks, in 1710. Her husband lived — but every child and grandchild of his name was lost that day, and he ended his life at Waterbury, Connecticut, with the one daughter he had left. Her third child, William, was at Hatfield and not in Deerfield that night. Whether this family descends from him or from his cousin William, Captain John Allis’s son, is not yet settled.

She lies with the rest of the dead of that morning in the Old Burying Ground at Deerfield, under a stone that reads: “The grave of 48 men women and children, victims of the French and Indian raid on Deerfield, February 29, 1704.” Her own family name was never written down. Those who afterwards gathered up Hampshire County’s records could call her nothing but “Alice, widow of Samuel Allis”, and she is remembered by her first name alone.

On 21 January 1704 she sat down with her second husband and her grown sons by Samuel to settle Samuel’s estate at last. William, the elder, took the house lot and the Hatfield lands and agreed to pay his brothers and sisters their shares and his mother twenty shillings a year for life. Alice signed with her mark, and she made sure that the little daughter she had by John Hawks would share in whatever was left. Thirty-nine days later the raid came down on Deerfield.

3082.s:
John Catlin was born about 1643, the son of a Catlin of Wethersfield, Connecticut, who died when the boy was an infant. He was of Wethersfield in 1662 — the year he married Mary Baldwin — and of Branford by 1665, and from there he went with the New Haven colony party that founded Newark in New Jersey. He was no farmer there. In 1676 he kept Newark's first school, in his own house, as the custom then was; the townsmen's vote engaged him to “do his faithful, honest and true endeavour to teach the children or servants of these as have subscribed … english and also arithmetick as much as they are capable to learn and he capable to teach them.” In 1678 he was the town's attorney — not a lawyer, but an “honest brother” charged to see that all town orders were executed and to punish any breach — and he was a selectman from 1676 to 1681.

About 1683 he moved north again, by way of Hartford, to the frontier town of Deerfield in Massachusetts, where he was one of the early permanent settlers. In 1685 he bought the Frary part of home lot 32, four acres on Deerfield street, and lot 33 from John Parsons in the same year; lot 36 was his as well by 1704 — three home lots on the one street. In the town records he is given the title “Mr.”, which in a New England town book is a rank and not a courtesy, and he took a prominent part in the town's affairs.

On the night of 28 February 1704 there were 291 people under Deerfield's roofs. Before the next morning was out, all but a hundred and twenty-six of them were dead or being marched through the snow towards Canada, three hundred miles away. No family in the town suffered more than John Catlin's. He and his son Jonathan were killed defending their house, which was then taken and burned with all his buildings; another son, Joseph, was killed later that morning in the fight in the meadow; a third son, John, and three of his daughters were carried off. Two of those daughters, Elizabeth, the wife of James Corse, and Mary, died on the march. The roll of the town's dead sets him down in four words: “John Catlin, (?) 60.”

The house that gave the raid its surviving relic still stood in Deerfield until 1848, and was photographed before it came down: Capt. John Sheldon's, built about 1698, which held out while half the village burned. Its front door, hacked through, is kept in Memorial Hall in the village to this day.

His line survived for one accidental reason. His daughter Sarah had married Michael Mitchell about 1694 and was in a household of her own that night. The captured son came home from Canada, and by about 1715 had built a new house on his father's ashes; he was a housewright, and was always known in Deerfield by tradition as “Master Catlin.” The forty-eight who died in the raid lie together in the Old Burying Ground at Deerfield, under a brownstone block raised over the common grave.

3083.s:
Mary Baldwin was baptized at Milford, Connecticut, on 23 June 1644 — the same day her mother Hannah joined the Milford church and the first four Baldwin children were all baptized together. Her father was Joseph Baldwin, one of the first settlers of the town. On 23 September 1662 she married John Catlin, and in a tangle that is rare even in a small colony she married the son of her own stepmother: her father's second wife, Isabella, was the widow of the elder John Catlin.

She went with her husband from Branford to Newark in New Jersey, where he kept the town's first school, and about 1683 to Deerfield on the Massachusetts frontier. They had ten children. Her father remembered her in his will of 20 December 1680: “I doe give to my Daughter Mary Cattlin of Arthur Cull fortie shillings” — the Arthur Kill, the channel behind Newark Bay, where she and John were then living.

On the morning of 29 February 1704 her husband and one son were killed defending their house at Deerfield and it was burned; another son was killed in the Meadow Fight; a son and three daughters were carried off towards Canada, and two of the daughters died on the march. Mary was taken with the other prisoners to the Sheldon house, the largest in the town, which the attackers had kept as a holding place for captives. A wounded French officer was brought in and laid on the floor, calling for water, and Mary Catlin fed him with water. Someone asked her how she could do that for her enemy. She answered, “If thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him water to drink.” The Frenchman was carried away, the captives were marched off, and Mrs. Catlin was left behind. Afterwards a little boy who had been hidden in the house came out, and she told him to run and hide. The boy said, “Mrs. Catlin, why don't you go and hide?” She said, “I am a captive; it is not my duty to hide, but you have not been taken, and it is your duty to hide.”

The story came down in her family and was written out a century later by a descendant, Lucy D. Shearer. Deerfield's historian printed it, and accepted its explanation of why she lived: this was the place “where Mrs. Catlin relieved the wounded French lieutenant, and secured her own freedom by her practical Christianity.” Her own people thought it was the water she gave the dying officer that left her standing in an emptied house. The house outlasted her by a century and a half — the “Old Indian House” stood until 1849, and its scarred and battered door is in Memorial Hall at Deerfield still. She did not long survive the raid, and she lies in the Old Burying Ground at Deerfield.

ph.c: The Old Burying Ground at Deerfield, where Mary Catlin was buried five weeks after the raid; the brownstone block marks the common grave of the forty-eight who were killed on 29 February 1704. — Find a Grave contributor 'Cindy Selensky Foster', photographed Sept 2023

6144.s:
William Tuttle came from Ringstead, a village on the Nene in Northamptonshire. The parish register there records John, son of William Tootell, baptized on 8 December 1631; Anne, his daughter, on 20 January 1632/3; and Thomas, in the first weeks of 1634/5. Who his own parents were is not settled. The likeliest answer is Symon Tootell of Ringstead, who signed as churchwarden in 1622 and was buried there on 15 June 1630: a William, son of Symon, was christened in the parish on 26 December 1607, but the surname in that entry is hard to read and Symon’s will has not yet been read.

In April 1635 he sailed from London on the ship Planter, which put into Boston about the first of July. The clerk wrote him down as “Husbandman Willm Tuttell 26,” with Elizabeth, 23, John, 3½, Ann, 2¼, and Thomas, 3 months: the same three children, in the same order. In his household were two girls, Cicely Clark and Mary Bill, and both surnames belong to Ringstead families. Also aboard was the household of Richard Tuttell of Ringstead, whom the genealogies make his brother, with an Isbell Tuttell, aged 70, whom they make their widowed mother; and John Tuttle, later of Ipswich, whether brother or cousin is disputed. The passenger list calls him a husbandman, a man who farmed his own ground. He had a merchant's interests too: a petition surviving in Boston shows him among the owners of the ketch Zebulon of Ipswich, asking the General Court for two guns to arm her for a voyage to the Indies. The court refused.

Two of his sons were baptized at Charlestown, Jonathan in 1637 and David in 1639, and by June of that year the family had moved to the new colony at Quinnipiac. On 4 June 1639 the planters met in Mr. Newman's barn and signed the church covenant that founded New Haven; William Tuttle's name stands on that list between Benjamin Ling and Ezekiel Cheever, near the head among the principal men. In the first division of land in 1640 he was rated at £100 of estate and seven persons in the family. In 1641 he held the home lot of Edward Hopkins, afterwards governor of Connecticut, and in 1656 he bought from Joshua Atwater a house, home lot and barn on the green. That became the Tuttle homestead, and the family held it for thirty years. Long after, the first building of Yale College was raised on the same ground.

He had land across the water at East Haven as well, enough of it that a stream there is still called Tuttle's Brook and the rise above it Tuttle's Hill. In 1651 he joined Jasper Crane and about fifty others in the New Haven colony's attempt to plant a settlement on the Delaware; the Dutch governor at Manhattan seized the party, held them prisoner and sent them home, and the petition of protest that followed — “the humble petition of Jasper Crane, William Tuttle and many others” — went to the commissioners of the United Colonies. The venture cost him money he never recovered, and after it he turned to farming and to town business.

At that business he was constant: fence viewer for Mr. Davenport's quarter in 1644, laying out allotments and settling boundaries; a juror again and again, his title of “Mr.” always carefully written, which in a New England town record is a rank and not a courtesy; sworn constable in March 1666-7; one of the commissioners who finally settled the line between Branford and New Haven in 1669 and between New Haven, Milford, Branford and Wallingford in 1672. When the meeting house was seated in 1646-7 — the seats graded by descent, public trust, piety and estate — Mr. Tuttle was voted into the first cross seat at the upper end, nearest the pulpit. He turns up in smaller things too. In 1646 he and Jeremy Watts were fined for falling asleep at the watch house. In 1664 a girl caught pilfering tried to drag his fourteen-year-old daughter Mercy into it; the charge collapsed, and before sentence William Tuttle asked the court, “with great affection,” to deal gently with the girl and place her in a pious family.

The town he helped found was drawn out, house by house, a lifetime after he died. A plan of New Haven ‘with all the buildings in 1748’, engraved in 1806 from General Wadsworth's survey, names every householder and his trade across the nine squares — and the Tuttle name is still scattered through it: a Widow Tuttle on the north road, a Noah Tuttle to the east, an Enos Tuttle, miller, by the harbour, and an Ab. Tuttle who was the sexton. The long hip-roofed building marked ‘Yale Colledge, Built 1717’ stands on the block beside the green where the family homestead had been.

He died suddenly in the first days of June 1673, leaving no will; his inventory was entered just after that of his neighbour Benjamin Ling, taken on the sixth. It came to £499 8s 6d: oxen, steers and cows; a house, barns and home lot at £110; nine acres of peas sown and plowed; rye, oats, flax and a hundred and seventy pounds of bacon; one silver spoon; and two matchlock guns with a flask and match, bandoleers, a fowling piece, a sword and a cutlass. The appraisers stopped at the foot to ask the court whether the food the family was living on — pork, bacon, candles, malt, rye, oats, corn and salt, sixteen pounds’ worth — ought to be counted at all. A deed he had agreed to was found unsigned. His widow Elizabeth took out the administration herself, and his Branford division lands were still being parcelled out to his children on 14 February 1705, thirty-two years after he died — his son Simon's deed of that year conveys “all my right in Branford division set to my father, Mr. William Tuttle, now (Feb. 14, 1705) laid out for his children.” The last remainder of the estate was not divided until 1709, thirty-six years after his death, when it was split into eleven parts and a grandson appealed the division to Hartford. He lies somewhere under the Old Green at New Haven; the exact spot is not known. Among his descendants is his great-grandson Jonathan Edwards, who studied and taught on the very ground where William Tuttle's house had stood.

6145.s:
Elizabeth Tuttle was born in England about 1609. She was about twenty-six when she crossed to New England in April 1635 on the ship Planter with her husband William and their first three children — John, Hannah and Thomas — from Ringstead, Northamptonshire, in a party that also held the household of Richard Tuttell of the same parish, whom the genealogies make her husband's brother; an Isbell Tuttell, aged 70, whom they make his widowed mother; and John Tuttle, later of Ipswich. They landed at Boston about the first of July, and a year later, on 24 July 1636, “Mrs. Elizabeth Tuttell” united with the church in Boston, where she brought two sons to be baptized: Jonathan in July 1637 and David in April 1639. Within weeks of that second baptism the family had gone to the new plantation at Quinnipiac, which became New Haven.

She bore twelve children and, in a century when that was rare, every one of them lived to grow up: John, Hannah, Thomas, Jonathan, David, Joseph, Sarah, Elizabeth, Simon — from whom this family descends — Benjamin, Mercy and Nathaniel. Her own standing in the town is legible in the dullest of records. When New Haven seated its meeting house in 1646-7, the seats graded by rank, Mrs. Tuttle was placed in the fifth seat in the middle among the wives of the leading men; in 1655-6 in the fourth long seat; in 1661-2 the clerk simply wrote “Sisters Miles, Peck, Lindon, Tuttle and Gibbard.”

Her husband died suddenly in June 1673, leaving no will. Elizabeth took out the administration herself — at a court in June 1674 she appeared to confirm a sale he had made, and is entered as “widow and relict and lawful administratrix,” signing with her mark. She stayed on at the homestead on the green, where she had lived since 1656, and kept it another eleven years; in all she lived there twenty-eight.

The widowhood was hard. In November 1676 her daughter Sarah, married to John Slauson of Stamford, died — struck down, it was afterwards said, by her own younger brother Benjamin after a quarrel. Sarah was dead on 17 November 1676; Benjamin, unmarried, made over his property to his brother-in-law Richard Edwards on 18 June 1677, and was hanged at New Haven that same month.

Elizabeth spent her last years with her youngest son, Nathaniel, and died on the last day of 1684. The will she left was presented to the New Haven court on 28 July 1685 and refused: “the other children objected and the court would not allow it.” Her inventory, taken on 3 February and coming to £294 7s 3d, was thought by a later reader to show “a ladylike refinement in apparel and household appointments.” The appraisers had to reckon with her grown children as they went: “A rug not entred their sister Hood had,” “Another rug Symon had,” and four swine “which Nathanll saith should not have been in.” The “sister Hood” was probably her daughter Anne, the wife of John Hurd of Stratford. Her gravestone, cut with the old-style date “Age 76: 31:10:1684 — Elisabeth Tutle” (month ten being December under the old calendar), was carried with the others from the Old Green to Grove Street Cemetery in 1821 and stands today in the row along the north wall. Part of its epitaph has crumbled away, but it was copied before it went: “The blest live as They are: the blest That live at Rest.”

6148.s:
Abraham Doolittle was born in England about 1620 — possibly at Kidderminster in Worcestershire, where an Abraham son of Edward Doolittle was christened on 20 August 1620, though another Abraham Doolittle was buried there as a grown man in 1706 — and was in New England by 1640. He was at Boston that year and at New Haven by 1644 — the monument later raised over him says 1642 — and from there he never left the colony's service: corporal, freeman, marshal of New Haven Colony from 1662 until the colony was swallowed by Connecticut, townsman, sergeant of the first train band, deputy to the General Court for New Haven and later for Wallingford, town treasurer. In the earliest records the name is written “Dowlittle.” On 10 November 1669 he sat as a juror at New Haven on the same panel as William Tuttle and Roger Alling — his own brother-in-law — in a court presided over by the deputy governor.

That same year he was chosen to superintend the affairs of the new settlement inland, and he became one of the founders of Wallingford. He and John Peck were on the ground there in 1668, two years before the town was incorporated. He was one of four trustees who managed the plantation until the incorporation in 1670, one of the committee that gathered its first church, and deputy for it in 1668 and 1672. During King Philip's War his house was one of those fortified, and he served on the town's vigilance committee in 1675.

He married twice. His first wife was Joan Alling, the daughter of a Kempston blacksmith, the mother of his first four children, Abraham, Elizabeth, Mary and John, born 1650–55 — John, born 14 June 1655, is the son from whom this family descends. The genealogists say she died about 1661; no record of her death has been found, but she was gone by July 1663. On 2 July 1663 he married Abigail Moss, daughter of his fellow Wallingford founder John Moss. In all there were thirteen children, and when he died on 11 August 1690, aged seventy, seven sons and three daughters survived him; his will, signed that May, names his wife, the seven sons and the three daughters. He wrote it, he said, “that love & concord may be preserved, & contention & discord prevented after my decease among my surviving relations”, and spent three pages parcelling Wharton’s Brook and the west rocks acre by acre among ten children — including ten acres of Boston saltmarsh that his childless brother John of Rumney Marsh had left him in 1681. He lies in the Center Street Cemetery at Wallingford, where the town replaced his worn original stone in 1918 with a tall granite monument that sets out his whole public career — and gives his first wife a line of her own. John is counted a child of that first marriage, though no record of the marriage itself survives.

6149.s:
Joan Alling was baptized at Kempston in Bedfordshire on 12 October 1617, a daughter of James Allen, the Kempston blacksmith, who in his will of 1657 left ten pounds to “my daughter Joane the nowe wife of Abram Dowlittle livinge nowe alsoe in newe England” and ten more to her children. Her brother was Roger Alling, who became treasurer of the New Haven Colony and a deacon of its church — so when she crossed the ocean she was coming to a family already planted near the top of the colony's affairs.

She was the first wife of Abraham Doolittle of New Haven and the mother of his first four children: Abraham, born 12 February 1650; Elizabeth, 12 April 1652; Mary, 22 February 1654; and John, 14 June 1655 — the son from whom this family descends. No record of the time names her as their mother, because New Haven’s clerks wrote down only fathers. But her father’s will of January 1657 left ten pounds to “her children”, and Abraham’s children then living were exactly these four, carried to the font together at the First Church on 24 April 1657. A fifth, Abigail, was baptized in May 1659 and died young; the family genealogists add a daughter Sarah. In January 1662, when the town assigned seats in the meeting house, “Sister Dowlittle” sat in the seventh long seat for women — very probably Joan. She died before July 1663, when Abraham married again; when she died, and where she lies, are not recorded.

The town of Wallingford remembered her all the same. When it raised a new monument over Abraham Doolittle in 1918 it cut a line for her near the top: “First wife Joane Alling is buried in New Haven.”

6150.s:
John Peck was born about 1638, the son of Deacon William Peck of New Haven, the London merchant who had come over on the Hector. He grew up in the colony his father helped found, and became a freeman there in 1669. On 3 November 1664 he married Mary Moss, daughter of John Moss, in New Haven.

In 1668, two years before Wallingford was incorporated, he and Abraham Doolittle were already on the ground there, and John Peck settled in the new inland town and stayed. The first of his ten children were born at New Haven and the last six at Wallingford; the eldest, Mary, born 4 March 1666, married John Doolittle, so that the two men who had broken the ground together became grandfathers to the same children.

John Peck died at Wallingford in 1724, about eighty-six years old; Mary outlived him by a year, dying 16 November 1725 aged seventy-eight. They lie in the Center Street Cemetery, in a plot that is now the ninth stop on the town's walking tour, but no stone for either of them survives — none was standing when the burying ground was surveyed stone by stone in 1934, and the two markers standing in the plot today belong to a later John Peck and his wife.

6151.s:
Mary Moss was baptized at New Haven on 11 April 1647, one of the eleven children of John Moss — the long-lived Wallingford founder who was said to have died at 103 — and of a mother whose name has not survived. On 3 November 1664, aged seventeen, she married John Peck, son of Deacon William Peck; the ceremony was performed by William Jones, afterwards deputy governor of Connecticut.

Her first children were born at New Haven and the last six at Wallingford, where her husband and her father were both among the founders. There were ten in all. The eldest, Mary, born 4 March 1666, married John Doolittle of Wallingford and is the one through whom this family descends. Mary Moss outlived her husband by a year and died at Wallingford on 16 November 1725, aged seventy-eight. She was buried in the Center Street Cemetery, but no stone for her was standing when the yard was surveyed in 1934, and none stands there now.

6152.s:
William Allis was born in England, probably between 1613 and 1616; the family tradition puts his birthplace in Essex or London and brings him over with Winthrop's fleet in 1630, but nothing outside the family's own telling confirms it. He is certain from 13 May 1640, when he was made a freeman of Braintree, Massachusetts, and the Braintree town book then carries him through the 1650s as a selectman, as “Deacon Allis”, and as a commissioner, with Thomas Meekins holding land next to his. This family descends from him through one of his sons, John or Samuel: each had a son named William at Hatfield, and which of those cousins was the Sunderland William is not yet settled.

In 1641 he married a woman named Mary, whose surname has not survived. Their children were born at Braintree: John in 1642, Samuel on 24 February 1647, two boys named Josiah, two named William, Hannah, and Mary. About 1661 he moved the family west to Hatfield on the Connecticut River.

There his title stops being a courtesy and becomes a command. When King Philip's War set the valley towns to garrisoning themselves, the commands were parcelled out: thirty-nine men under Pynchon at Springfield, twenty-nine at Westfield, twenty-six at Northampton, thirty at Hadley — and thirty-six at Hatfield, under Lieut. Wm. Allis, the largest force in the valley after Springfield's. Six more soldiers were ordered to him, to be employed through the winter getting out timber for the fortifications at Hatfield and Deerfield. In the same war, on 19 May 1676, his son William, aged twenty, was killed in the Falls Fight at Turners Falls.

His wife Mary died on 10 August 1677. On 25 June 1678 he married Mary, daughter of John Bronson and widow of John Graves of Haddam — and died ten weeks later, in September 1678. A Deerfield land redistribution of 1680 notes it in brackets, as a thing everyone in the valley knew: “[Lieut. Wm. Allis had died September, 1678.]”

6153.s:
Mary married William Allis in 1641 and spent the next twenty years at Braintree, Massachusetts, bearing a family of eight. The town register records the births without ever giving her a surname: “Mary Allis the dauter of wilom Allis and mary his wife was born the (25)(8)(53)”; “William Allis the sonne of William Allis and Mary his wife was borne the (10)(11)1655”; and, on the same page, the death of a baby — “Josia Allis the sone of William Allis and Mary his wife dyed the (15)(8)1651”. She buried two sons named Josiah and a first son named William in infancy before the William who lived — and that William was killed in the Falls Fight at Turners Falls on 19 May 1676, a year before she died.

Her son Samuel, born 24 February 1647, is the child through whom this family descends. About 1661 the household moved west to Hatfield, and she died there on 10 August 1677; what of is not known. Her husband remarried the following June and was dead himself ten weeks after that.

Her surname is gone for good. Her own family's genealogy prints a literal blank where it should stand — “In 1641 William Allis married Mary ____ and their eight children were born in Braintree” — and the Braintree register, which had three chances at it, calls her only “Mary his wife” and carries no marriage entry at all. An old family story that she was killed in the Hatfield raid of September 1677 is false: she had been dead five and a half weeks when it happened, and the violent death the story was reaching for belongs to her daughter-in-law Alice, killed at Deerfield in 1704.

12300.s:
William Peck was born in 1601 and was a merchant in London. In 1637 he sailed for New England on the Hector with his wife Elizabeth and their young son Jeremiah, in the company of Theophilus Eaton, Edward Hopkins and the Reverend John Davenport; the ship reached Boston on 26 June. He went with that company to Quinnipiac, and in June 1639 he signed the Fundamental Agreement that founded New Haven. He was made a freeman there on 29 October 1640.

His home lot was on George Street and his shop stood on the south-easterly side of Church Street, fronting it. He was never a rich man, but he was a trusted one. He was one of three men who inventoried the estate of Sergeant Thomas Jeffrie in 1661. In December 1662 he stood up at a New Haven town meeting to tell it that the town's elders were not getting enough to eat: there was not wheat and malt enough to go round. With Roger Alling he was appointed a trustee of the fund, £918 in all, that paid for the colony's collegiate grammar school. From 1659 until his death — thirty-five years — he was deacon of the First Church of New Haven, and that is the name he kept.

Elizabeth died in December 1683, and about a year later he married Sarah, the widow of William Holt; his will, drawn 9 March 1689, mentions the second wife and his four children, all of them Elizabeth's. His will survives in the New Haven probate book. In it he left the house, barn and shop to his sons Jeremiah and Joseph, a share of the household goods to “my son John Peck now of Wallingford”, and the best feather bed to his daughter Elizabeth Andrews. Sarah, who had a marriage agreement giving her the use of the house for life, chose twelve pounds instead, “by her desire & to her better satisfaction”. The inventory taken after his death holds a surprise. Among his scales, tobacco, spectacles, psalm books and looking glass was an “instrument for drawing teeth & barbering”: it seems the old deacon also cut hair and pulled teeth. He died in October 1694 while staying at the house of his son Joseph at Lyme, more than forty miles from home. His stone was moved with the rest from the Old Green to Grove Street Cemetery in 1821 and still stands against the north wall there, giving in its own worn letters the age he reached and the day he died: “Here lyes Deacon William Peck, aged 93, deceased Octobr 14, 1694.”

3078.s:
Samuel Davis was born about 1645, probably at Roxbury, Massachusetts, and probably a son of William Davis of that town. He came up to Northampton in 1668 and was made a freeman there in 1676.

He kept choosing the exposed edge. Besides his Northampton land he held shares in the valley’s silver and lead mine venture, which he sold to Medad Pomeroy, and he put his name down as a subscriber to Harvard College. In 1682 he was a grantee of Northfield — a town that had already been burned twice — and in 1685 he was among the men who went back to rebuild it. In March 1676 his wife was one of a long list of Northampton women fined for wearing silk “in a flaunting manner.”

He married twice: first, on 4 March 1668, Hannah Edwards, who died on 11 September 1680; then, in 1681, Elizabeth, daughter of William Smead. He had two sons, Samuel, born 1672, and John, born 1677, and three daughters whose names were never set down. Samuel Davis died at Northampton on 26 July 1690, in the epidemic that swept the town that summer.

One of those three daughters was, in all likelihood, the Elizabeth Davis of Northampton who married William Allis of Hatfield in 1703–4 and is this family’s ancestor: his was the only Davis household of that generation in the town, though nothing on record names her as his.

Hannah Edwards was born at Springfield, Massachusetts, in February 1645, a daughter of Alexander Edwards, afterwards of Northampton. On 4 March 1668/9 she married Samuel Davis of Northampton — a young man newly come up the river from Roxbury — and she died on 11 September 1680, after a dozen years of marriage. Her husband married again the following year and lived another nine.

The town clerk of Northampton entered two of her children in the town book: a son, John, born in May 1677, and a daughter, Elizabeth, born on 20 June 1679, each written down as the child of “Samuel and Hannah Davis”. That Elizabeth is very probably the Elizabeth Davis of Northampton who married William Allis of Hatfield in 1703–4 and carried this line on, though no record yet joins the baby of 1679 to the bride of 1703. Hannah died in September 1680, the year after Elizabeth was born, and Samuel married again the next year.

52.s:
Benjamin Nott — the name was written Knott about as often as Nott — was born in Ohio about 1815 to 1817 and farmed in Adams Township, near Lowell, in Washington County. His mother was Polly (Roach) Nott. His father was very probably an elder Benjamin Nott “of Adams” died insolvent in 1822, leaving a widow Polly; he was one of several Nott householders in that corner of Ohio, and if he was the father, as seems likely, the boy was orphaned as a small boy on a broke farm on Calls Creek.

On the evening of Sunday 13 March 1836, in Morgan County, up the Muskingum, he married Margaret Kirk; their son John W. swore to her maiden name sixty-four years later. By 1850 they were farming in Adams Township, both thirty-three, with five children — Henrietta, Lucina, Frances, Pearly and William — and a Virginia-born woman of sixty-eight, Polly Morris, living with them — Benjamin’s mother, remarried since his father’s death. A year later she deeded him her fifty acres and took them back on a lease for her life; in 1861, “aged and infirm,” she left “my son Benjamin Nott” her share of her own father’s estate. In 1860 the household stood at Lowell: Benjamin forty-three, a farmer; Margaret forty-three; P. J. fifteen; William F. thirteen; and Jos M eleven. That eleven-year-old is believed to be Joseph McGee Knott, who named Benjamin and Margaret as his parents and Lowell as his birthplace at the end of his own life; the ages do not quite line up, so the link is probable rather than certain.

In July 1861, at forty-six, he volunteered for Company A of the Thirty-sixth Ohio Infantry — enlisted 29 July 1861, a private, discharged 4 September 1864. By 1870 the family had moved to Marietta, where the household was Benjamin fifty-three, Margaret fifty-two, John W. twenty-three, Sarah twenty, a baby Henry, and three boarders.

His last years were hard. In December 1890 the probate court recorded “P. J. Nott, guardian of Benjamin Nott, an Insane person” filing an inventory — the guardian was his own child, the P. J. of the 1860 household. He died at Marietta on 6 May 1891 of la grippe, the influenza that went round the world between 1889 and 1891, and the estate was settled that July: charged with nothing at all, credited with $10.91, and that sum found due the child who had cared for him. He lies in Oak Grove Cemetery at Marietta, lot 90, block 19, under an upright stone.

53.s:
Margaret Kirk was born about 1817 — in Ohio by her own household’s reckoning in 1850 and 1860, in Virginia by the 1870 enumerator and her gravestone’s compiler. On the evening of Sunday 13 March 1836, in Morgan County, Ohio, up the Muskingum, a justice of the peace named A. Rich married her to Benjamin Nott. The Kirks of Meigs Creek in Morgan County were a real family, and one of them kept a cabin that sheltered Virginia migrants walking west in 1817, which may account for a daughter whose birthplace was once written as Virginia; which Kirk was her father is not known.

Their first child, Henrietta, was born the next year. By September 1850 they were farming in Adams Township, Washington County, near Lowell: Benjamin and Margaret both thirty-three, with Henrietta, Lucina, Frances, Pearly and a two-year-old boy, William, who later went by John W. Living with them was a woman of sixty-eight named Polly Morris, born in Virginia — Benjamin’s own mother, as her will of 1861 would make plain. In 1860 the household at Lowell held a boy of eleven entered as Jos M — Joseph McGee Knott, who named Benjamin and Margaret as his parents at the end of his life — and in 1870 the family was at Marietta, Margaret fifty-two.

Benjamin went to the war in the Thirty-sixth Ohio, came home an invalid pensioner, and in his last months was under his own child’s guardianship as insane. He died at Marietta on 6 May 1891, and on 1 June Margaret applied for a widow’s pension, which was granted. Long afterwards her son John W., swearing to a marriage licence in 1900, gave his mother’s maiden name as “Margaret Keirk.”

A Mrs. Margaret Nott of Lowell, aged eighty-three, died on Sunday 15 January 1899, and her body was carried down the Muskingum by the steamer Sonoma for burial at Oak Grove Cemetery, Marietta, where Benjamin lies. The paper called her the widow of “the late Thomas Nott” — but Thomas H. Nott was her son, and the stone she shares with Benjamin reads MARGRET NOTT HIS WIFE 1817–1899, so it was almost certainly she.

54.s:
Erwin R. Lamb — Irvin on his own gravestone, Irwin in the Jonesboro papers; the three spellings are one man — was born on 19 March 1840 in Wayne County, Indiana, the second of the ten children of Elias Lamb, carpenter and farmer, and Susannah (Bish) Lamb, who had married at her father’s house in Clay Township on 23 March 1837. His grandparents were Joseph and Lydia (Adamson) Lamb, Quakers who had brought the family from Randolph County, North Carolina, to Wayne County in April 1829, eleven years before he was born. He was reared on his father’s farm in Clay Township and stayed in the county until he was a grown man.

On 14 March 1860 he took out a licence in Wayne County to marry Melissa J. Bailey, the daughter of a neighbouring farming family; the minister married them the next day. It was a double season: his elder brother Azel had married Sarah Ann Bailey three months before, in the next township. That summer the newlyweds were still under his father’s roof in Clay Township, on a farm worth eleven thousand dollars. Four children came — Alma S., Martha E., Frank A. and May Belle — and then, on the evening of Monday 29 November 1875, after a few days’ illness, Melissa died at Newport in Vermillion County, aged thirty-one. The family had moved there in 1870 with his parents.

On 18 May 1879 he married Mrs. Mary Elizabeth (Jackson) Hall, the widow of a soldier of the 125th Illinois Infantry and the daughter of Arthur Jackson, an early Vermillion County settler who had given three sons to the Union and lost all three. She brought five Hall children with her. In 1880 the two families were together on Main Street in Vermillion — Erwin forty, “Mary E.” forty-one, his own Mattie, Frank and Bell, and her Effie. By 1888 he was living at Newport. In May 1890 he was very probably the Erwin Lamb of Plainfield, Indiana, who came down to Terre Haute to stay with two of his children — his daughter, by then Mrs. Mattie Ford, and his son Frank — who were keeping house together on north Third Street.

He did not stay in Indiana. He and his wife were settled at Jonesboro, in Craighead County, Arkansas, in a house on Krewson Avenue, by 1911 at the latest, and he kept the books for other men to the end of his working life: for many years he was clerk at the Old American Hotel. He was a member of the First Methodist church and a regular attender until his health failed. He spent seven weeks in St. Bernard’s Hospital in 1914.

His last illness is in the Jonesboro papers almost day by day. He had been ill at home for ten days in October 1918 and in poor health for eight months; on Monday 17 February 1919 an infected foot was amputated at St. Bernard’s, and the paper noted that at his age the operation was a shock to his nervous system; he was reported resting nicely, then continuing to improve; the surgeons went back and took the leg off below the knee for gangrene; and he died at half past twelve on the morning of 27 February 1919, aged seventy-eight. One paper called him “a splendid man”; the other, “an old resident of the city… highly respected by everyone, making a friend of every acquaintance.” Six men carried him. His survivors were given as his wife and his step-children — A. W. Hall and Mrs. C. C. Conger of Jonesboro, Mrs. Josephine Schweizer of Danville, Illinois, and Mrs. Effie Townsend of Richmond, Illinois. His own children, his daughter Martha among them, were not mentioned. He was buried at Jonesboro, under a plain marble block cut IRVIN R LAMB.

His widow Mary outlived him by two years. She had turned seventy-nine at a party at the First Methodist Church in August 1917; after his death she lived with her daughter Bertha Conger, and she died at the same hospital on 20 February 1921 after a long illness, and was buried from that church. Martha Ellen Lamb was his daughter, though her birth year was written down two or three years apart in different places, so that tie is not quite beyond doubt.

55.s:
Melissa J. Bailey was born on 24 July 1844 in Wayne County, Indiana. In 1850 she was the youngest child in the Green Township house of her father, John Bailey, a Virginian, and his wife Martha, a North Carolinian. When her father died in August 1863 she was one of his thirteen heirs, and in January 1869 she received her share of his estate, $582.85, as Mallissa Lamb. The Baileys and the Lambs farmed adjoining ground in Clay Township — Ithamar Lamb, Milo Bailey and Lewis Strickler were living on one tract of school land there — and she married the boy from the next farm.

On 14 March 1860, aged fifteen, she took out a licence with Irvin R. Lamb, and the minister married them the next day. Three months before, Irvin’s elder brother Azel had married another Bailey, Sarah Ann — two brothers and two Bailey brides in one winter. That summer she was living with her husband in his father’s house in Clay Township. Four children followed: Alma S., Martha E., born at Richmond in August 1865, Frank A. and May Belle. About 1870 the whole Lamb connection moved west to Vermillion County.

She died at Newport at about eight o’clock on the evening of Monday 29 November 1875, after a few days’ illness, aged thirty-one. Her funeral was preached at two the following afternoon in the Methodist Episcopal church by the Rev. Milton B. Wood, and she was buried at Newport. The local paper, which knew her, called her “a United Brethren in belief” and “a kind mother, an affectionate wife, a noble woman and highly esteemed by every person in Newport.” Her daughter Martha was ten.

124.s:
George Nease was born in Virginia on 10 December 1819 — his own death record says 21 November 1820 — into one of the Nease families of Mason County who had come down from the Shenandoah Valley with the Roushes and settled both banks of the Ohio.

On 12 March 1849 he took out a licence to marry Nancy Roush: she was seventeen, he was twenty-nine. He and Henry Roush signed the bond, and with it the clerk filed a note from an Anthony Roush, made with his mark: “let George Nease have lisons to git maried to nancy Roush.” Their eldest, Susan M., was an infant in the house in 1850, when he was thirty-one and Nancy eighteen, and a six-year-old Lewis J. was there in 1860, in a household the enumerator spelled “Neoce.” He farmed in Graham District, and he and Nancy raised their family there; their son Lewis married Martha Love in 1877 and twenty years later gave his own daughter in marriage to a Roush.

George Nease died on 21 November 1899 in Mason County, and Nancy gave the county the particulars — she is entered as “Nancie Nease, wife.” It was one of the few years the register asked for the dead man’s parents, and the clerk wrote “Samuel and Catherine Nease,” a first name that does not match the Emanuel and Catharine Nease who were the only Nease couple of that generation in the county. A deed he signed himself in 1865 answers it. With his brothers and sisters he sold his share of the home farm as one of the “Heirs at law of Emanuel Nease deceased”.

He lies at Broad Run. His marker is a small modern block cut GEORGE NEASE 1818 - 1898 — a year adrift at each end from everything else that records him.

125.s:
Nancy Roush was born on 16 February 1832, the eleventh child of Anthony Roush and his first wife Elizabeth Rickard — a parentage her family’s own book records and no document has yet confirmed, though it was an Anthony Roush who gave consent for her marriage.

She married George Nease in March 1849, at seventeen. She was under age, and the licence papers keep a scrap of paper reading “Mr Thomas Lewis let George Nease have lisons to git maried to nancy Roush your oblige your friend Anthony Roush,” with Anthony’s X mark and the marks or names of Henry and David Roush beneath it. Henry carried it to the courthouse on 12 March and swore that Anthony had made it. By 1850 she was eighteen with an infant daughter, Susan M., in a Mason County household headed by George, thirty-one. Her son Lewis was born in November 1854, and in 1860 he was six years old in a house the enumerator called “Neoce.” She raised her family in Graham District.

In November 1899 she buried her husband and gave the county the information for his record herself. She lived another fourteen years a widow, and died on 21 July 1913, aged eighty-one years, five months and five days — somebody in that house still had her birthday written down eighty-one years on. Dr. D. A. Sayre gave the cause as congestion of the lungs.

She is buried at Broad Run beside George, under a small modern marker cut NANCY NEASE 1828 - 1911. Hers and George’s are a matched pair of the same late pattern, and both are wrong in the same direction, which is what replacement stones cut from memory look like. One thing is worth saying plainly about her: in February 1897 her granddaughter Bertha Nease married John G. Roush of Mason County, and in doing so married straight back into Nancy’s own birth family.

249.s:
Catharine Nease was born in Virginia between about 1793 and 1797, most likely at the beginning of January 1797. She married a Nease of Mason County — Emanuel, by the stone that lies over her — and they farmed on the Virginia bank of the Ohio, in the dwelling immediately after Jacob M. Roush’s; the Neases and the Roushes were already neighbours there. Her sons included George, born on 21 November 1820, and Levi A. In 1850 she was fifty-three and keeping house, her husband fifty-eight.

He died in the 1850s, and she went on alone for more than twenty years. In 1870, at seventy-four, she still had her own house in Graham District, with an eighteen-year-old of the family in the next dwelling who “works on farm.”

She died in July 1878, aged eighty-one years and six months — the age cut on her stone. She lies at Union Cemetery in New Haven, where that stone now lies flat among the leaves, broken in two across the line naming her husband. Her own family name before marriage is uncertain; Aumiller has come down with her, and nothing yet confirms it.

Anthony Roush was born on 23 January 1792 in Shenandoah County, Virginia, near Solomon’s Church, and was baptised there on 18 March 1792 with Michael Levermore standing sponsor. He was the seventh child of Henry Roush and his wife Dorothy — a Henry who at twenty-three had served eighty-eight days as a private in Captain John Tipton’s company and been paid off at Romney in October 1775, and for whom his younger brother Jonas later stood substitute.

The family came down into the Ohio Valley, and Anthony with them. On 11 July 1812, when he was twenty, Henry Roush sold him seventy-five acres for three hundred dollars. About 1810 he had married Elizabeth Rickard, a sister of the Rickard brothers of that neighbourhood, and in 1820 and 1830 an Anthony Roush with a young family was living across the river at Letart, Ohio, among the Roush households there. Whether that was he is not yet settled. After Elizabeth he married Catherine Hoffman, in Mason County on 11 January 1837; she bore him Moses and Phoebe and was dead within four years, and on 21 March 1841 he married a third time, Lydia Pounds, probably the Lydia, born in New York, who was fifty-seven and his wife in 1850. Young men and women named Pound were living with them in 1860, probably her children. He had a long family, and Nancy, born on 16 February 1832, was the eleventh child; she married George Nease in 1849, at seventeen, and the consent for it carries the X mark of an Anthony Roush. In 1850 he was fifty-nine, a farmer who could not write his name, living in Mason County with a wife named Lydia, born in New York, and sharing his house with his son Henry and Henry’s young family.

He fell heir, in all likelihood, to a share of his father’s portion of the six-thousand-acre estate in Graham District, Mason County — land that had been fought over in the courts since a petition of 1806.

He lies in the Rickard cemetery, in the White Church community of Mason County, under a small stone with no epitaph cut on it.

251.s:
Elizabeth Rickard was a sister of the Rickard brothers of Mason County, in what was then Virginia, and about 1810 she married Anthony Roush, a young man of the Shenandoah Valley Roushes whose family had settled in the same neighbourhood on the Ohio. Who her own parents were is not known.

She bore Anthony a long family, among them Nancy, born on 16 February 1832, the eleventh, who married George Nease in 1848 at sixteen. Elizabeth was dead, or the marriage was over, before Anthony married Catherine Hoffman.

No date of birth and no date of death has come down for her, and her grave is not identified — though the burying ground at White Church, where Anthony lies, carries her family’s name. Of her own life nothing survives but that one phrase, “a sister to the Rickard brothers,” and the children she raised.

500.s:
Henry Roush was born in 1752 in Shenandoah County, Virginia, one of the oldest of the children of John Adam and Susannah Roush.

He was twenty-three when the war began, and he was in it from the first season: a private in Captain John Tipton’s company, eighty-eight days’ service, paid off at Romney on a receipt dated 25 October 1775 for £6 12s. In the summer of 1781 he was drafted again and his younger brother Jonas went in his place — Jonas swore to it half a century later, applying for his own pension. The Daughters of the American Revolution carry Henry as Patriot Ancestor A098977.

He married Dorothea about 1777 and they raised ten children in Shenandoah County near Solomon’s Church — Michael, Christina, Henry Jr., Elizabeth, Susannah, Anthony, Dorothy, Eva and Balser among them. Anthony, born 23 January 1792, is the son through whom this family descends. Henry gave the two and a half acres the church and its graveyard stand on, and in 1793 he put his hand to the Solomonburg deed, signing “HENRICH ROUSH” in German on the same page where his wife made her mark. It is why the descendants who later marked his grave called him the Church Builder.

He followed the Roush migration down the Ohio — to Mason County in 1798, and on to Letart Falls in Meigs County, Ohio, about 1800 — and he settled his children on land as he went: a deed to Henry Jr. in October 1805, seventy-five acres to Anthony for three hundred dollars in July 1812, and in June 1817 land to his son Balser and to his daughters Susanna Linscott and Catharine “for natural love and affection.”

He died on 26 October 1831, aged seventy-nine, and lies in Plants Cemetery above the river at Plants, Meigs County. The little stone set over him then — “Henry Roush died October 26, 1831, aged 79 years” — has been joined by a granite block carrying a plaque from his descendants: “HENRY ROUSH / 1752-1831 / ‘THE CHURCH BUILDER’ / ONE OF NINE BROTHERS / WHO FOUGHT IN THE / REVOLUTIONARY WAR / ERECTED BY HIS DESCENDANTS.” A bronze tablet at its foot reads “HENRY ROUSH / PVT CAPT TIPTON’S CO / VA STATE TRP / REVOLUTIONARY WAR / 1752 † 1831,” naming the very company he had served in fifty-six years before he died. The markers were dedicated by the Sons of the American Revolution at the Roush family’s annual meeting on 19 August 1933, the same afternoon as his brother George’s, a few miles down the Ohio.

501.s:
Dorothea — Dorothy to the neighbours who wrote her name down, Dolly in the family — married Henry Roush Sr. in Shenandoah County about 1777. Her maiden name has never been recovered; the family thought she was a Nease, Nehs as that family spelled itself in German, and there were Neases standing as baptismal sponsors for her children.

She bore ten children in the neighbourhood of Solomon’s Church — Michael, Christina, Henry, Elizabeth, Susannah, Anthony, Dorothy, Eva and Balser among them. Anthony, born in January 1792, carries this line. In 1793 she witnessed the Solomonburg church deed: her husband signed his name in German, and she signed “DOROTHY ROUSH (her mark)” on the same page. In 1796 a John Nease was serving as a church trustee beside Henry and Dorothea.

She went with the family down the Ohio to Letart Falls in Meigs County, Ohio, and she died about the same time as Henry, in 1831 or near it. She lies beside him in Plants Cemetery. Her stone was already past reading when the family went looking for it a century later — the “inscription … is now too far gone to be recovered, but it seems undoubtedly to be his wife Dorothy” — and a broken, wholly illegible stone still stands beside his monument today. Her grave counts as unmarked.

290.s:
He was, if his family's own story is true, a small boy found alive on the North Carolina coast sometime between 1735 and 1745 after a shipwreck. He could tell them only that his name was Billie Pigford and that he had sailed from England with his parents, who were never found. A Dutch family took him in. In March 1740 or 1741 the county court dealt with him formally: Rebecca Perry petitioned to be allowed to keep the boy herself, and the court bound him instead to Benjamin Fussell. He was called Lost Billie for the rest of his life, and his great-granddaughter was still telling the story in 1896.

Whatever he came from, he ended a landowner on both banks of Sill's Creek, in the Penderlea country where New Hanover County runs up against Duplin — and in 1790 his was the only Pigford household in the whole state. He married a woman named Sarah, remembered in the family only as “a woman of Dutch descent,” and they raised a large family: William, Jacob, Timothy, Solomon, Edward, Martha and Margaret, and probably a daughter Elizabeth, who married an Eakins of Moores Creek.

On 27 March 1801 he had his will written out. It gives Sarah all the household furniture and moveable effects and everything else not otherwise left, “to be by her disposed of amongst her children as she may think proper,” together with the plantation he lived on and all the land east of Sill's Creek for the term of her life. Timothy got the land on the west side of the creek. Solomon got the home place after his mother's death — and in return was bound to help his brother Timothy build “a dwelling house, kitchen, corn crib, smoke house, dairy, and in clearing ten acres of land.” To the rest of the children he left one shilling sterling each. The filed original ends with his name written out, “William Pigford (Seal),” witnessed by William Jones; a later transcription that gives him an X and “his mark” is not borne out by the paper.

He died before March 1803, when the New Hanover Court of Pleas and Quarter Sessions proved the will — and had to do it the slow way, since the witness himself was not there to swear to it: William Bloodworth stood up instead and swore that the signature was in William Jones's own hand. Both the Sons and the Daughters of the American Revolution carry him as a patriot for signing a 1779 petition from the inhabitants of New Hanover, Duplin and Bladen counties, asking that the county be divided so that militiamen could reach their musters; in 1779, though, there were two William Pigfords in the county, father and son, and which of them put his name to that sheet is not known. He and Sarah lie somewhere in the Penderlea area in unmarked graves.

291.s:
Sarah was the wife of William “Lost Billie” Pigford of Sill's Creek, in the Penderlea country of New Hanover County, North Carolina. Family tradition, set down about 1896, says only that Lost Billie “married a woman of Dutch descent.” Her own surname was never written down anywhere that survives — the family's historian hunted through the marriage records of both New Hanover and Duplin counties for it and wrote in 1967 that “her family name continues to be beyond the reach of this recorder.”

They had a large family: William, Jacob, Timothy, Solomon, Edward, Martha, Margaret, and a daughter Elizabeth, who married an Eakins.

Her husband's will of 27 March 1801 begins with her, and it trusts her with everything: “First; I give and bequeath to Sarah, my dearly beloved wife, all my household furniture, moveable effects and all other of my estate… to be by her disposed of amongst her children as she may think proper; and also the plantation whereon I now live, with all the improvements thereon; and all the land I possess adjoining the east side of Sill's Creek, for the term of her life.” She was named executrix. Her son Solomon was to have the home place only after her death, and until then was under orders to help his brother Timothy put up a house. She is believed to lie in an unmarked grave in the Penderlea area, near the old Pigford burying ground.
