108.s:
Elias Lamb was born on 24 September 1814 in Randolph County, North Carolina, about sixteen miles north of Asheboro, the son of Joseph and Lydia (Adamson) Lamb, Quakers. In April 1829, when he was fourteen, his parents took the family out of North Carolina and settled in Clay Township, Wayne County, Indiana, where they farmed until they died. Nine children had been born to them; seven grew up.

He was reared on his father’s farm and learned the carpenter’s trade, which he worked at alongside farming all his life. On 23 March 1837 he married Susannah Bish at the house of her father, John Bish, in Clay Township; the licence had been issued the day before, and Richard Jobes, Justice of the Peace, joined them. When the wedding was paid for he took stock of what he owned and found “a few carpenter tools and $20. in money”; her dowry was about twenty-five dollars’ worth of goods, including a heifer calf. They spent part of the twenty dollars on simple furniture and began housekeeping on his father’s farm on 7 June 1837. In April 1839 they bought a farm adjoining it; that September they swapped farms and moved three-quarters of a mile south, and there they stayed thirty-one years. In 1841 he and Susannah left the Society of Friends and united by letter with the United Brethren church, to which he belonged for the last forty-one years of his life.

Ten children were born to them, five sons and five daughters, of whom one, an infant son, died in June 1844. In politics he was a Free-Soiler until 1856 — “that is he believed it wrong for one man to enslave his fellow man” — and then a Republican from the year Frémont ran.

In November 1870 they sold up and bought the Montgomery farm near Perrysville, in Vermillion County; in March 1873 a farm a mile and a half north-west of Newport; and on 3 March 1887 the house in Newport where they spent their last years. On the night of 12 October 1883 burglars broke into the Newport house and beat Elias badly — one eye closed, a bullet grazing Susannah’s head and splitting her ear — until he reached the yard bell-rope and rang the alarm. He never fully recovered from it; three years on, the paper said he had received injuries from which he would probably never recover.

Their golden wedding fell on 23 March 1887. Fifty-eight relatives and friends came; a neighbour, M. G. Rhoads, read out a history of the two old people; two ministers performed the marriage ceremony over again; a senator made some remarks; and then everyone went in to a sumptuous dinner. The presents were listed in the paper down to a china catsup mug and a silver butter knife. They counted that day nine living children, twenty-nine grandchildren and eight great-grandchildren — forty-eight in all, most of them in the room.

In February 1887, a month before the golden wedding, he made his will. He wrote that he had already given his four eldest — Azel Edwin, Irvin, Elizabeth Jane and Merritt — “at divers times… all I intend for them,” left Susannah the widow’s portion and the income of the rest for as long as she stayed his widow, and named the five younger children to share it after her. He also set aside money for his own gravestone: “a plain monument put up at my grave at an expense not exceeding Fifty Dollars (suitably lettered).”

He took sick one Monday in late August 1890 and died at four o’clock on the Sunday morning, 31 August, within a month of his seventy-sixth birthday. The funeral was preached at the United Brethren church by his pastor, the Rev. R. B. Van Allen, and “his remains were followed to the Thomas cemetery by a large concourse of relatives” — the burying ground at Newport, where the plain stone he paid for still stands, cut ELIAS LAMB DIED AUG. 30 1890 AGED 76 YEARS.

109.s:
Susannah Bish was born on 17 November 1818 in Fairfield County, Ohio, about eighteen miles east of Columbus, a daughter of John and Ann Elizabeth Bish. She was brought up among Lutherans, of Dutch or German descent, had what her family called “a very limited education in the old fashioned ‘deestrict schools’,” and learned “the various mysteries of house keeping.” In 1836 she came with her parents to Wayne County, Indiana, and settled in Clay Township.

On 23 March 1837, four months past her eighteenth birthday, she married Elias Lamb at her father’s house. Her dowry to the “joint stock company” was about twenty-five dollars’ worth of goods, including a heifer calf. They kept house first on his father’s farm, then on farms of their own three-quarters of a mile away, for thirty-one years. Ten children were born to her; one, an infant son, died in June 1844. In 1841 she and Elias left the Society of Friends — his people’s church, not hers — and joined the United Brethren by letter.

Her own family stayed close by. Her sister Mary Ann, born near Dayton, Ohio, in July 1823, married first William Petty and then Jesse Sykes and lived until 1915; her brother John married Sintha Johnson on 8 October 1842, a wedding written into the marriage page of the Bish family Bible, which a generation later recorded a second Lamb–Bish match, William D. Lamb to Pally A. Bish.

The family moved to Vermillion County in November 1870, and in 1887 into a house in Newport. Four years before that, on the night of 12 October 1883, burglars broke in on them; Elias was badly beaten and a bullet grazed Susannah’s head and split her ear. Their golden wedding, on 23 March 1887, drew fifty-eight relatives and friends, two ministers to perform the ceremony over again, and a table of presents — a tidy and a handkerchief from Mrs. Petty, three towels from Mary J. Sykes. They counted forty-eight descendants, most of them present.

She outlived Elias by eighteen years. In her last years she made her home with her son-in-law Levi S. Clendenning near Sugar Grove, Illinois, and she died there at three o’clock on the morning of Wednesday 8 April 1908, at ninety. Eight of her children survived her. The funeral was held in the church at Sugar Grove the next morning, and she was brought back to Indiana and buried beside Elias in the Thomas burying ground at Newport, under a stone that says only SUSANNAH, wife of E. LAMB.

110.s:
John Bailey was a Virginian, born about 1793. A Wayne County history of 1872 tells his road west: out of Kentucky to Richmond, Indiana, about 1810, then to Perry Township, and in 1859 to Clay Township, where his son Milo was already farming. By 1850 he and his wife Martha were in Green Township with seven children at home, from Harriet, twenty, down to Malissa, seven.

The Baileys farmed among the Lambs. Thomas Lamb lived two doors away, and in a single winter two of the girls of his house married two Lamb brothers: Sarah Ann married Azel E. Lamb in December 1859, and Malissa married Irvin R. Lamb in March 1860, at fifteen. The two families went on doing each other’s business for years; in 1872 Milo Bailey and Irvin’s father stood surety together for Irvin in the county court.

John Bailey died on 5 August 1863, without a will, leaving his widow Martha, twelve grown children and the children of a daughter, Julia McPherson, who had died before him. For months his family simply got on with it: the widow and all the heirs but one, who was “out of the country”, agreed to let two of the sons, John A. and Milo, settle the estate without the court. In February 1864 the two brothers took out letters anyway, on a $22,000 bond with Joseph Lamb as surety, signed by the county clerk Solomon Meredith, lately a general at Gettysburg. The farm and stock came to more than $11,000 in personal property and $5,000 in land; it took five years, four settlements and a lawyer before, in January 1869, the widow received her third and each of the thirteen heirs $582.85 — among them his daughters Sarah A. Lamb and Mallissa Lamb.

216.s:
Joseph Lamb was born in North Carolina about 1782. He married Lydia Adamson there in November 1806, her brother Samuel standing bondsman — the clerk wrote her name “Lidya Addison” — and they were members of the Society of Friends. Nine children were born to them, of whom seven grew up: Ezekiel, Esther, Smith, Elias, Mournen, Joseph and Ithamar. The family was living in Randolph County, about sixteen miles north of Asheboro, in 1814, when his son Elias was born there.

In April 1829 he took the family out of North Carolina for Indiana — the ordinary Quaker departure from the slaveholding South — and settled in Clay Township, Wayne County, on land adjoining Perry Township that a widow, Eve Shoemaker, had first taken up in 1821. He farmed there for the rest of his life, and his sons and his wife’s brother settled around him: when the Clay Township school section was sold in 1832 the buyers included Samuel Adamson, and his son Ithamar was still living on that land forty years later.

Lydia died first — in 1844, his son Elias remembered, though the year is also given as 1837. Joseph died on 29 July 1855, aged seventy-three, and lies in Sugar Grove Cemetery in Wayne County under a small marble stone, weathered but still readable: JOSEPH LAMB DIED 29th Day of the July of year 1855.

217.s:
Lydia Adamson married Joseph Lamb in North Carolina in November 1806; the marriage bond was made out for “Lidya Addison,” and her brother Samuel stood bondsman. He later married Joseph’s sister Naomi, so two Adamsons married two Lambs. They were Quakers. Nine children were born to them, of whom seven lived to grow up, among them Elias, through whom this line descends.

In April 1829 she came north with her husband and children to Wayne County, Indiana, and settled in Clay Township; her brother Samuel was one of the buyers when the township school section was sold in 1832. She did not live to be old in Indiana. Her son Elias gave her death as 1844; it is elsewhere put at 11 November 1837, at Economy in the same county.

Almost nothing of her own survives. The county’s history of its first settlers names her husband and all seven of their grown children without once naming her, and she is the only one of the four Lambs and Bishes of her generation on this chart with no stone — none at Sugar Grove beside Joseph, and none anywhere else that can be found.

218.s:
John Bish lived in Fairfield County, Ohio, about eighteen miles east of Columbus, where his daughter Susannah was born in November 1818. He may be the John Bish who married an Anne Campbell in Rockingham County, Virginia, in November 1810. He and his wife Ann Elizabeth raised ten children to maturity.

In 1836 he brought the family to Wayne County, Indiana, and settled in Clay Township. 6156.s:
William Davis was born about 1617 and lived at Roxbury, Massachusetts, where he was made a freeman in 1673. His children come into view in a single entry in the Roxbury church book in 1649, when the congregation received the children of a newly admitted member: “John Davis, Samuel Davis, Joseph Davis — Children of William Davis whose wife was admitted & so brought her children to p'take of this blessed ordinance.” Samuel, born 21 February 1645, is the son through whom this family descends, and the same church book marks his going: “Samuel Davis dismissed to North-Hampton”, when he went west up the Connecticut valley.

He married twice. His first wife was Elizabeth, who died or was buried on 4 May 1658. He married second, that October, Alice Thorp, and the Roxbury clerk wrote her end in one unsparing line: “Alice wife of William Davis who dyed in child birth undelivered.” He was probably a brother of Tobias Davis of the same town — a household that has to be kept carefully apart from his, because it held a Samuel too.

He made his will on 6 December 1683 and died three days later, on the 9th, aged about sixty-six. That the Samuel who settled at Northampton is the same boy brought to the ordinance at Roxbury in 1649 is probable rather than certain.

Elizabeth was the wife of William Peck, the London merchant who became deacon of the First Church at New Haven. They were married in London, and in 1637 she crossed to New England with him and their young son Jeremiah on the Hector, in the company that would found New Haven; the ship made Boston on 26 June. Their home lot in the new town was on George Street, and her husband's shop fronted on Church Street.

All four of William Peck's children were hers — Jeremiah, John, Joseph and Elizabeth — and they are the four named in his will. John, born about 1638, is the son in this line. She died on 5 December 1683, away from home: she was visiting her son at Lyme, forty miles down the coast, when she died. Eleven years later her husband died in the same place, at their son Joseph's house.

She lies in New Haven. Her grave was on the Old Green with the rest of the founding generation and was moved to Grove Street Cemetery in 1821, where a small rough stone against the north wall, eight feet from her husband's, carries nothing but a date and two initials: 1683, and under it E P. Her maiden name was never written down by anyone who knew it.

12302.s:
John Moss was at New Haven by 1639, in the first years of the colony, and he is one of the three names — with Doolittle and Peck — that between them made Wallingford. He served the older town first. He was one of the commissioners New Haven chose to settle its disputed boundary with Branford: they met on 5 October 1669 and, after full debate, set the bounds and ended the case for ever. Through the 1640s, 1650s and 1660s the colony's records carry him as a trainband corporal, a representative and a deputy. In 1670, when Wallingford was incorporated, he moved inland with the rest, and the town's historian, writing in 1870, called him flatly “the ancestor of all who bear the name in these parts.”

He and his wife had eleven children baptized at New Haven between 1640 and 1655. Among them were Mary, baptized 11 April 1647, who married John Peck in 1664 and is the one in this line; Abigail, who married Abraham Doolittle as his second wife; and a second John, born 1650, who carried his father's name and has been taken for him ever since.

He died in 1707, and the striking thing said of him was said everywhere: that he was 103 years old, and the oldest man who had ever died in Connecticut. The claim was local and old — the stonecutter carved it, and it was repeated from a Wallingford pulpit at the town's centennial in 1770 — and whether he truly reached it is another matter. His stone stands in the Center Street Cemetery at Wallingford, a heart cut into its face, and inside the heart: “Mr John Moss, born 1604, died 1707, Æ 103.”

961.s:
Susannah married John Adam Roush about 1739, soon after he landed at Philadelphia, and went with him down into the Shenandoah Valley to the farm on Mill Creek. She was the mother of the whole American Roush family — ten children, seven of them sons, and every one of the sons went into the Revolution. Her own maiden name is lost; Sehler, or Schlern, circulates in family trees, but no source for it has ever been produced.

Very little else of her life was ever written down. In 1773 a grant of four hundred acres on Mill Creek was made “to him and his wife Susannah.” She stood as a baptismal sponsor at the Old Pine Church in 1770, and again on 5 January 1786 — nine months before her husband died — that second time as a grandmother. After his death the church’s list of communicants carries “Susannah Roush, widow” in 1788, 1790, 1792, 1795 and 1796, and then never again.

She died at or about 1796, ten years after her husband, and was buried beside him at the Old Pine Church. “The grave of the wife, Susannah, is not marked,” the family’s historian wrote, “but there is no reason to doubt that she lies by his side.” When the old stones were moved to St Mary’s Pine Church Cemetery at Mount Jackson in 1868, nothing of hers went with them, because there was nothing to move. In 1936 the Roush and Allied Families Association cut her name into the bicentennial monument there — “1713 – HIS WIFE, SUSANNAH – 1796” — the only stone that carries it, and the only thing that gives her a birth year at all.

Alec descends from her three times over, her grandson John and her granddaughter Regina having married each other. This is the first of the three, through her son George.

965.s:
Susannah married John Adam Roush about 1739, soon after he landed at Philadelphia, and went with him down into the Shenandoah Valley to the farm on Mill Creek. She was the mother of the whole American Roush family — ten children, seven of them sons, and every one of the sons went into the Revolution. Her own maiden name is lost; Sehler, or Schlern, circulates in family trees, but no source for it has ever been produced.

Very little else of her life was ever written down. In 1773 a grant of four hundred acres on Mill Creek was made “to him and his wife Susannah.” She stood as a baptismal sponsor at the Old Pine Church in 1770, and again on 5 January 1786 — nine months before her husband died — that second time as a grandmother. After his death the church’s list of communicants carries “Susannah Roush, widow” in 1788, 1790, 1792, 1795 and 1796, and then never again.

She died at or about 1796, ten years after her husband, and was buried beside him at the Old Pine Church. “The grave of the wife, Susannah, is not marked,” the family’s historian wrote, “but there is no reason to doubt that she lies by his side.” When the old stones were moved to St Mary’s Pine Church Cemetery at Mount Jackson in 1868, nothing of hers went with them, because there was nothing to move. In 1936 the Roush and Allied Families Association cut her name into the bicentennial monument there — “1713 – HIS WIFE, SUSANNAH – 1796” — the only stone that carries it, and the only thing that gives her a birth year at all.

Alec descends from her three times over, her grandson John and her granddaughter Regina having married each other. This is the second of the three, through her youngest son Jonas, who stood at Yorktown.

1000.s:
John Adam Roush — Johannes Adam Rausch — was born in 1711 in the Palatinate, and the family has always said Darmstadt. He crossed to Philadelphia in the closing months of 1736 and took the oath of fidelity there. The tradition carried down into the twentieth century was that he and two companions, forbidden to emigrate, were hidden inside hogsheads by a friendly cooper, loaded aboard, and let out at sea. He landed too poor to pay his passage, hired himself out near Philadelphia, stayed on past his term because he was paid unusually well, and then married and went down the Shenandoah Valley.

He settled on Mill Creek in what was then Frederick County — later Dunmore, then Shenandoah — and farmed it; the family says he kept a mill and a tannery as well, and more than thirty land transactions stand in his name or his sons’. In 1773 a grant of four hundred acres on Mill Creek was made “to him and his wife Susannah.” By then he had been in the valley more than thirty years and had raised a large family: the sons Philip, John, Jacob, Henry, Daniel, George and Jonas, and the daughters Mary Magdalene, Eleanor and Elizabeth. The family has always said that nine sons went out of that house.

Every one of those sons went into the Revolution, and so, in his sixties, did he: he furnished supplies to the army between 1780 and 1783 and took a Shenandoah County claim certificate, number 2453, for the property impressed from him. The Daughters of the American Revolution carry him for it as Patriot Ancestor A098982. One son was a captain with two of his brothers in the ranks; two of them substituted for each other; one of them witnessed another’s pension application fifty years later.

He was a Lutheran, and the family were tanners and builders of churches. He died on 19 October 1786 near New Market in Shenandoah County and was buried at the Old Pine Church. His gravestone survives — a rough slab cut in German by someone who spelled by ear: ANO 1711 GEBOHREN JOHANNES RAUSCH GESTORBEN DEN 19 OCTOBER 1786. The Adam had already dropped out of his name. When the old burying ground’s stones were moved to St Mary’s Pine Church Cemetery at Mount Jackson in 1868 his went with them, and it is kept upright there under glass with a Sons of the American Revolution patriot star beside it. Susannah outlived him by ten years and lies beside him in a grave that was never marked. In 1936, two hundred years after his crossing, the Roush and Allied Families Association raised a monument over the two of them that names their children one by one and reckons their descendants, living and dead, at about forty thousand American citizens.

Alec’s descent reaches him three times over, because two of his grandchildren married each other. This is the third of the three paths, and it runs through his son Henry Sr., the Church Builder who lies at Plants Cemetery in Ohio — a son by the family’s own settled account rather than by the word of any surviving record.

962.s:
Michael Zerckel — the name was written Zirkle, Zerkel, Zerchel, Sircle, Circle and Zickel, and twice differently on his own family’s gravestones — came south with the Zirkle brothers out of Pennsylvania into the Shenandoah Valley. His parents were Ludwig Zirkle and Eve, and he was their eldest son: when he and his wife Catherine sold land in Dunmore County on 16 November 1776, the sale carried fifty-four acres “patented to my mother, Eve Sircle, now deceased … and descended to Michael as eldest son and heir of Eve.”

He settled near Forestville, on Holman’s Creek, in the country that became Shenandoah County — a neighbourhood where the Zirkles, the Neases and the Roushes lived within a few miles of each other and married one another for a century. His brother Andrew built the stone mill at Quicksburg that still stands. In 1776 Michael’s own name was on the roll of the Dunmore County militia under Captain Jacob Holman, the same captain Henry Roush had served under the year before.

He and Catharine had fourteen children, though whether she was mother to all fourteen is uncertain — her own stone would make her sixteen when the eldest was born. That eldest, Catharine, married George Roush. Mary, born 20 June 1770, married Henry Nease in June 1791, and the marriage papers carry her father’s consent signed “Michel Corckel.” His son Henry followed the Roushes and the Neases down the Ohio to the Graham District of Mason County and founded the Zirkle family there. His children’s marriages are a large part of why the Roush, Nease and Zirkle families are braided together in Alec’s tree in three separate places.

He died on 2 October 1811, aged seventy-six years, eight months and three days. A cracked slab in the Zerchel–Nehs burying ground, on the east bank of Holman’s Creek northeast of Forestville, is very probably his: cut in German with a Pennsylvania-German compass star at its head, HIR RUET MICHAEL ZICKEL IST GEBOREN DEN 29 JANER 1735 UND GESTORBEN DEN 2 OCTOBER 1811 UND SEIN ALTER WAR 76 JAR 8 MO 3 DA — born 29 January 1735, died 2 October 1811. The ground has long been unfenced. “The old graveyard used to have a good many tombstones in it,” a Forestville man wrote shortly before his own death, “but for many years it has been unfenced. Now cattle graze over the bodies of our forefathers, most of the tombstones have disappeared.”

963.s:
Catharine was the wife of Michael Zerckel of Forestville in Shenandoah County, Virginia, and the mother, by the family’s account, of their fourteen children. The eldest, another Catharine, married George Roush; a second daughter, Mary, married Henry Nease in 1791; a son, Henry, took the family name down the Ohio to Mason County behind the Roushes. Her own family has never been traced.

She appears with her husband in a Dunmore County deed of 16 November 1776 — “Michael Sircle and Catherine, of Dunmore County, to Ludwick Fulmor” — the earliest surviving line that gives her a name of her own.

She was born on 12 July 1747 and died on 16 November 1830, aged eighty-three years, four months and four days — exact to the day — by the stone that stands beside Michael’s in the Zerchel–Nehs burying ground on Holman’s Creek. It is very probably hers: carved with a compass star matching his and lettered in German by what looks like the same unschooled hand, HIER RUHT CADARINA ZERCEL. SIE WARD GEBOHREN JULIUS DEN 12 IM JAHR CHRISTI 1747 UND GESTORBEN NOVEMBER DEN 16 1830, ALT 83 JAHR 4 MONAT 4 DA. Those dates leave a puzzle the family never noticed: a woman born in 1747 would have been sixteen when Michael’s eldest daughter was born in August 1763, which is very young but possible — and if that is not what happened, then she was Michael’s second wife and not that daughter’s mother at all.

6164.s:
The first husband of Isabel, and the father of the John Catlin who settled at Deerfield, was a man of Wethersfield, Connecticut, whose estate was appraised at £69 on 17 July 1644. He left a widow who married twice more and a son who was then an infant.

What he was called is not settled. Deerfield's historian, numbering the Catlins, heads his genealogy “1. CATLIN, CATLING, CATTELL, John, of Weth.; estate appraised July 17, 1644, amt. £69” — but an earlier authority said twice, flatly, that the baptismal name of Isabel's first husband is unknown. The doubt is about his name, not about where he stands: he is Isabel's husband and the father of John Catlin of Deerfield either way. At least four men named John Catlin lived in Connecticut in that generation, and the Thomas Catlin family of Hartford — whose son John married Mary Marshall in 1665 — is a separate family altogether.

6165.s:
Isabel was married three times and outlived two husbands before she was fifty. The first was a Catlin of Wethersfield, who died by the summer of 1644 leaving her a small estate and an infant son, John. She married second James Northam of Hockanum, on the Hartford side of the river. The town of Hadley granted him a home lot, but, as a neighbour later swore, “it pleased god to take him away by death before he came,” and by December 1661 the town had granted his widow a hundred-pound allotment of her own. Her son John broke and fenced that land for her. She married third Joseph Baldwin of Milford, by then settled at Hadley on the Connecticut River, whose own first wife had died in 1661.

That third marriage closed a circle. Her son John Catlin had married Mary Baldwin, Joseph's daughter, in 1662; so her son's wife became her stepdaughter, and Mary Baldwin found herself married to the son of her own stepmother. The two families interlock twice in a single generation.

She held land at Hadley in her own right: a court pleading of 1692 names her as one of the town’s first settlers, granted an allotment rated at a hundred pounds, about 1661 as far as a torn date can be read. After her death her son John sued her third husband’s grandson for that land, naming her in one breath as “Isabel Catlin, alias Isabel Northam, alias Isabel Baldwin.” She was probably a sister of Lawrence Ward of New Haven, Branford and Newark, which is likely how the family came to be in Newark at all. Her maiden name was never written down. She died at Hadley, Massachusetts, on 5 December 1676, holding the land in her own name. Her husband Baldwin kept it, and left it to his grandson. Sixteen years later her son John, by then of Deerfield, sued for it. Old neighbours swore that she had always “owned” him as her son, and in October 1693 a jury at Boston gave him his mother’s land.

6166.s:
Joseph Baldwin was among the first settlers of Milford, Connecticut, in 1639, one of three brothers who came over together and were given home lots there after a first stop at New Haven. He married Hannah, who joined the Milford church on 23 June 1644, when their first four children were all baptized at once; Mary, who married John Catlin, was one of the four. Hannah died in 1661, and about 1663 Joseph moved north to Hadley in Massachusetts, where he was made a freeman in 1666. He married twice more: Isabella, the widow of the elder John Catlin and afterwards of James Northam, who died in 1676; and Elizabeth, the widow of Luke Hitchcock and then of William Warriner.

On 20 December 1680 he made his will, and its first words say exactly where he was and how he felt: “In the Name of God Amen the twentieth day of december, One thousand Six hundred and eighty, I Joseph Baldwin Senr of Hadley in the Countie of Hampshire within the Colony of the Massachusetts: being together with old age and of life now Sick and weake of body but of good and perfect Memory, thanks and praise be to Almighty God for it.” He left his wife the use of his house and land at Hadley for her life, excepting the half of his lands he had already made over to his son Joseph; the other half, with the houses and the moveables, went to that son. Then he went through the daughters one by one — five pounds to his “Loveing Daughter Hanah Hull” of New Haven and five pounds to her daughter Mary Hull when she should reach eighteen; forty shillings to “my Daughter Mary Cattlin of Arthur Cull”, across the water on the Arthur Kill in East Jersey; seventeen pounds to Elizabeth Warriner of Springfield; ten pounds to Sarah Bartlett of Northampton; and, for a daughter already dead, Mrs Hawks, five pounds each to her children John and Hannah Hawks when they came of age — and confirmed to his three sons Benjamin, Jonathan and David the gifts he had made them out of his Milford lands. He signed it before two witnesses, Chiliab Smith, who made his mark, and Samuel Partrigg.

Nearly four years later, on 30 October 1684, he had the will read over to him again and ratified it, appointing his grandson Joseph Baldwin junior his sole executor in place of the son, who had died before him. He lived only four days more, and died on 3 November 1684. The inventory of his estate was taken on the 8th by Lieutenant Smith, Chiliab Smith and Samuel Partrigg: £165 8s 7d in all, of which his house, barn and home lot at Hadley stood at £50 and ten acres of land at £45, with debts of £10 14s 3d, leaving a net estate of £154 14s 4d.

In the town he had helped to found at the other end of the colony, Milford set a granite boulder by the Wepawaug bridge among its founders' memorials: JOSEPH BALDWIN, OBIT 1690, HANNAH HIS WIFE. The date cut on it is wrong by six years.

6167.s:
Hannah was the first wife of Joseph Baldwin, one of the first settlers of Milford, Connecticut. She joined the Milford church on 23 June 1644, and on that same day their first four children were baptized together — among them Mary, who grew up to marry John Catlin. Four sons and five daughters are credited to the marriage in all.

She died in 1661 at Milford, and her husband left the next year for Hadley in Massachusetts and married twice more. Nothing of her own origins is known: a surname, Whitlock, and a wedding at High Wycombe in Buckinghamshire in November 1636 are claimed for her by later family writers with nothing behind them. Milford remembers her the way the colony usually did. On the founders' boulder by the Wepawaug bridge her husband's name is cut in full, and under it: HANNAH HIS WIFE.

74.s:
William Payne was born in Virginia about 1791–93, and by the 1840s he was farming in Lauderdale County, Mississippi. In 1850, at fifty-seven, he headed a household of eleven: his wife Mary, thirty, born in North Carolina; four boys born in North Carolina who carried the Eakens surname and were orphans in his care — John W., sixteen, James O., fourteen, Lewis T., twelve, and George W., ten; four younger children born in Mississippi, the eldest of them Sarah H., aged eight; and an eighteen-year-old named Martha Moore.

The arrangement was formal as well as domestic. He was guardian of the Eakens boys, his wife Mary was administratrix on the Eakens estate, and a William Eakens served as administrator alongside her. He was, in short, a Virginian in Mississippi raising another family’s orphaned sons beside his own young children — and in May 1861 a daughter of that house, Sarah Hudson Payne, married Joel W. Eakins, who bore the same surname as the boys he had raised.

He married Mary Eakins, the widow of Andrew Eakin, at Lauderdale on 28 May 1840, two years before Sarah was born, and became guardian of her four Eakin sons; for nine years after the wedding the court went on calling her by either name as she wound up her first husband’s estate. In June 1851 the court granted him guardianship of the property of two of his younger children, Orrigon and Joel, whom it called “his minor children”. Whether Sarah was his own daughter has not been formally proved, and so his place at the head of this line is still graded a likelihood rather than a certainty.

75.s:
Mary, whose maiden name is not known, was born in North Carolina between about 1812 and 1820 — the census-takers could not agree on her age. She was first the wife of Andrew Eakin, and after his death she took out letters on his estate in Lauderdale County, Mississippi, as its administratrix. Four boys born in North Carolina were his heirs: John William, James Owen, Lewis T. and George W. Eakin.

On 28 May 1840, as Mary Eakins, she married William P. Payne at Lauderdale; the licence had been taken out three days before, and a member of the county Board of Police married them. The Eakin boys grew up in the Payne house with William as their guardian, and in May 1842, two years into the marriage, Sarah was born — the eldest of the four children born there in Mississippi, with Ann, Origon and Joel after her.

For nine years the court went on calling her by both names as it worked through her first husband’s affairs: “Mrs Mary Payne” in April 1849, “Mrs Mary Eakin” a month later, and in August 1849, when she handed what remained of Andrew Eakin’s estate to her husband as the boys’ guardian and was discharged, “Mrs Mary Payne late Mary Eakin”. In 1860 the family was at Markwell, in Beat 2. William died before 1880, and Mary, a widow, was then living in the household of her son Joel.

162.s:
Daniel Jones was born about 1806 in North Carolina, one of a Jones sibship that drifted to Alabama a few at a time. His brother Joel went out to Sumter County ahead of the rest and died there about 1843, and an undated power of attorney has the others acting over his estate — “Daniel Jones, Elijah Jones, Sarah… and Absalom Price” over the estate of “our dec’d Brother Joel Jones.” Daniel went too, and the Alabama births of his younger children put his own arrival in the middle 1830s.

He was in Sumter County and of full age by 1839, when he stood surety on a $2,200 Orphans’ Court guardianship bond. In 1850 he was farming at dwelling 1186 — Daniel Jones, forty-four, born North Carolina; Susan, thirty-five, born North Carolina; and Elizabeth 13, James 12, Margaret 10 and Mary 6, all born in Alabama. Two doors up the road lived Henry Stephens with Daniel’s eldest daughter Sarah Ann as his wife, and six houses beyond that Henry’s father Moore.

Moore Stephens was more than a neighbour. In March and April 1853 the two men, with Jesse Thomas, were jointly bound for $1,200 and then $2,800 on the administration of Thomas Fowler’s estate, and in January 1854 for $5,000 on the guardianship of Willis Thomas’s two small children. In October 1854, after Sarah’s death, Henry Stephens married Daniel’s second daughter Elizabeth.

By 1860 he had crossed into Mississippi, to Newton County, where he had bought land as early as 1854; Henry Stephens and his family went too. Susan disappears from the record, and by 1869 Daniel had a wife named Martha L. In February of that year, with months to live, he and Martha gave land to his daughters for five dollars apiece. He died later that year, “late of” Newton County. On the last day of 1869 the Sumter County probate court appointed Henry Stephens guardian of three of his boys, each “a minor heir of Daniel Jones deceased”.

In August 1873 his heirs divided the rest of his Newton County land by lot: his daughters Elizabeth Stephens, Melissa Williamson, Mary and Margaret, his son James, and Sarah’s three sons, Calvin, Caswell and John, who signed in Sumter County before a justice of the peace. The grandsons could inherit only in their dead mother’s place, and that is how we know Sarah Ann was Daniel Jones’s daughter.

163.s:
Susan Jones — her maiden name is not known — was born about 1815 in North Carolina. In 1850 she was the wife in Daniel Jones’s household at dwelling 1186 in Sumter County, Alabama, with four children about her, all born in Alabama: Elizabeth 13, James 12, Margaret 10 and Mary 6. Elizabeth, the eldest of them, became Henry H. Stephens’s second wife in 1854.

Whether she was also the mother of Sarah Ann Jones is not known, and that doubt is why she is drawn here as a possibility rather than a settled ancestor. Sarah was born about 1833, when Susan would have been only about eighteen, and an earlier wife who died before 1837 fits the household just as well. No marriage of Daniel and Susan has been found, and nothing records what became of her after 1850.

78.s:
Benjamin Asbury Simmons — B. A. Simmons on his gravestone and Ben on most people's tongues — was born on 26 October 1818 in Georgia, in Troup County by his family's reckoning, and came as a young man with his people into Sumter County, Alabama. His father was very probably Robert Simmons of that county — who was married by 1845 to a wife named Ann S., though whether she was Ben’s mother no record says — who in the fifth item of a will written on 6 March 1845 set down: “I hereby appoint my Son Benjamin Asbury Simmons my executor to this my last will and testament.” The same will shows how that household looked after its women: the daughters' share was granted “to them and the heirs of their bodies; and not to be subject to the debts of their husbands.” The will was proved on 15 November 1855. Ben's brothers and sisters were Mariah Jane, who married a Bustin, William Miles, John Christopher, Robert H., an E. W. and Susan H., who married a Boyd and died young in 1852.

He married Adeline on 11 May 1847, when he was twenty-eight and she was seventeen. Their children's birthplaces trace a family moving back and forth along the state line: Alabama in the late 1840s, Mississippi in the early 1850s, Alabama again by the end of that decade. By 1870 he was at Cuba with Adeline and six children in the house, and he was still there in 1880, with a sixteen-year-old daughter among them whose name the clerk wrote down as “Dellon” — Rebecca Anna Dillon Simmons. Two of his daughters married the same Swain man, twenty-two months apart. Eugenia married J. L. Swain first and died young, leaving a little girl named Lela. Dillon married him next. When the probate court divided Ben's land in 1895 it listed all seven of his heirs by name, and among them was “Dillon Swain, adult wife of J. L. Swain.” Lela, still a minor, took her dead mother's share.

He was a miller as well as a farmer. When he registered to vote at Cuba on 3 July 1875, entry 64 of the Sumter County book, he wrote his own name in a strong, practised hand, where most of the page made marks, and the registrar gave his living in three words: “Mill & Farm.” His was a slaveholding family before the war — in 1855 his brother Lewis was taxed for twenty-nine enslaved people, Robert H. for fifteen and William M. for two.

He ended his life on his own place near Cuba Station, Sumter County, Alabama, with a mill’s tools and an iron safe among his goods, and died on 6 April 1894, aged seventy-five. Adaline took out letters on his estate that August and sold his horse, cows, buggy and shop tools on the premises the Friday before Christmas. He was buried just across the state line at Kewanee, in Lauderdale County, Mississippi. His marble headstone in the churchyard at Salem Baptist, carved with two clasped hands, reads B. A. SIMMONS, HUSBAND OF ADALINE SIMMONS, BORN OCT. 26, 1818, DIED APRIL 6, 1894.

79.s:
Adeline was born on 7 October 1829, probably in Walton County, Florida, though in later life she was put down as Alabama-born as often as Florida-born. Two of her children's death records give her maiden name as Peavy; that, and a suggestion that her father was Levi Daniel Peavy, are not yet proven. She married Ben Simmons on 11 May 1847, at seventeen, and bore nine or ten children over the next twenty years, the last about 1867 when she was thirty-seven. At least two did not live out infancy.

She kept house at Cuba, in Sumter County, Alabama, through the war and after it, with a few years in Mississippi in the early 1850s that show up only in where her middle children were born. In 1870 she was “Adline,” forty-one, with six children at home; in 1880 she still had a sixteen-year-old daughter under the roof, written down as “Dellon.” It is through her daughter Dillon that Alec's line runs. When Ben's land was divided in 1895, a neighbour swore that Dillon was one of Ben's children, and Adeline had been his wife without a break since before Dillon was born.

A sepia photograph of her survives from about 1875: a woman seated in a dark dress with a lace collar and a tasselled ribbon at her throat, hands still, looking straight out.

Her husband died in April 1894. She outlived him by six years and died at Kewanee, in Lauderdale County, Mississippi, at seventy. Her tall marble headstone at Salem Baptist, beside his, was cut with a weeping-willow panel: IN MEMORY OF ADELINE, WIFE OF B. A. SIMMONS, BORN OCT. 7, 1829, DIED SEPT. 25, 1900, AGED 70 YRS. 11 MOS. 16 DAYS.

58.s:
Mathew Chalmers was born in Scotland about 1821 and crossed to America as a young man; with him and his wife the Scottish side of this family begins. He married Ellen King, another Scot, and by the middle 1850s they were settled at Orange, in Essex County, New Jersey, where all their children were born.

He made his living in trade and was out of it early. In 1870, at forty-nine, he was a retired dealer in stores with real estate worth $4,600 and $1,500 more in personal property — a comfortable house in the second ward of Orange holding his wife Ellen, forty-four, and four New Jersey-born daughters: Ellen B., thirteen, Margaret, seven, Catharine, four, and Sarah, one.

Catharine — Katharine — became a schoolteacher, went out to Detroit, and married the Paterson silk manufacturer Harry B. Frost there on 10 June 1896. Margaret married a Jordan; Sarah never married; both were still at East Orange in 1932, when Katharine died. Two of his grandchildren were christened with their grandmothers’ maiden surnames, Katherine King Frost and Harry Bell Frost, which is how this family marked descent.

He died in 1893, when Katharine was twenty-seven and teaching school, and he lies at Rosedale Cemetery in Montclair, four miles from Orange, under a flat granite stone cut MATTHEW CHALMERS, 1821–1893, with his wife Ellen’s beside it.

Ellen King was born in Scotland about 1823 — Ellen B. King, as her stone has it — and crossed to America as a young woman. She married Mathew Chalmers, a fellow Scot, and lived at Orange, in Essex County, New Jersey, for more than half a century.

They had four daughters, all born in New Jersey. In 1870 she was forty-four and keeping house at Orange with her husband, a retired dealer in stores, and the girls: Ellen B., thirteen, Margaret, seven, Catharine, four, and Sarah, a baby of one. Catharine — Katharine — born in January 1866, became a schoolteacher and married Harry B. Frost of Paterson at Detroit in 1896; her first child, born at Paterson in September 1898, was christened Katherine King Frost, carrying her grandmother’s maiden surname, which is how this family remembered its women. Margaret became Mrs. Jordan and Sarah stayed Miss Chalmers, and both were living at East Orange as late as 1932.

She was a member of the North Orange Baptist Church, and Katharine was a Baptist at East Orange for many years after her.

Mathew died in 1893 and she was a widow eleven years. She died at her home, 262 Centre Street, Orange, in 1904, after a long illness, eighty-one years old; the day is given both as 30 March and as the end of May. Four daughters survived her. She was buried at Rosedale Cemetery in Montclair, beside Mathew, under a stone cut ELLEN B. KING / WIFE OF / MATTHEW CHALMERS / 1823–1904.

34.s:
Henry Bradley was born in Alabama about 1836, of South Carolina parents, and spent his life in Barbour County. He fought for the Confederacy. A Henry Bradley, aged twenty-four, is on the roll of the Clayton Guards, the company raised in his own town for the 1st Alabama Infantry and mustered at Pensacola in 1861, alongside a brother, Abraham; and the state’s register of maimed soldiers lists “H. Bradley, clerk” of Barbour County, 1st Alabama, wounded at Atlanta on 28 July 1864 — very probably him, and the wound that would kill him twenty-odd years later. On 8 July 1867, in the first registration taken in Alabama under the Reconstruction acts, he signed the Board of Registration’s return of qualified voters for Precinct No. 9 — line 97, “Bradly Henry” — on a page where his neighbours are set down White and Colored alternately down the column, and a tick against his name says he came back and used the vote. A Bell and a Cox registered at the same table: the two families his daughters would marry into were in the same room.

That December he married. Barbour County issued a licence to “Henry Bradly and Elvira Loveless, both of full age” on 18 December 1867, and the judge of probate signed the authorisation the following day. He was thirty-one; she was eighteen. By June 1880 there were five children in the house at Clayton — Ida J. nine, Anna V. seven, Henry R. five, Alice three, and Katie seven months old — and he was farming then as well as keeping the court’s books.

He was also clerk of the circuit court of Barbour County, and he died in office. On Monday 21 February 1887 erysipelas set into the old war wound; congestion of the lungs, stomach and bowels followed, and he died at his home in Clayton at one o’clock on the morning of Sunday 27 February, aged fifty. He was buried at Clayton at ten the next morning with Masonic honours. He had left his family well provided for by the standards of the place and the time — nine thousand dollars of life insurance in all: two thousand with the Knights of Honor, two thousand with the A.O.U.W. and five thousand with the New York Life. Petitions for a successor were circulating within two days of the funeral, four men applied for the unexpired term, and in the second week of March the governor appointed Capt. John C. McNab to the clerkship.

Four years later his widow died too, and in the autumn of 1891 the county took his two youngest, Alice at fourteen and Katie at twelve, into guardianship. In the summer of 1893 a Eufaula weekly printed, four times over, the Barbour County probate court’s settlement of that guardianship, and with it the names of all five of his surviving children — the account of the guardian of “the following named minor children of Henry Bradley, deceased, to-wit: Ida Parker, wife of Lee Parker; Annie Fortner, wife of W. J. Fortner; Henry Bradley, Alice Bradley and Katie Bradley.” Five children, two of them married off already, two of them still wards of the court.

He lies at Clayton City Cemetery, inside a rusting iron rail in the old part of the burying ground, under a draped marble tablet carved with swags and a wreath and with the square and compasses of the Freemasons cut into its arch. It reads HENRY BRADLEY, BORN APR. 25, 1836, DIED FEB. 27, 1887, though the day-figures are worn now past certainty. Beside him, under the same rail, stands a second stone: ELVIRA, WIFE OF HENRY BRADLEY, who outlived him by four years. A draped monument with a Masonic emblem inside its own iron enclosure is not a poor man’s grave.

35.s:
Elvira Loveless was born in Alabama in August 1849, of Alabama parents. At eighteen she married Henry Bradley of Barbour County on a licence issued at the courthouse on 18 December 1867 — “Henry Bradly and Elvira Loveless, both of full age” — and J. S. Williams, judge of probate, signed the authorisation to marry them the next day. Whoever married them never sent the licence back: the printed return underneath it, “I hereby certify that the above named persons were duly married by me on the ___ day of ___”, was left blank, so the county book records the authority and never the wedding.

She bore at least eight children and buried three of them — one at birth in 1870, a boy of eleven in 1879, a baby in 1884. Five grew up: Ida, born about 1871, who married Lee Parker; Annie, who married a Fortner of Dothan; a son Henry; and the two youngest, Alice, born 8 October 1876, and Katie, born in 1879. In 1880 the census-taker found her at Clayton, thirty-one and keeping house, with all five of them under her roof.

Her husband, the clerk of the circuit court, died of an old war wound in February 1887. Three years a widow, in January 1890 she bought Jake Fortner’s house at Mt. Andrew and moved the family there, and her daughter Annie was married in that house the following September. Then, on a Sunday afternoon in the summer after, it was her turn. She had dressed her children for Sunday school that morning; when she was taken ill they sent for the doctor, and sent too late. She died at Clayton on 14 June 1891 of cholera morbus, aged forty-one, and the paper called her “Mrs. Bradley, relict of former Clerk Henry Bradley,” leaving five children.

Four months later a Barbour County court took the two youngest, Alice and Katie, into guardianship. The order speaks only of the father, because that is the form of words the clerk used; in fact the girls had lost both parents.

She lies at Clayton City Cemetery beside her husband, inside the same iron rail, under a draped marble tablet with a star cut into the arch and a worn verse on the plinth. It gives her no surname at all — only ELVIRA, WIFE OF HENRY BRADLEY, born in August 1849 and dead in June 1891, the day-figures too worn now to be certain of.

64.s:
John Bell was born on 13 January 1807 in South Carolina, and came to Alabama a young man of about twenty-three, when his parents brought the family out of Darlington District about 1830 and settled in the Barbour County neighbourhood the family never left. He was in Alabama by 1836, because in that year he served as a private in Captain White’s company, Regiment of Alabama Volunteers, in the Creek War; he took his pay for it in land. He was settled in Barbour County before 1837, and every one of his children was born in Alabama — the eldest, Mary, about 1836 or 1837.

He began buying early. On 19 July 1838 John H. Miller sold him about 189 acres in Township 10, Range 26 for five hundred dollars, Ann Caroline Miller releasing her dower the same afternoon. In January 1841, from Alabama, he sold off a forty-acre Georgia gold-lottery lot in what had just become Forsyth County for thirty dollars, and signed the deed himself — John F Bell — in a generation where a great many men made their mark. In April 1853 President Franklin Pierce signed his bounty-land patent: warrant 4615, forty acres and eleven hundredths of an acre, for the Creek War service. He sold that same forty to William Bounds in 1858, and for a generation afterwards his neighbours’ deeds navigated by “the east corner of the Bell forty.”

His household can be followed across half a century. In 1840 there is a boy and a girl under five in the house. In 1850 he is forty-three and farming, with his wife Laney — South Carolina born, like him — and Mary 13, William 11, John 9, Kervin 4 and Laney 2. Two of those children matter to this family: William, who died a Confederate pensioner in 1924 and whose estate was divided out among his nieces and nephews; and John, who became John T. Bell and fathered Thomas Jefferson Bell. By 1860 he was returning four thousand dollars in land and ten thousand in personal estate, and in the Alabama cotton country of that year a figure like that is largely a statement about people: he probably owned the handful of men and women set down under a John Bell of Barbour County in that year’s slave schedule. In July 1867 he registered as a qualified voter at Precinct No. 9. In August 1870, at sixty-three, he had Laney at sixty-four and two grown children still at home, Mary and Archibald — and his son John T., twenty-seven, was farming the very next place with a wife and four small children. A few doors further along, his daughter Melissa, twenty-one, was keeping house for her young husband, Marion Farrior. By June 1880 he was seventy-two and a widower, and he told the enumerator that both his own parents had been born in South Carolina.

He farmed into old age. In 1876, at sixty-nine, he gave a crop lien in his own voice — “I John F Bell being indebted to J. C. Jones … thirty five dollars … to make a crop the present year on my plantation in Barbour County Alabama.” On 1 August 1890, at eighty-three, he divided the home place by deeds of gift — 203⅓ acres each to his son Curvin and his daughter Mary, each gift to take effect only after his death, “I however, holding and retaining the ownership and comfort of said above described lands during my natural life time.” The boundary runs past “the big gate leading to the house” on the public road from Clayton to Louisville. So there was no estate left to probate when he died on 21 November 1890: he had given the farm away and kept the comfort of it.

The following November his heirs petitioned to sell 604 acres containing “the John Bell homestead and out houses” for division — in equal thirds to William, to John T., and to the five children of the daughter who had married a Farrior. The boundaries of that tract name his neighbours, and they explain a good deal: the Daniel Norton land to the south, which is why two Bell wives later married a Norton, and the old William Beasley place, in whose little family burying ground he himself lies.

65.s:
Laney was born in South Carolina about 1806 and came out to Alabama as a young wife, with her husband John Bell’s people, about 1830. In August 1840 she was keeping a house in Barbour County with a baby boy and a little girl in it — William, born in February 1839, and Mary. By 1850 there were five children: Mary 13, William 11, John 9, Kervin 4 and a small Laney of 2 named for her. In 1860, at fifty-three, she was the mistress of a prosperous place; her husband returned four thousand dollars in land and ten thousand in personal estate that year. In August 1870 she was sixty-four and keeping house with her grown daughter Mary and her son Archibald still at home, and her son John T. Bell was farming the next place along with a wife and four small children of his own.

Then she is gone. Her husband was a widower by June 1880, living with a lodger and a girl of fourteen, his children grown and scattered. She was buried, almost certainly, in the Beasley family’s little burying ground on the farm that bounded theirs, where her son William would be laid in his turn — a rail-fenced square of a dozen markers now standing in second growth, with her death given as 17 June 1873. No stone of hers has ever been photographed.

Nothing says in words that she was John T. Bell’s mother, though she was John Bell’s wife through all the years his children were born, so her place here is a near certainty rather than a proved one. There is one small puzzle left of her. Three different enumerators in three different hands wrote her name down, and all three wrote Laney. But her eldest son, dying in 1924, gave his mother’s name as Viney. Which of the two she answered to, nobody now alive knows.

Also recorded as: Archibald "Archy" Bell

Full dates: b. about 1770–1775; d. before 22 October 1839, Sumter District, South Carolina

⭐⭐ A candidate with a documented life and no document tying him to us. He is graded hypothesis deliberately — but for a narrower reason than this node used to give. ⭐ Archy Bell’s own will names a son JOHN BELL: “the remainder I will & bequeath to my beloved children to be equally divided between them, viz, John Bell, Celey Amoson, Harriett Bell, Martha Bell, William Wesley Bell, and Jane Bell” — verified in the signed original, the clerk’s certified copy and the recorded will book [BELL-430]. ⚠ What is NOT documented is that this son John is OUR John F. Bell of Barbour County, Alabama. The open question is an identification, not a relationship — and a “John Bell Senr” was witnessing deeds in Darlington in 1820, so uniqueness cannot be assumed. What follows is the case, which is now a strong one.

⭐ He left a will [BELL-147]. Made 4 October 1839 and filed at Sumter District on the 22nd, it leaves his wife Margaret the 275-acre plantation for her life or widowhood, then to five children — Benjamin Sumter, Margaret Louisa, Ezekiel Dixon, Hugh McCallum and Columbus Campbell Bell. An 1846 partition establishes that those five are the children of a second marriage. The residue he leaves to six more: ⭐ “John Bell, Celey Amoson, Harriet Bell, Martha Bell, William Wesley Bell, and Jane Bell.”

⭐ That earlier family is dated, and it is dated to the right decade. William Wesley Bell is in the 1850 Darlington census aged 30, born 1811×1820 [BELL-160] — restated 10 Sep 2026 (self-correction #384): the 1860 census and an 1866 ration book both read ~1811 against 1850’s ~1820, and on the 1811 reading he has no slot in Archibald’s 1830 household at all. So the six were born roughly 1805×1820 — the window in which John Bell was born, 13 January 1807, and the window of Archibald’s marriage to Martha, who released dower in 1809 and 1817.

⭐⭐ And his household held a boy of exactly the right age, twice [BELL-159]. The 1820 Sumter schedule (page 115, indexed “Arel Bell”) tallies one male aged 10 and under 16 — John was thirteen. The 1830 schedule (page 66, indexed “Achable Bell”) tallies one male aged 20 and under 30 — John was twenty-three, and his family left for Alabama “about 1830.” Archibald himself is 45-and-upwards in 1820 and 50–60 in 1830. ⚠ But the bracket is not exclusive: of the seven Bell households on the 1830 Sumter schedule, the elder John Bell’s (p. 93) also holds an anonymous male 20–30 [BELL-166] — the census cannot choose between the two roofs.

⭐ The neighbours run for twenty-six years. Robert Severance is the household directly below him in 1820, sells him land in 1836, and his estate bounds Archibald’s farm in 1846. William Copeland is on the 1830 page and witnesses the will. The Amosons are on both pages, and a daughter married one of them.

⭐⭐ 11 Sep 2026 [BELL-721] — A NEW DEED, A SECOND DOWER RENUNCIATION, AND HIS NAME IN A CLERK’S OWN PEN. Archibald Bell → John B. Divine, 22 Feb 1817, Darlington Deed Book G p. 204: 127 acres “between Bay Branch and Newmans Swamp,” provably the tract he bought from James Hudson in 1810. ⭐ MARTHA BELL renounced dower on it on 24 Feb 1817, by mark, before John Huggins J.P. — a SECOND certified renunciation, eight years after the 1809 one, before the same magistrate. ⭐⭐⭐ And the proof clause calls him “ARCHEY BELL” — image-verified, in the same hand that wrote “Archibald” three times on the same page. That is the Arel/Achable/Archable index-mangling problem caught at its source: his neighbours called him Archey. ⚠ His residence formula oscillates and is quoted rather than smoothed: 1807 “of the same place” (Darlington) · 1810 “of the district of Sumpter” · 1817 “of the State and District aforesaid” (Darlington) — he held land in both. The 127 acres left the family in 1818 (Devine → James Reynolds). Outstanding — and these are the reasons the grade has not moved [BELL-148, BELL-162]: ⛔ No instrument names John Bell as his son, and none places the will’s John Bell in Alabama. ⭐ And the negative is stronger than “not found” — the receipt class most likely never existed. Record Book M, read at the ink [BELL-526]: no return was EVER filed on this estate. Archy Bell’s block (pp. 238–241) ends at Evan Benbow with nothing after it and the Ordinary’s printed qualification line “was duly qualified on the ___ day of ___ 18__” was left blank forever — while the estate on the facing page, in the same clerk’s hand, got a full return filed 20 Jan 1840 with $38.00 coming in from “W. Montgomery OF ALABAMA.” So the one document class that would style a legatee “John Bell of Alabama” moves from unfound toward improbable. ⛔⛔ The cheapest test that could have settled this is now PERMANENTLY closed, not merely unrun [BELL-562]: [BELL-162] named searching the estates of Thomas Bell and John Bell of Sumter as the one action that could materially raise this node — but the Sumter Probate Court’s own General Index to Estates 1784–1960 holds nine Bell entries in total, and there is NO John, Thomas, William Jr., James, Drury, Jesse, Benjamin or Robert Bell estate in Sumter County at any date, ever. The two-roofs problem can never be resolved from probate. ⛔ Two other Sumter Bell households in 1820 — Thomas Bell, on the line immediately above him, and John Bell — also held a boy of John’s age, and if those men are his brothers then the rivals are his nephews, sharing every neighbour and every migration route. ⛔ And the rival persists: in 1830 the elder John Bell’s household (the probable “John Bell Senr” of the 1839 bond) still holds a male 20–30, while Thomas Bell’s household has vanished from the schedule entirely, leaving his boy unlocated [BELL-166]. ⚠ The Darlington-vs-Sumter question has narrowed sharply: beyond the shared “Archy”/“Archibald” usage and the three surnames that cross the creek with him (Huggins, Chaney, Newman), the February 1839 resurvey of his own home plantation — the Sumter estate tract itself — is headed “South Carolina, DARLINGTON DISTRICT” by the deputy surveyor [BELL-170]. His home paperwork crossed the line; a single instrument equating the two men in words is still wanting. ⚠ The 1820 and 1830 tallies also leak by one boy, which is unexplained. ⭐ And the exclusion now runs one way [BELL-172]: no John Bell of the will’s generation is documentable in Sumter or Darlington District in 1840 or 1850 — the one right-age Sumter candidate resolves to James P. Bell by his own will — so the will’s John left the home districts, and ours is the only located right-age John with any documented tie to them. ⭐⭐ 12 Sep 2026 — THE NAMED RIVAL THIS FIELD HAS BEEN MISSING, AND HE IS STILL STANDING: A JOHN BELL OF YORK DISTRICT [BELL-735–BELL-746]. Under the Genealogical Proof Standard a convergent case is not proof while a named competing candidate stands unexcluded, and this one is age-perfect in two consecutive censuses — male 20–29 in York in 1830, male 30–39 in 1840 (roll 516 p. 304, one enslaved person, immediate neighbour John Springs). His father has no name in any record, which is exactly why he cannot be retired. ⭐ What was done about him on 11–12 Sep, so nobody re-runs it: all 324 York documents whose OCR contains “John Bell” were harvested and read — 93 kinship contexts, every one a false positive; not one instrument names his father, mother, sibling or child; the Withers will of 27 Oct 1845 (his last trace) shows him as a subscribing witness and nothing else, signing plain; all thirteen Bells in the 1850 York schedule were read off the manuscript — no John, no Bell widow, three of seven households not York-rooted; the mangled-surname escape is closed in both 1850 and 1860 and in both York and Chester (the one B400 collision, “Ball John 37 NC,” is excluded as North-Carolina-born); and no estate or guardianship was ever opened for any John Bell in York. ⚠ But he did NOT simply vanish: a John Bell was decreed against in York in 1848 and a “John Bell Junr” stands on Dr J. B. Hunter’s books in 1851 — so “absent from the 1850 schedule” is a fact about the schedule, not about the man (self-correction #437). ⛔⛔ A Catawba-leasehold argument that would have excluded him was raised and REFUTED by an adversary the same night [BELL-746]: the Pettus lease table’s “formerly X’s” field contradicts itself on the very tract, an unrelated adult James Davis was already leasing on Steel Creek in 1797, and the series — which names sons-in-law, daughters and heirs constantly — carries not one kin word in the rows at issue. ⭐ FOUR candidates now stand unexcluded: Christopher Bell of York’s seven unnamed heirs · Robert Bell of York’s own son John · a possible Broad-River-side York Bell family · an ordinary unrelated transfer. ⭐ 12 Sep, later — that last strand was TESTED and came back against it [BELL-748]: the 1833 York sale at which a “John Bell Sen” bought is Rev. William Dickson’s of CROWDERS CREEK — western York, the Broad River side — and not one Bell appears among his legatees, witnesses or receipt-signers. ⭐⭐ And an ironmaster’s ledger from that same neighbourhood carries two John Bells, tagging one “John Bell Mountain” while tagging a neighbour “James Moore Indian Land” two lines below in the same clerk’s hand — a clerk who used patronymics (“W’m Felts, James Son”) freely and reached for a place instead. So the Senior/Junior pair sits on the WESTERN side of the district while this rival’s whole documented world is EASTERN, on the Catawba Indian Land: “John Bell Senior of York” now reads as a third man, not as his father. ⭐ Excluded and off the board: the Pickens rival (born North Carolina, stated twice), John Bell Jr of Sumter (held a note in Aug 1821, when our man was fourteen), and the Georgia gold-lottery route (lot 891 was drawn by John F. BALL of Twiggs). ⭐⭐ What would settle it, named and reachable: the original 1830 Catawba lease — SCDAH holds the 128 originals returned in 1840, transfers signed and dated on the dorse, and Robert Bell’s son John signed cleanly three times in 1802–04, so a John Bell who MARKS that lease is a third man; and the Secretary of State, Papers Pertaining to State Grants on Catawba Indian Lands, 1798–1853, whose post-1840 neighbour affidavits recite who held a tract, from whom, and how — a series this project has never opened.

⭐ 22 Aug 2026 [BELL-484]: the Darlington Archibald (wife Martha, 1809–1820) and the Sumter Archy (wife Margaret by 7 Oct 1829) are now one man stated in the record — “Archd Bell of the district of Sumpter” buying the Darlington tract on 4 May 1810, and “Archey Bell … Margaret Bell the wife of the within named Archibald Bell” on one 1829 deed. His Boykin land came “sold to said A. Bell by General Cantey” — a purchase, not a descent from William Rasor Bell. He witnessed for Jonathan Newman of Sumter District in 1805 and beside a John Bell Senr in 1820 — association, never kinship. Still no document ties him to W.R.B.’s son Archibald; the estate bundle (Sumter Box 10 Pkg 3) was opened the same week — nine leaves, no division, no receipts [BELL-485].

⭐ [BELL-485]: his own estate packet is found (Sumter Bundle 113 Pkg 15): the original signed will of 4 Oct 1839 names wife Margaret, five younger children (Benjamin Sumter, Margaret Louisa, Ezekiel Dixon [#238 — not “Nixon”], Hugh McCallum, Columbus Campbell) and six older (John, Celey Amoson, Harriett, Martha, William Wesley, Jane) — and no father or brother; the sale bill shows the family buying its household back; J. W. Stuckey was guardian ad litem for the three youngest in 1846–47. 128.s:
Archibald Bell — Archy to his neighbours, who spelled it that way in the deeds they swore to — was born about 1770 to 1775, probably a son of William Rasor Bell, a planter of Salem in Sumter District, South Carolina, who died leaving nine sons, two daughters and a widow named Mary. Whether the John Bell he names first among his older children is the John Bell who went out to Alabama about 1830, and who is Alec’s ancestor, has never been settled, so his place on this chart is a likelihood and not a fact.

He farmed on both banks of Lynches Creek, the water that divides Sumter District from Darlington, and his own paperwork crossed the line with him: he is “of the same place” in Darlington in 1807, “of the district of Sumpter” in 1810, and “of the State and District aforesaid” in Darlington again in 1817. He bought land in Darlington in 1806 and sold a hundred and twenty-seven acres of it to John B. Divine on 22 February 1817, between Bay Branch and Newmans Swamp. His wife Martha released her dower on his land twice, in October 1809 and again in February 1817, both times before the same justice of the peace, John Huggins, whose family would later marry into his. He was witnessing and swearing to deeds across the creek in Sumter from 1810, and in 1812 James Hutson senior conveyed land to “Archd Bell of the district of Sumpter.” In 1815 he mortgaged a 345-acre tract on Lynches Creek to Zachariah Cantey — the same ground a surveyor had laid out for William Rasor Bell thirty years before.

Martha died in the 1820s, and he married Margaret, a Dixon widow with grown sons of her own. That is why one of his children is called Ezekiel Dixon Bell, and why John H. Dixon, his stepson, was the executor he trusted with everything. They had five more children, with names that read like a roll-call of his neighbours: Benjamin Sumter, Margaret Louisa, Ezekiel Dixon, Hugh McCallum, Columbus Campbell. He was sued in 1830 for a witness fee. He was still buying land in 1836, at sixty, from Robert Severance, who had been his next-door neighbour since at least 1820.

He made his will on 4 October 1839, weak in body but of sound mind, and it was filed on the 22nd. He left Margaret the 275-acre plantation for her life or her widowhood, and after her to the five children of the second marriage; the residue he divided among six more — “John Bell, Celey Amoson, Harriet Bell, Martha Bell, William Wesley Bell, and Jane Bell.” He left a set of blacksmith’s tools and thirteen geese. And he directed that the rest of his property be sold to pay his debts, “including my negroe boy Limus” — a boy of about fifteen whom he had already pledged to Henry Scarborough nine months earlier. When the appraisers came on 26 October they valued Limus at seven hundred dollars against an estate of eleven hundred and eighteen. Sixty-three per cent of everything Archy Bell owned was one enslaved child, and after the sale the boy passes out of sight.

His widow remarried a Severance, which tripped the widowhood clause in the will and forced the partition of 1846–47 — and the “Margaret Severance” who bought the plantation in May 1847 was the widow buying her own place back.

129.s:
Martha was the wife of Archibald “Archy” Bell of Lynches Creek, in Darlington and Sumter districts of South Carolina, and she is probably the mother of his older children — the six he named in his will of 1839, among them the John Bell who went to Alabama — though nothing says so, and her whole place on this chart hangs on her husband’s.

She appears twice, briefly, and both times because the law required a man’s wife to be asked. In October 1809, and again in February 1817, Archy sold land in Darlington District, and each time she came before a justice of the peace — the same man both times, John Huggins — who examined her privately and separately from her husband, as the statute said, to be sure a wife was not signing away her dower under her husband’s eye. She declared that she did it freely and voluntarily, without compulsion, dread or fear of any person whomsoever. In 1809 she made her mark.

She was still living in September 1820, when she gave up dower once more on the Sumter side of the creek. By October 1829 Archy’s wife was Margaret, a Dixon widow, so Martha died somewhere in that decade. Her maiden name, her age and her burial place are all unknown, and the two renunciations are the whole of what the world kept of her.

256.s:
William Rasor Bell appears out of nowhere in 1784, already styled planter, in Claremont County of old Camden District, South Carolina. He is here as the father of Archy Bell of Sumter, and that is the one step on this branch that nothing asserts — his will names a son Archibald, but no paper says that the Archibald of the will is the Archy who died in 1839.

In June 1784 he helped appraise Isaac Higgs’s estate in Kershaw District. In April 1787 he bought Micajah Stokes’s entire personalty — an enslaved woman named Ann, the horses, the beds, nineteen cattle, for £105 15s — and the very next day began giving it all back to Stokes’s children “for love, good will and affection,” which in that century usually means family. Ann was conveyed twice in two days between two households that were probably kin; she is the only person he is known ever to have held, and he held her for a day. His own household in 1790 was ten people and no one in slavery.

He took two surveys in 1785 — a hundred and fifty acres on Bare Branch in April, four hundred on Lynches Creek in June — and the grants on both issued to Samuel Boykin, who had paid the treasury fee, as was the local habit. His land lay on two watersheds at once: a later grant describes eighty acres “on Charleston Road between Black River and Lynches Creek, bounded N.W. by William Rasor Bell and Fred:k Bells Land,” and a 1787 grant to Frederick Bell recites its north-east line as “Land Surveyed for Wm Rasor Bell, Frederick Bell, Jonathan Newman and Lewis Mathews” — one line of one document carrying three surnames that stay beside this family for three generations.

He may have been a Patriot, on the strength of a single sheet of paper. Book G, stub number 30, in South Carolina’s Revolutionary indents: “Issued the 22d. April 1784 To Mr. William Bell for Eleven pounds Eight Shillings and Seven pence Sterling for two Horses impressed for Militia Use in October 1780.” It is the only William Bell indent in the state that no man has ever been attached to, and no lineage society claims it; whether the two horses were his, or one of at least six other South Carolina William Bells’, nobody can say.

On the day after Christmas 1803, “very sick & weak in body,” he made his will. It divides a plain farmer’s world among a wife and eleven children: the plantation and stock to Mary for her life, to be sold at her death or remarriage and the money divided among nine sons — “John Bell, Archibald Bell, Thomas Bell, William Bell, James Bell, Drury Bell, Jesse Bell, Benjamin Bell, & Robert Bell” — and feather beds to his two daughters, Mary and Elizabeth, Elizabeth also getting “One Cow & Calf which is now call’d hers,” the only line in the document about a child’s own particular possession. The witnesses were Lewis Bell, Mary Stuckey and a Douglas.

He was dead by 1809. Moses Gordon, the executor he had named, never served, and administration with the will annexed went on 15 April 1809 to Charles Williams of Georgetown District. Jonathan Newman — the neighbour Archy Bell had witnessed for in 1805 — appraised the estate.

His own parents are unidentified. The likeliest frame is the Raccoon Swamp Bell clan of Albemarle Parish, in Surry and Sussex counties, Virginia, where the patriarch’s 1746 will names five sons and no William; if he belongs there at all it is as an unnamed grandson. And the name Rasor — almost certainly his mother’s or grandmother’s family — has never been found anywhere.

257.s:
Mary was the wife of William Rasor Bell, planter of Salem in Sumter District, South Carolina, and she outlived him. His will names eleven children — nine sons, John, Archibald, Thomas, William, James, Drury, Jesse, Benjamin and Robert, and two daughters, Mary and Elizabeth — and presumably they were all hers. She is on this chart as the mother of Archy Bell of Sumter, and that step is her husband’s uncertainty as much as hers: nothing asserts it.

Her husband made his will on 26 December 1803, very sick and weak in body, and what he did with it tells you what a widow’s position was. He left her the plantation and the stock for her lifetime “for the benefit of my children, if she remains single” — the land to be sold at her death or her remarriage and the money divided among their nine sons. When the will was proved in March 1809 she was still living and had not married again.

Nothing else of her is certain. A “Mary x Bell” signs by mark on a Darlington-proved family deed of 1794 beside William Rasor, John and Frederick Bell, and that may be her or may be Frederick’s wife. Her maiden name is unknown. So is the date of her death — which is a pity, because her death is the event that sent the land to be sold among her sons.

512.x:
Also recorded as: John Bell of Camden District (candidate)

Full dates: b. probably c.1710–1730 (if Robert Bell of Bertie's son John, b. before c.1717); seated on Bear Swamp, Duplin Co., N.C. by 1762, there 1773; will dated 18 Oct 1786, Camden District, S.C. (abstract only)

⭐⭐⭐ A named, located candidate — still not tied in (22 Aug 2026). Holcomb’s 1978 abstract of a will dated 18 Oct 1786 names wife Mary, “eldest son Frederick Bell,” William Rasor Bell and “eldest daughter Penelope Stuckey”; the Kershaw General Index to Estates reads “Bell, Jno — Frederick Bell — Adm’r — Apt 6 — Pkg 180” (apartment and package read directly; year cell illegible). Independent support: John Stuckey of Duplin’s wife was Penelope (1779); Lewis Stuckey’s 1792 deed says his property “descended to me from my Grandfather John Bell” and by 1794 he is “now of the County of Salem, South Carolina”; in 1790 there was exactly one Frederick Bell in the state; and a 1787 Claremont deed puts Jacob Hurst beside Frederick [BELL-446–448, 458, 481, 482].

⭐⭐ The family this John probably belongs to is now documented in its own right: Robert Bell of Chowan and Bertie Co., N.C., died intestate 1738; his children signed for their shares — George (“his Eldest Son and heir at Law”), John, Archibald, Penelope — with William Byrd as son-in-law; the family moved to Duplin by 1754 (Archibald “of Duplin County” 1756), and Sampson County was cut out under them in 1784.
