512.s:
Whether this John Bell belongs to Alec’s family at all is unproved, and the whole line above him waits on it — but a life can be made out of him all the same.

He sat on Bear Swamp in Duplin County, North Carolina, before the Revolution, seated there by 1762 on good swamp-edge land among a kin-group of Bells, Kings, Snells and Herrings who had come down together out of Bertie County in the late 1740s. In 1765 he sold his plantation to his eldest son Frederick for a hundred pounds and went on living on it; he was still “Sr” in the Duplin papers in January 1773, and then he is gone from North Carolina altogether. Somewhere after that he made the four hundred miles south into the Black River country of South Carolina, where his son Frederick was settled by May 1777, and on 18 October 1786 he made his will in Camden District.

The will names his wife Mary, his eldest son Frederick, and his eldest daughter Penelope Stuckey, and it hands money to two more men, a John Bell and William Rasor Bell, without saying what either was to him. Frederick administered the estate.

His daughter had married John Stuckey of Duplin, and her life did not go easily: Stuckey and three others lost a judgment to the administrators of William Kenan for £1,658 11s 0½d, and the sheriff sold his plantation on the west side of Bear Swamp out from under him. A Duplin deed of 1822 was still tracking the ground as land “formerly owned by John Stuckey, which said land was sold by virtue of an execution.” But his grandson Lewis Stuckey had something of the old man’s: in a deed of 1792 Lewis says his property “descended to me from my Grandfather John Bell,” and by 1794 Lewis is “now of the County of Salem, South Carolina” — the family having followed the same road.

If he is who the Bertie County papers suggest — a son of Robert Bell of Chowan and Bertie, who died intestate in 1738 — then his own father could not write. Robert signed with a big interlocked R B, while John and his brothers all signed their names.

513.s:
Of this Mary there is one clause of one document. A will made in Camden District, South Carolina on 18 October 1786 names a wife Mary, alongside the testator’s “eldest son Frederick Bell,” William Rasor Bell and his “eldest daughter Penelope Stuckey.” So she was living that October, in the Black River country, married to a man who had come down from the Bear Swamp neighbourhood of Duplin County, North Carolina, with his grown children about him.

That is the whole of her. Her maiden name is unknown; nothing else she did was written down, or at any rate nothing else survives — not a deed, not a dower release, not a line of a census. She is here for her husband’s sake, and his own place in this family is unproved, so she stands or falls with him: if he is the wrong John Bell, she is simply a different woman.

12288.s:
Whether Symon Tootell was William Tuttle’s father is not yet proved, but the records make him the likeliest man. He lived at Ringstead, a village on the Nene in Northamptonshire, and he stood among its leading parishioners: in 1622 he signed the parish register as churchwarden, as “Symon Tootehill,” beneath the vicar James Southwell. He was already a man of property there in 1605, when the return of the county’s freeholders listed seven at Ringstead, among them “Symon Tootwell” and “John Weales.” On 26 December 1607 a William, son of Symon, was christened in the parish.

He was buried at Ringstead on 15 June 1630; the clerk first wrote the fourteenth, struck it out and wrote the fifteenth. He left a will, entered that year in the Archdeacon of Northampton’s court, and it still lies unread in book O at folio 212. Within five years the Tootells had gone. William and Richard Tuttell of Ringstead sailed on the Planter in April 1635 with their households, and with them went an Isbell Tuttell, aged seventy.

111.s:
Martha Bailey was born in North Carolina about 1802 and came west to Wayne County, Indiana, as the wife of John Bailey. In 1850 they were farming in Green Township with seven children. Two of the daughters of the house married two Lamb brothers in the winter of 1859–60.

She outlived her husband by eight years. She died on 7 September 1871 at the home of her son Milo, and the Sugar Grove correspondent of the Richmond paper gave her a line: “an aged and very respectable citizen.” Two ministers preached her funeral.

196.s: Daniel Fürstenberger lived at Walldorf, in the Wiesloch district of Baden, a few miles south of Heidelberg. On 10 February 1807 he married Veronika Haußer in the Lutheran church there. Their son Franz was born on 17 August 1826 and baptised the next day. Veronika died at Wiesloch in February 1840, and Daniel was named at her burial as her husband. He was a master shoemaker and a citizen (Bürger) of Wiesloch, the trade his son Franz would carry to America. In August 1835 he and Veronika buried three of their sons in five days: one of twenty on the 19th, Jakob, twenty-nine, on the 22nd, and Johann Heinrich, eleven, on the 23rd. Franz was nine. When and where Daniel died has not been found. He was married before. In 1803 he had married Anna Eva Binß, a divorced woman, and when she died in November 1806 he married Veronika within three months, entered in the register as a widower. He was probably the Daniel baptised at Walldorf in January 1781, son of the shoemaker Johann Fürstenberger and his wife Catharina. Their son Daniel, born in January 1808, became a shoemaker too. He married Anna Margaretha Walti in 1834 and lived on at Wiesloch until 1881.

152.s: Levi Swain was born about 1785 in North Carolina. In 1850 he was sixty-five and living in Lauderdale County, Mississippi, with his wife Margaret A. and a household of children that included a twelve-year-old Joseph and a ten-year-old Jacob, both born in Alabama. A Wesbrooks girl lived with them, and a young Crawford family next door. In November 1855 the two boys, by then “minors over 14 years of age,” went before the Lauderdale County probate court. About four hundred dollars was owed them from the estate of John G. Lee, lately dead in Monroe County, Alabama, and they asked the court to appoint “our father Levi Swain” their guardian so the money could be collected. Neither boy could write; both made their mark. The clerk headed the page “Guardianship of Joseph T & Jacob S Swain, Sons of Levi Swain.” Levi rode back and forth to Monroeville on the boys' business, five times in all, and in his final account as Joseph's guardian he recorded the cash paid over to his son. How John G. Lee was kin to the boys the record does not say; a family caption names Joseph's mother as Margaret A. Lee.

He left everything to his wife Ann S. for her life, and after her to his children equally — and twice, in two separate clauses, he wrote that whatever fell to his daughters or granddaughters was theirs and the heirs of their bodies, “and not to be subject to the debts of their husbands.” He named his son Benjamin Asbury Simmons executor and gave him power to sell the land “without having to proceeding in Court.” The will was witnessed by James Lake, D. A. Stewart and Price Williams, and it lay unproved for ten and a half years, until November 1855. He was born about 1780 in North Carolina. In the autumn of 1850 the census-taker found him at Paynesville, seventy years old, living with his daughter Susan and her husband James Boyd and their three small children. Susan died young, and when Robert's estate was settled in 1857 her children took her share. His son Benjamin, who carried out the will, is Alec's ancestor through Dillon Simmons Swain.

68.s: Robert Bradley was born about 1809 in Edgefield District, South Carolina, the son, his family said, of Hobbs Bradley, an Irishman who had come by way of Delaware. His family remembered that he married Elizabeth Kemp in 1831 and then brought her to Alabama, but the census shows him already in Pike County in 1830 with a wife and a baby son. He settled near the village of Clayton in Barbour County, and he served in the Indian war of 1836. They had ten children. In 1850 he was farming there with eight sons and a daughter at home, and when the war came, his son remembered, Robert and eight of his sons fought for the Confederacy, and three of the sons did not come back. He died at his home on or about 10 June 1890, without a will. His daughter Mattie, who had nursed him for the last eight years and seven months of his life, administered the estate and paid out of it for a tombstone over his grave. The court divided what was left among his surviving children, the two sons of his late son Ezekiel, and the five young children of his late son Henry.

248.s: Emanuel Nease was born in Virginia about 1792, a son of Henry Nease, who on one spring day in 1817 gave him a hundred-acre farm in Mason County “for the natural love and affection which I bear” him and gave his brother Henry the farm next to it. Emanuel farmed in Mason County, on the Virginia bank of the Ohio, with his wife Katharine. In 1850 he was fifty-eight and she fifty-three, living next door to the Roushes. On 4 October 1853 he signed his will in his own hand. Every one of his sons, it says, had been given a horse, four sheep and two hogs on reaching twenty-one, and he left the same to his youngest, Levi, so that he would not be short; everything else went to Katharine, and after her to all his children, “sons and daughters Share and Share alike without any differance whatsoever.” He was dead by July 1854. In March 1865, a month before the war ended, his children met to sign over the home farm to the youngest, Levi, keeping their mother’s right to live on it for the rest of her life. George Nease signed among them, “as Heirs at law of Emanuel Nease deceased”. That deed settles whose son George was, though George’s own death record, filled in thirty-four years later, would call his father Samuel.

Nathaniel Bell was born in Manchester between about 1804 and 1808 and made his life in the silk town of Macclesfield, twenty miles south. In all likelihood he is the Nathaniel Bell, silk weaver of Sutton, on the edge of the town, who on 30 June 1837 brought two children to St George’s chapel to be baptised on the same day — James, and Frances, already five — though that identification is not yet proven. He was probably already a widower: a Maria Bell of Sutton, twenty-eight, was buried at Prestbury in June 1834, and in 1841 a “Nath Bell”, thirty-three, a silk weaver born outside Cheshire, was living at Bank Top in Macclesfield with no wife, a boy George of ten already winding silk, and Frances, nine. By the early 1840s he had a second wife, Ann (their marriage has not been found); their son William was christened at Macclesfield in February 1843, when Nathaniel called himself a weaver, and their daughter Mary in June 1845, when he was already a trimming maker. She was dead by 1851, though her burial has not been found. By 1851 he had risen in the trade: the census found him a widower and a silk manufacturer on Chestergate, the town’s main street, with Frances, nineteen, a son William, a daughter Mary and a resident servant. Fourteen years took him from the loom to the counting-house. On 10 June 1857 he stood witness in Prestbury church when Frances married George Frost, a silk throwster, and signed the register himself.

By 1861 he had moved into the finer end of the trade: a gimp manufacturer — a maker of silk trimming braid — at 1 West Bond Street, a widower still, with William and Mary at home. William followed him into it and married Jane Pegg, a shoemaker’s daughter, at Prestbury in 1865. By 1871 Frances was in Paterson, the house had emptied, and Nathaniel, sixty-five and still making gimp, lived at No. 63 Oxford Road with only a servant, Louisa Cottrill, a silk winder from Sutton — on the same street where his daughter’s husband’s family had lived twenty years before.

They had a son, James, born about 1828, and a daughter, Frances, born in 1832. She probably did not live to see either of them grow up: a Maria Bell of Sutton, twenty-eight years old, was buried at Prestbury parish church on 1 June 1834, and the register gives no more than her name, her township and her age. 113.s:
Sarah Frost was a Somerset woman, born at Bridgwater, near the mouth of the Parrett, around the turn of the nineteenth century — a long way from the Cheshire silk town where she spent her married life. By 1822 she was the wife of George Frost, a Macclesfield silkman, and that July their son George was baptised in the town’s parochial chapel; a second son followed in October 1824 and was christened Edmund Hayman.

On census night in March 1851 she was keeping house in Oxford Road, Macclesfield, a married woman in her fifties with no husband at home that night. Around her were five grown children — Mary, thirty-one, at domestic work; George, twenty-eight, a journeyman silk throwster and already a widower; William and Nathan, both in the silk trade — and three small grandchildren, Eliza Ann, Mary Elizabeth and little George Thomas Hatton Frost. Her neighbours were Cheshire and Staffordshire people; she was the West Country woman of the street. Thirteen years later her son George took his second family to Paterson, New Jersey.

105.s:
Polly Roach was born about 1782 in Virginia, the daughter of William Roach. By the time she was in her thirties she was married to Benjamin Nott and living in Adams Township, in Washington County, Ohio, among neighbours who included Price, Daniel and Anna Roach. In 1820 the Nott household held a wife of her age and nine others, four of them boys under ten. One of those boys was Benjamin, born on 8 May 1817.

Her husband died in 1822 owing money. On 4 October that year the court made Polly his administratrix. The following September his three lots in Cats Creek, 234 acres, were auctioned for his debts at the house of a neighbour, Lewis Morris, all except her widow’s dower. Commissioners had set that off in December 1823: fifty-three acres off the south end of lot 16. By then she had remarried, and the dower was recorded to “Mrs Mary Morris late Widow of Benj’n Nott.”

Her second husband does not survive in the record. By the 1830s she was paying tax on land in her own name. In July 1836 she bought a hundred acres in the Rainbow Mills allotment from Percival Nott, another Nott of the township. In 1850 she was sixty-eight and living in her son Benjamin’s house. On 1 September 1851 she signed her fifty acres over to him, and the next day he leased them back to her for the rest of her life; she promised to keep the place “in as good repair as they now are in.” Five years later the two of them sold it.

On 23 April 1861, “aged and infirm,” she made her will with her mark. All she had left to give was her share of her father’s estate, about six hundred dollars held in a bank at Alexandria, Virginia, and a claim for bounty land she had filed under the act of 1855 that had never been granted. She left both to “my son Benjamin Nott.” She was dead within seven weeks.

104.s:
Benjamin Nott was a farmer in Washington County, Ohio, in the years after the War of 1812. He was taxed at Big Run in 1816 and in Adams Township in 1817, and that winter he stood as surety, with Anna, Price and Daniel Roach, for Anna’s appearance in court. In 1820 the census taker wrote him down as Benjamin Knotts of Adams: a man between twenty-six and forty-five, with a wife of about the same age and nine others in the house, four of them boys under ten. He owned three lots of the Ohio Company’s Cats Creek survey, seventy-eight acres each.

He died in 1822, before his forty-sixth year, and he died in debt. His widow Polly took out letters of administration on 4 October. Two years later his land was auctioned to pay what he owed, and it was gone except for her dower. Benjamin, almost certainly his son, was five when he died. That son grew up to farm the same township, served three years in the 36th Ohio, and named a son of his own Benjamin as well.

12298.s: James Allen was a blacksmith at Kempston, a parish of scattered hamlets just south-west of Bedford, where he was baptised in 1586 and where he raised his family. Two of his children crossed the Atlantic: his son Roger, who became treasurer of the New Haven Colony, and his daughter Joan, the wife of Abraham Doolittle. When he made his will in January 1657 he remembered them both by name as “living now in New England”, leaving each ten pounds and ten more to be shared among their children. He kept a feather bed and bolster back for Joan: they would go to her sister Martha “in case my daughter Joane comes not to demand the same within twoo yeares. If she doth then I will both the featherbedd and feather bolster shalbe hers.” The rest went to the children who had stayed: William, Martha (Mrs. Richard Parkes), the children of Mary Warren, and his son John, who inherited the house at Kempston Wood End and the close called Nine Leyes. He was buried at Kempston on 29 December 1657. His son William and William's daughter Elizabeth followed him to the churchyard within weeks, and Roger sailed home from New Haven to settle the estate, back again by August 1658.

6158.s: Alexander Edwards came out of Wales about 1640, sailing from Bristol, and settled first at Springfield on the Connecticut River. There, on 28 April 1642, he married Sarah, the widow of John Searl. His daughter Hannah was born at Springfield in February 1645. The family later moved up the river to Northampton, where Alexander and Sarah are recorded together as parents in 1657 and 1659, and there he died on 4 September 1690. His daughter Hannah married Samuel Davis of Northampton in March 1669 and died young, leaving a son John and a daughter Elizabeth. When Samuel Davis died in the epidemic of July 1690, Alexander, then an old man himself and signing his will by mark, set aside thirty shillings apiece for his Davis grandsons John and Samuel in settlement of a piece of land their father had expected; he died that September. Twenty-three years later, when his grandson John Davis died at Hatfield, it was Alexander’s son Benjamin, John’s uncle, who stood bond for the widow.

496.s:
Henry Nease is first seen in Mason County, on the Virginia side of the Ohio River, as an old landholder dividing his farm. On a single court day, 15 April 1817, he went before the county court and gave two of his sons farms side by side, “for and in consideration of the natural love and affection which I bear” them: 119 acres to Henry and 100 to Emanuel, for a dollar each. He had bought the 331 acres in 1813 from John Roush, out of the great tract the Roush brothers had won at a chancery sale of the Rev. William Graham’s lands, so the Neases and the Roushes, whose grandchildren would marry, began as neighbours on one survey. Henry kept the last 112 acres and lived on them, but by 1823 he owed his neighbour Nicholas Yager $164.64 and pledged the land for it, and on 19 March 1825 he and his wife Mary, who signed with her mark, made it over to Yager. In that deed Henry himself called the two farms he had given away the conveyances “to his Sons Henry Ness Junr & Emanuel Ness”.

Emanuel’s hundred acres stayed in the family for almost fifty years. In March 1865 Emanuel’s children signed them over to their youngest brother, Levi, keeping their widowed mother’s right to live on the farm for the rest of her life.

The family’s own history says that Henry came from the Shenandoah Valley, where a Henry Nease married Mary Zerckel in 1791. No record yet joins that Henry to this one.

Mary Nease is known from a single day. On 19 March 1825, in Mason County, Virginia, she and her husband Henry signed away the last 112 acres of their farm to a neighbour. Henry signed his name; Mary made her mark, an X between “Mary” and “Ness” written in by the clerk. Two justices then took her aside, out of her husband’s hearing, as the law required, to ask whether she signed of her own free will. She said she did.

She was very probably the mother of Henry’s sons Henry and Emanuel, though no record yet says so. The family’s own history names Henry’s bride of 1791 as Mary Zerckel, of the Shenandoah Valley.

136.s: Hobbs Bradley was living in Kershaw District, South Carolina, by 1806, when he bought land on Grannies Quarter Creek. The Kershaw people believed the family had come from the Eastern Shore of Maryland; his grandson’s family remembered him as an Irishman who had come by way of Delaware. In 1825 his uncle Solomon Bradley died in Kershaw claiming no relation in the world but Hobbs, and a neighbour swore to the court that Hobbs had children named John, Abram, Salathiel and Ezekiel, and two daughters. The court heard that Solomon, an old man who had left his brother John behind in Maryland at sixteen, had told Hobbs: “I do not mean to make you my heir but your son John.” Neighbours swore the two men were as alike as any two men they had ever seen; others said there was no kinship at all. When Hobbs went to see his uncle he sent for his own mother to keep house — “an old crooked creature”, called the widow Bradley, who flew into a passion because he did not send a horse for her. By then Hobbs had already left Kershaw “for the state of Alabama”, and in 1825 he and his wife Sarah sold the land they had left behind. He won a quarter of Solomon’s estate and was still collecting on the decree in 1830. The sons scattered west into Alabama, Mississippi and Arkansas; one of them, Robert, settled near Clayton in Barbour County and named his first son Hobbs. In June 1827 he was living in Autauga County, Alabama, near a married daughter, the wife of John Peeples, and he gave their son, his grandson John Peeples Jr., a two-year-old brown bay mare colt, taking care that it could never be seized for his son-in-law’s debts. He signed with his mark. In 1832 he was in Pike County, where Robert and Ezekiel Bradley were living by 1830, and sold eighty acres there to his son Salathiel. By 1835 he had moved on to Barbour County, where his son Salathiel sold him the house and plantation he was already living on, 35 acres near the village of Clayton; two years later, in 1837, the old man sold it again, signing as always with his mark. The family later said Hobbs died in Edgefield District, but the records show him alive in Alabama in the late 1830s; where and when he died is not known.

Jefferson M. Shoemake was born in Alabama about 1836 or 1837, to a father from North Carolina and a mother from South Carolina. On 3 September 1860, in Clarke County, he married Mary Hutto, a schoolteacher’s daughter who had been a student that summer. During the war he served as a private in Company D of the 32nd Alabama Infantry. In 1870 they were farming at Webbs Mill in Clarke County, near Woods Bluff, with five children, the eldest a girl called Eliza.

Sometime in the later 1870s the family moved to Mississippi, where two more children were born. By June 1880 they were back across the line in Choctaw County, Alabama. Jefferson was forty-three and farming, with Mary and nine children at home. Eliza, nineteen, was still at school.

He died on 13 August in the 1880s, probably 1887. In 1899 Mary was granted a Confederate widow’s pension as his widow, and she signed for her first payment of $11.88 in her own hand.

Open objections: (1) five married daughters are entered under their own names and Patsy is not; (2) John Bailey could in principle be an assignee who bought a share, which nothing read excludes; (3) there are several Thomas Lambs in Wayne Co. (a Thomas Sr. and a Thomas Jr. in 1841, and one said to have married Massey Adamson). This estate is identified by its date and the widow Hannah. The John Bailey of p. 461 is very probably node 110, and the rival “John Bailey, son of Hugh” (#582) stays open there. Route to ok: the petition for sale or partition of his real estate, c. 1851–53 (Wayne Co. Probate Order Book F, Complete Record), which normally lists heirs by relationship; or deeds from his heirs (“John Bailey and Martha his wife”). His wife Hannah (b. ~1782) is not charted: she is his widow, but no record makes her the mother of his children. Her maiden name “Lewis” and a 1798 Randolph Co., N.C. marriage are compiled only (WikiTree Lamb-1589, citing Ruby Manning, A Brief Genealogy of the Thomas Lamb Family, 1942). Her death is said to be 19 Oct 1865.
222.s:
Thomas Lamb was born in North Carolina about 1770 and came west with the great migration of Carolina families into the Whitewater country of eastern Indiana. By 1850 he was eighty, farming in Green Township, Wayne County, with his wife Hannah. His daughter Patsy and her husband John Bailey lived two doors away.

He died on 15 July 1851 without a will. Two years later the county court divided what money was left among his widow and eleven heirs: married daughters scattered under new surnames, sons, and the orphaned children of his son John. John Bailey signed for two of those shares, one for his wife and one for the orphans, who had chosen him as their guardian.
